review_text: The 1st Vitacura Jazz Festival was held in the Bicentennial Park. Vitacura is one of the most affluent suburbs of Santiago and is full of magnificent high-rise apartment buildings and corporate headquarters and many parks. The Bicentennial Park stretches along the Mapocho River. I finally found a statue of the liberator of Chile, Bernardo O’Higgins, there. The festival was held in a fenced area near the extraordinary civic centre building. We arrived very early and sat on the steps of the building and watched cyclists and skateboarders and roller-bladders and families with small children and/or prams streaming passed. The concert started with a set by Claudia Acuna, a Brazilian singer with a great voice. Her band was made up of Chilean musicians, including a very fine pianist names Felipe Riveros who I had not heard of before. Their set of about an hour consisted of two songs in English, a couple in Portuguese and a couple in Spanish, mostly standards except for one lovely piece written by the pianist. Acuna’s singing, however, was a bit disappointing. She doesn’t come across as pure and magical as she does on her recordings. The pianist, however, was a revelation. He had a bright and enthusiastic touch and his solos were lively and consistently interesting. Acuna was followed by the burly and bearded Chilean trumpeter Cristian Cuturrufo. He played a too short set. He seemed to be playing well within himself and I suspect he feels more comfortable playing in a small sweaty jazz club than a large outdoor stage. Kenny Barron and his trio were the headliners of the evening and they played nearly ninety minutes of glorious jazz. Barron is a magisterial pianist, elegant and eloquent, free-flowing with seemingly endless ideas and variations on standards and originals. And he played two Thelonious Monk songs so I was one very satisfied jazz fan!

review_text: This was the second time we attended events at El Teatro del Lago. Although the Semanas Musicales of Fruitillar are 43 years old, the theater was just finished a year ago. We chose three days worth of events and spent two nights in Fruitillar. The Don Quijote Ballet with the Ballet de Santiago was beyond words. Fabulous! We next attended one of the most creative performances I have ever since: HumAnimal, p "children's performance" by the Circo da Silva of Rio. If you EVER have a chance to see them, don't miss it, or at least check them out online. Third was yesterday's talk by a Chilean astronaut, which was quite interested and opened us up to a totally different world. Last night, the Gala de Estrellas ballet was also impressive, though not nearly as colorful as Don Quijote. The performers were top-notch. I just wish Fruitillar were closer to Pucon, where we live, because they are now offered events year-round. The problem is that food options in Fruitillar are disappointing and expensive, except for Se Cocina (pricey but exceptional).

review_text: There are plenty of options in terms of hot springs around pucon, but Los Pozones came recommended to us by our AirBnb hosts (both of whom were local tour guys), as well as reading about it online. You can a take a bus from town (about £2 per person one way) and this takes 45 minutes.Entry was cheap (this is one of the reasons we went for this option over some of the more luxury options) at about £9 per person for 3 hours, although this increases by about £2 to go in the evening. We got there for 11:30am (the pools open at 11) Don’t expect luxury. The facilities are basic (a couple of log cabins to change in) and no facilities in terms of refreshments (so bring your own). However this experience is rustic and completely natural and this is what it’s all about in my opinion. There are 7 naturally heated, gravel pools by the bank of the river - all of which have varying temperature from cool to boiling hot and in between. I’ve read a few reviews stating the water wasn’t hot at all, but I can honestly say I could not get in the first pool as it was literally scalding hot. The pool we eventually settled on was just like a hot bath and was perfect. If you’re looking for a completely natural experience for a good price than look no further than Los Pozones!

review_text: While visiting Chile we decided to do a trip do Cajon del Maipo. We came across this company in the city centre in Santiago where they had a little tent on the square. Even though it looked trustworthy enough, unfortunately our first impression was wrong and it all ended up as a very bad experience for us. There was four of us, our friends who we were visiting in Santiago and the two of us, interested in the tour. The company representative, Andrea Matos, completely blanked us as we don't speak Spanish and only talked to our friends who had to translate to us. We should have walked away when being ignored, unfortunately we did not. After Andrea booked us for the tour, we opted for paying on the morning of the tour and just as well. Andrea told our friends to translate for us that she will add us to Whatsapp group where we'd get an info about a pick up location and time. This happened on Monday, we had the tour booked for Wednesday. When by Tuesday evening still no info, our friends tried to ring and text Andrea, with no reply. Obviously, we did not get to go on the tour that day which was really disappoining, but luckily we had one spare day in Santiago the following week so we were able to book this tour with Turistik, much more professional company, where we were told straight away when and where we would be picked up in the morning, showed a picture of the bus so we had an idea what to look for and received confirmation email straight away. So my advice is do not fall for this scam, don't book with Somos Tour even though they might be the first ones you find in Santiago, as they have their little desk based on Plaza de Armas, there is plenty of other companies organizing this tour and in a more professional way. Lamentamos profundamente que hayan sufrido esta mala experiencia, hemos enviado una solicitud a la administración de TripAdvisor ya que Andrea Matos no es funcionaria de Somos Tour y esta situación no corresponde a nuestra empresa. Sabemos la importancia de entregar un buen servicio al cliente y definitivamente solidarizamos con ustedes por la mala experiencia que les tocó vivir. Ya hemos enviado nuestros antecedentes a TripAdvisor y deseamos que su próxima visita a Chile realmente puedan disfrutar la experiencia de Somos Tour. Saludos Cordiales, Raúl Soto Avello Gerente Comercial Somos Tour

review_text: I coordinated with Al Ramirez last minute to set up a Casablanca Valley Wine Tour. He was quick to respond to my emails and it only took 2 days to work out the details! Our tour guide and driver were polite and professional, (thank you Rod!). He chatted with us throughout the tour and even took us to a wine store so we could purchase some wine when the winery sold out. Chilean wine is different from Argentinean wine, so your satisfaction with the tour will largely depend on the type of wine you prefer. Chile seems to have a lot of interesting blends, i reccommend purchasing a bottle from Bodega Re. The lunch is not included with the tour price, but we enjoyed it. We chose to dine in Vina Mar winery, quite possibly the most beautiful winery i've ever seen. The food is "fancy" but very filling with large portions, so come hungry. We got dropped off right in front of our hotel in Santiago, with bags full of Chilean wine and stomachs full of Chilean cuisine. If you are looking to hop between Valparaiso and Santiago, this beats taking a crowded bus or expensive flight. Thank you Al Ramirez Wine Tours! Review of: Tasting Valparaiso: Valparaiso City & Wine Experience

review_text: Let me begin by saying that the fact that they LEFT TWO PEOPLE BEHIND on the daytrip to Valpariso/Vina del mar, sort of trumpets anything else that happened on the day trip. The guide didn’t notice until the bus had already pulled away from one of our stops, so we circled around for 45 minutes trying to find them. The poor guys that got left had their bags on the bus as well! The guide told us that this had happened before (!) We spend most of the time on the bus, which was unfortunate, as we were told we would have time to explore the city. Additionally, as I see someone else has mentioned in their review, they take you an overpriced seafood restaurant and expect you to sit at a long, white table with all of the bus passengers and pay inflated prices. We specifically asked if we would have a choice of places for lunch as we know that familiar tourist trap, and were told yes. We had none of this and left the restaurant to find something else, meeting the bus again before we moved onto our next stop. I would recommend taking a local bus to Valpariso or Vina Del Mar and exploring the cities yourself rather than take this trip. We shared our experience with Turistik and received a 25% refund, but I wanted to warn others about our experience. Imagine what a nightmare it was for the two men on our trip that were left behind in a strange city without their belongings. We appreciate your comment dear traveler, it is very important for us to know about your experience.

review_text: I've had a chance to do the Torres del Paine W trek and the Perito Moreno Big Ice Trek with Flashpacker in December 2017. I initially discovered the agency on Instagram and really liked how simple and detailed everything was on the website. From day 1, LeAnn has been extremely helpful and responsive and figured out all the details of our itinerary while suggesting ways to make the trip better and more feasible. We met a lot of other travelers who booked everything on their own and I honestly don't want to think about the headache of booking everything individually, in Spanish. Plus, the prices we got for the W trek were unbeatable. We had an issue in Puerto Natales, Chile with our reservation and it was a Sunday: when we picked up our trekking package, the extra kayak tour in Grey Glacier was not inside, and LeAnn was very responsive even on a Sunday afternoon and clarified everything quickly (it turned out it was a 3rd-party reservation). Also, few days before the trip, she checked on us to make sure we were all set. I definitely recommend Flashpacker if you're doing some off the beaten path trip: prices are clear, itineraries and inclusions are detailed and most importantly, they are responsive. Looking forward to traveling again with you!

review_text: My wife and I took a star tour with Jorge at the beginning of July and it was the best part of our week trip to San Pedro and the Atacama Desert. We came to the Atacama Desert because it is one of the best places in the world for stargazing. Jorge picked us up at our hotel at 7:30 and took us to his location outside the town with about 10 telescopes. We sat outside under the stars for 45 minutes while Jorge gave an historical overview of astronomy, telescope details, and basics of the night sky. His knowledge and enthusiasm is incredible and while more expensive than a group tour of up to 12 people, it was definitely worth it. Other star tours have 12-24 people. After the overviews Jorge provided snacks and cocoa - it was appreciated since the temps can drop quickly in the desert after sundown. Then we looked at the sky with the various telescopes including Jupiter, Saturn, and stars and galaxies. The galaxies were pretty amazing. He took pictures of us with the sky as a background including one where he 'wrote' our names on a wall next to us with his laser pointer which was on the shot due to the long exposure. He then setup my camera on a tripod and adjusted the settings to get several pictures of the night sky featuring the milky way and the Southern Cross. We finished around 10:30 and Jorge drove us back to our hotel. Some notes: Try to visit around the time of new moon or after/before moonrise/set since the moon cuts done on visibility. San Pedro noted for having clear nights about 320 of 365 days a year, (although we had clouds 4 of the 6 days we were there). Winter is supposed to have less rain and better viewing in general. Thanks again Jorge!

review_text: My first tour at La Chascona had been so wonderful that it was the first thing I wanted to introduce to my new girlfriend on our recent trip to Chile. What a disappointment this turned out to be. That first time there was a lively guided tour with wonderful details, wonderful stories and intricate details. A history skillfully told by a lovely young lady who clearly enjoyed her work. She shared stories, anecdotes and tidbits of information about the house, the writer and his long time love. It was wonderful. Now she is replaced by a little plastic box called "self guided tour." The passion is gone, the stories are canned. The interaction is gone and there's no place for questions. No smiles, no laughter. Just zombie tourists pressing numbers on a plastic toy containing the life of a historic figure. The house that was built for love and sustained by passion and intellectual banter is now reduced serve that family we all see at every local restaurant. Passionless, emotionless and speechless. All staring at their phone while life passes by. It makes me very sad to see a once wonderful experience completely ruined.

review_text: We were going to see the penguins on Isla Magdalena in the afternoon and had some spare time on our hands in the morning so we decided to visit the Cementerio Municipal in the middle of Punta Arenas. There is free parking at the flower shop across from the main entrance, there is no fee to enter, and just past security there are clean restrooms. And yes there is security. The Cementerio is divided into two sections. The main one is the old fashioned above ground tombs and mausoleums dating back to the 19th century. Some are simple, others are very striking and ornate. Not sure if these are considered gothic or classical (I slept through that lecture in Art History) but no matter, they are quite interesting. Over all, the Cementario is not as big or complex as the Recoleta in Buenos Aires, but it’s the same idea. In addition, the topiary is really quite effecting: large busy greens that appear to “sway”. The second part of the Cementerio is the modern section and it’s like a rundown apartment block with small shelves for the remains. The dreary design and poor workmanship (its already crumbling) is a bit sad. But since this is the current generation’s cemetery, families still visit and leave flowers and remembrances to their loved ones and the effect of fresh flowers makes up for the rest of it. Its very touching and certainly absorbing to just walk through. My wife and I thought we would be there 20 minutes, just take a quick lap around the grounds. Instead we were there for an hour and half! If you have any time at all in Punta Arenas, I would recommend the Cementerio Municipal.

review_text: Took a tour from La Serene with Eco tourism (30,000 CLP each). 2 hour coach ride from La Serena with a stop for coffee at the restaurant where we would eat lunch. Once at the coast we took a small boat out to the islands. We toured one of the islands to see the wildlife, Humboldt penguins, pelicans other seabirds, sea lions and sea wolves, then as we headed away from the island the spotter saw a whale and so we set off for its location. After a few minutes we got closer and then waited with baited breath to see if it would continue to surface, and luckily it did. We then toured the larger island to get to the smaller island which you can land on (for 1 hour). We had a quick walk up the hill to get a view from the top and then went back to the beach for a swim (v cold water). On the way back we were lucky again to see a school of dolphins which came very close to the boat. We were told that to see a whale and dolphins is quite unusual so don't necessarily expect to see them. On the way back to La Serena we stopped at the restaurant for late lunch which was very good (nice fresh fish as you would expect)

review_text: We went on board the navimag from porta natales to Porta montt and it was one of the worst experiences of our six month travels. The on board addition of cows transported live for slaughter who were crammed in horrific conditions, made to stand for 4 days and not able to lie down and whose stench only intensified sea sickness- which was already unbearable- made the trip horrendous. The navimag charges western prices and therefore opens itself up to certain standards and scrutiny. With those prices comes a responsibility. Although we appreciate that animal treatment in chile is of a different standard to what we're used to we felt like some of that high price should have gone to the poor animals. Trying to fall asleep at night with the distressed sound of the animals and the over powering stench made the experience incredibly unpleasant. If you want to take the navimag we hope you will also take the time to raise these issues with the crew as the more people who protest the more navimag must take responsibility for these issues

A type of grape brandy, the ABA distillery founded in 1921 remains in operation by the grandson of the original founder. We had a tasting of 4 types of Pisco and an information tour. We then visited the small town of Vicuna and the lovely square. A glimpse of an authentic small town and the people who live there. Samantha kept us on track to complete our tour on time and we stopped at a viewpoint to see the varied rocks and a scenic view of the Elqui Valley, proceding back to La Serena. I highly recommend this tour company with their good communications, excellent guide and driver. Review of: La Serena: Full day Tour to Elqui Valley

review_text: We went with my partner in August, we knew that it would rain and that the road would not be in the best conditions, we stopped at the entrance to Route 5 where the open sign appeared. We continued, when we arrived at the gate the park ranger urged us to go to Chigualdad because there we canceled the entry. She gave us the go-ahead to cross part of the flooded road, we confirmed with her. We continued the road to Chigualdad, the park ranger had warned us that we were going in case something happened to us at the crossing. We advanced on a bad road until we found the road cut off, a small river that crossed had taken away part of the bridge and road, no one knew!! They let us pass and continue, in the end we turned back and there the water had already risen, we tried to cross but the truck couldn't, we tried to get it out between us, we moved forward but we couldn't raise it any further, already reaching the goal, walking, all of us wet, we told him I showed the park ranger who was also with another park ranger the photos and videos of the road block, they didn't know. There's my point, it's okay, I know, it's understandable that few people go at this time but they should be there for everyone, there was no sign, none of the park rangers walked the path to find out how far the park could be open, minimal information about handle for the safety of visitors. They were good to us, very kind and we received help, but the truth is that this point can be improved. We passed outside today on Route 5 and the open signs were still there! as if the road was closed.

review_text: After reading all the glowing reviews, my wife and I attempted to book a tour with Santiago Adventures and were ignored. We sent an e-mail requesting a tour which went unanswered for 24 hours. We then phoned them directly and were told that they were in a meeting, but would respond to our e-mail after the meeting. Still waiting for a response and our vacation ends tomorrow. My advice; try another provider. We were disappointed that Mr. Evans provided us such a harsh negative review of our company given the fact that we actually never confirmed a service with him and he never took a tour with us. Mr. Evans contacted us mid day on October 13 for a bike tour that he wanted to depart on the morning of October 14 - essentially giving us 6 hours to respond and organize a tour. This is not feasible given the high level of detail that goes in to organizing our tours to ensure the high level of quality we provide. Unfortunately, the problem was confounded by the fact that our entire sales staff was off site on October 13. Since Mr. Evans did not provide an alternative date and we could not respond in the six hours he allowed, our staff did not respond to him the following day. We have since updated our website to clearly state that we do not necessarily respond to requests for tours with less than 48 hours in advance. Our recommendation is to take his 1 rating with a grain of salt and book your tour with us with some anticipation. Best regards, Brian Pearson, Owner Santiago Adventures

review_text: With the construction of highrise towers -since 2001, still in progress- the coastline of Puerto Montt dramatically changed. From a laid back small town known for salmon fishery, it became a major hub and gateway to the southern end of the country. Modern shopping center, major banks, new busterminal and an impressive promenade all the way to Pelluco 7km away. I am hesitant to call it progress, but at least there is ample space for pedestrians, sportive activities and creative expression. If you want to get an idea of how it was, head for Coihuin village further east.

review_text: It was a beautiful yet challenging hike. Excellent views from atop the volcano. Please note that once you arrive at the base, if you are offered to take the chairlift up the first 1400 feet, you will have to pay. This was something we didn't know about and I'm unsure of whether I didn't understand when they told me or if it was not mentioned at all. Just be prepared. It is probably best to take the tram as those who do so simply wait for the rest of the group to reach them. Takes about 30 to 40 minutes for this initial climb. The guides were very good, speak English and do a good job of explaining the safety protocols in the short amount of time they have to do so. Takes just about 5 hours to complete the climb. I definitely recommend this climb as the views are spectacular and the workout is awesome! And it's nice to say you've climbed up a 9000 foot volcano.

review_text: A nice "half-day" evening tour just in the vicinity of town but which to me was kind of "more physical than fun" is how I would describe this tour where there was a walk along the stretch of soft sand "requiring more effort than a regular walk" to the top of the ridge for a sunset view (the fifth & the last stop of the tour) and where there was also a walk through the salt cave which involved "a bit of crawling" due to some tight spaces inside (the second stop of the tour). But despite the physical part of the tour, "absolutely worthwhile" were what seen down below from the two viewpoints where you can see down below from each of the two viewpoints a "kind of contrasting" sight of an uneven "wave-like" landscape (formed by these round-shaped mounds & long-shaped ridges) & a "perfectly smooth" surface of sand pretty much side-by-side with each other; it was about an hour at the first viewpoint which was actually just the tour's first stop directly reached by tour van just shortly after the entrance area for tickets, and it was about an hour & a half for the second viewpoint at the tour's last stop (with a "fairly arduous" walk-up to the top of a ridge as mentioned above) where the 1.5 hours spent also included about 15 minutes to get above then about 10 minutes along the top of the ridge to the end area for the view of the sunset at about 8 pm then the time for the way back down. And between those "two highlights" at the tour's beginning & end are the salt cave (the second stop for about half an hour with tight parts to go through inside as mentioned above but really quite fun with "some salt" to see on the interior walls & a nice clearing area above the other end of the cave), the vertical rock monument called 'Tres Marias' with maybe some spiritual significance (the third stop just for about 10 minutes) and the stretch of road to walk alongside a "rock wall" (the fourth stop for about 10 minutes to walk from one end of the wall to the other which I would say is pretty awesome for some great pics). I booked the tour with the nice tour operator named Marianne who I met just alongside the "main street" of San Pedro upon my arrival in town (her office called Lickan Antay on Calama St.), and yes 13,000 chilean pesos which is about 20 US$ (plus 3,000 pesos at the site itself for the entry ticket) was a pretty good deal for a "nice coverage" (with I believe all the "essential stops") of this vast valley. And yes, by doing this tour, I also got to compare this moon valley with the one in Bolivia (in La Paz), both awesome but "different types" of moon valley in regard to landscape (that one entirely covered by vertical formations not seen here) & size (that one just a relatively small valley to see in a "one-stop" tour).

review_text: It took me a fair amount of researching mostly Spanish websites to find out where this bus goes from so I thought I'd share the info here. It does indeed go from Panaderia los Griegos but for those of you without intimate knowledge of the whereabouts of la serena's bakeries, an address would be useful. It is on the north side of calle Francisco de Aguirre on the corner of los Carrera. It still costs 4500chp each way and leaves at 9. The bus was waiting from about 8 though and I wouldn't leave it too late as our bus was full by 845. I think it is still run by Hector and Eduardo and looks like a solid operation with no sign of stopping any time soon. As for Punta de choros, it is fairly touristy but not as bad as say San Pedro, the boat and island trip is good for wildlife spotting. If you go to isla damas, don't forget to get a conaf ticket, separate from the boat ticket. There is nothing in English, or no-one in any language telling you this, not even our guide checked we had this. To find the conaf office, you'll need to squeeze between some parked trucks, go round the back of a boat, past a makeshift campsite at the back of a cafe and through a gate. There you'll probably find about ten conaf staff standing round doing nothing but if you're lucky, they'll be able to find the one person allowed to operate the till to sell you a ticket (6000chp each). The boat trip does have a questionable impact on the wildlife but conaf, for all their flaws, seem to be monitoring things and trying to keep the human impact to a minimum. Overall, a trip worth doing (as others have said, so much cheaper than a tour). Don't forget a jacket and suncream!

review_text: My husband and I backpacked the W Trek with a tour group, and it was honestly one of the best experiences of our lives! It is true what they say about the park - you'll experience all four seasons over just a few days. So make sure to pack layers...you'll need it! Also brace for very strong winds. There were a few times we could literally lean our entire body weight into the wind, and have it support us completely. Using trekking poles will help combat the gusty winds, and will help keep tension off the joints overall. There are plenty of full bathrooms (with showers) along the route. All the refugios have full restaurants where trekkers can purchase food and drinks. Day 1 - Hiked to the base of Las Torres. This is a fairly strenuous hike, as you'll gain (and then lose!) about 3,000 feet of elevation. On this day, we experienced snow...even though it was summertime there! However, it was more than manageable. There is a rest stop at about the halfway point, which is a good place to stop for lunch. Day 2 - Hiked to the Los Cuernos refugio. This day, we traversed Lake Nordenskjold, which was stunningly beautiful and icy blue in color! There are a few steep uphill sections, but the hiking this day is very straightforward. This day was fairly cool and overcast, but dry. Day 3 - Hiked to Paine Grande camp. We first hiked from the Los Cuernos camp to the French Valley overlook, which was my favorite part of the trek. We saw/heard avalanches up high, and were able to gaze upon Paine Grande...the highest point in the park! The hiking this day is also fairly strenuous, as there's quite a bit of elevation gain (and then loss) to the overlook. On this stretch, the sun was out in force...most of us sunburned! Day 4 - Hiked a short distance to Grey Glacier overlook. The winds off the glacier were quite biting and strong, but it was so neat seeing the large glacier. It was a great finish to a wonderful trek!

review_text: Recently spent time at El Tatio and enjoyed the experience. Just being at 4,200 metres (13,800 ft) is fantastic - I love the scenery at this altitude. My partner and I went with our own guide, so didnt need to get up at 4.30 am thankfully. Still it was certainly cold on arrival (about minus 7) but once you start walking around you forget about the cold. We also meet a postdoc research fellow from one of the Chilean university undertaking various measurements at one of the geysers and our chat was really interesting. We stayed for breakfast, prepared by our guide, including his special scrambled eggs cooked on site. This was a wonderful experience, and meant that by the time we had finished, El Tatio was just about deserted, the fumaroles have subsided and it is quiet. Take the opportunity to see if it offered.

review_text: This park really is so beautiful. I did the two main day hikes in the area, the three lakes hike, and the San Cristobal hike. The San Cristobal hike is definitely a bit more difficult, with a greater elevation change, but it was my favourite of the two. It isn't as popular, so I saw only 7 other people the whole day. And the vegetation and landscape is really varied. It took me 3 and a half hours up, and 3 hours down. The three lakes hike is pretty easy, although a bit muddy. The whole circuit took about 6 hours with a number of stops. I really recommend that you try to stay a couple of nights in this incredibly beautiful park. You can either camp, or there are some Refugio's and Hospedaje's. I stayed in Refugio Tinquilco, and it was just fantastic (see my review for more information). And if you stay overnight, you can hit the trails early, and beat the hordes of day trippers that come from Pucon!

review_text: I booked this tour asking for an English speaking operator as I don't speak Spanish. The website information said 'Guide just in your language (no language mixed during the tour)' & 'Small-group tour limited to eight people per vehicle', well there were 21 in the group and I was the only English speaking person including the driver (no English whatsoever). We made our way up the mountains and stopped at Parque Farallones where I went in as I thought the rest of the tour had. By the time I came out 15 minutes later, the bus had gone, left me behind. I was fortunate enough to find an English speaking Argentinian girl working there who called the Tour Operator & he said that he would come back for me, no time given. I then had the misfortune of blacking out for around 20 seconds, helped by Paramedics and then ultimately flown by helicopter to hospital where they carried out test for 5 hours, only to find nothing wrong with me, and costing me $2,250 US Dollars. I have since been in contact with the Tour Operator who has given me every excuse known to man, from the last minute driver change, to it being my fault for going into the ski park and costing me 30,000 Pesos. And an offer to give me a free airport transfer, though I'd never know where I'd end up. DISASTER!!! Review of: Small-Group Tour to Valle Nevado and Farellones from Santiago

I also loved how he paced the day, we could enjoy watching the birds and not feel rushed to get to the next spot. Jurgen brought a scope and made the ebird lists for each spot. I highly recommend this company and Jurgen Schulmeister as a guide.

review_text: We booked the astrophotography tour with Feel Atacama. Even though the sky was mostly cloudy, the tour was not canceled. The tour should last 3 hours. We took the bus for about 15 minutes near San Pedro, where we got a drink and snacks for the first half hour. no one said anything, it was a strange atmosphere. We were then divided into 2 groups. One group was told something about the starry sky for 15 minutes, but apart from the moon there was hardly anything to see because of the clouds. We were allowed to look at the moon through a telescope. The other group was photographed individually sitting on a tree trunk. Then it was changed. After an hour the tour was over and we were back on the bus. We had imagined astrophotography to be something completely different; we are ambitious photographers and had cameras and tripods with us... We complained in writing to Feel Atacama, initially we were offered a replacement tour 2 days later, but that was not possible for us. When we asked for a refund we never heard from Feel Atacama again.

review_text: HecTours provided a city tour of Santiago, Chile for me and my wife on 12/12/17 and tour the next day to Portillo, a ski resort northeast of Santiago. The Santiago City tour consisted of a walking tour thorough the central portion of the older city. We walked past numerous governmental buildings, the National Cathedral, and the financial district. During the remainder of the tour we drove through many of Santiago's picturesque neighborhoods. Our guide was personable, well-informed, and contributed a good deal of background information about the sites that we visited. Our trip to Portillo exposed us to the Chilean countryside. We drove north to Los Andes, then turned east toward the Argentine border. The 29-turn switchback road as we gained altitude toward the ski resort was memorable. As we returned toward Santiago, we left the major highways and toured through Chilean wine country. The scenery was outstanding. We thoroughly enjoyed a stop for lunch a a rustic restaurant in Los Andes, La Ruca, which had fine selection of Chilean food. The Corn Pie was wonderful. This tour lasted most of the day. Our guide for it was the same person that escorted us around Santiago. The fact that we had gotten to know our guide on the previous day contributed greatly to the success of our second tour. We give high marks to HecTours for helping to make our visit to Santiago so interesting.

review_text: an unforgetable cruise with navimag to laguna san rafael, not only because of the impressive glacier san rafael! the puerto eden from navimag has space for 208 passengers. the round trip from puerto montt takes 5 days and if you want to immerse yourself in a real chilean exeperience you should book this trip. 95% of all passengers were 60+ chileans which wasn't unique to our trip. navimag doesn't promote this cruise to foreign tourists but rather to chilean senior citizens, which makes the whole trip a patriotic-find-our-identity-totallyweirdbizarre-experience (e.g. national songs sung on the spur of the moment all the time or group shouts of "chi-chi-chi-le-le-le, viva chile"). there are events organised every night: party, karaoke, kind of carnival set up as a competition between "alianza roja" and "alianza azul" and bingo. the food is average but ample. take lots of drink with you! if it's sunny, take advantage of the human size chessboard on the top deck. and enjoy the dolphin sitings. the rooms are cramped, especially when you have to share with old folk, but despite all the weirdness, and sometimes boredom on the loooong and slooooow journey to and from the glaciar, you come away with a feeling that you've had quite a worthwhile experience, certainly like nothing else. and the glaciar itself (zodiac rides to get near the wall to watch the ice calving followed by a glass of whiskey on glacial ice) well, that takes the whole thing to exceptional. unfortunately the glaciar part is only a couple hours of a very long journey so be prepared to meditate.

We tasted both whites and reds. The snacks were wonderful and complemented the wines perfectly. We had a great discussion about the history of wines in the area. Next we headed off to Bodegas RE, a small, but very impressive, family winery. The winery is owned by Pablo Morande and his children. This family has been growing grapes in the area for nine generations. The Bodegas RE in in a new facility with state of the art wine making equipment. The wines, both red and white, were excellent. The clay pot special reds were really special. We tasted the wines in the cellar tasting room. Our last stop was at the House-Casa del Vino. Again, we toured and tasted in a beautiful modern winery. Our tour started with a wonderful lunch paired with five wines. It was the best! We then toured the vineyard and the winery. By this time we were pretty full of wine and food, but we did our best. The shop attached to the restaurant had a good selection of gifts. The wines were very good, but we were ready to head out to the Santiago Airport. Jose was an excellent host, and he was very knowledgeable about wines and the area. He spoke excellent English. The cost of the whole trip was less than the ship's trip from the port to the airport. Uncorked Wine Tour gave us an excellent tour, lunch and transportation. Review of: Best Wine Tasting in Santiago

review_text: Three of us went in a private vehicle and were taken to most of the star attractions within Santiago. The city itself is beautiful, nestled under snow-capped mountains and the historic buildings are wonderful. We discovered exquisite old buildings and visited a modern museum along with seeing important government buildings. We walked through the city trying some local street vendor drinks and visiting a Haiti cafe which was an experience and possibly one of the highlights. The marble counter and the girl in the short skirt who serves and the retro coffee equipment all add to the colour of these cafes and the coffee is good. The views from the old castle were wonderful even though the climb up the narrow steps was a little arduous. But you have to do these things and the reward of the vista at the top is worth it. If you only have a short time in Santiago, this private tour is a good option. Unfortunately, the traffic was bad the day we took the tour. However, the driver made sure we got to see all that was of interest and extended the time by around 2 hours! Review of: Private Tour: Santiago City Sightseeing

review_text: The Petrohue river in March is fairly low and the rapids are fun but not huge. (I think I took an innertube on a Washington River in rapids about the same size.) And, AlSur accurately advertises them as Class III. HOWEVER, AlSur made the trip the best. Our guide 'Chris' was fun, spoke great English, but above all, hit all the rapids perfectly to make the most of the every inch of the river. The equipment, from wetsuits to the rafts, was of top quality. We had a smaller raft with 7 people total, where the guide uses a paddle not oars to steer. Try to get on one of these, not on an oar boat; they do not ride the smaller rapids as well. We had a typical day, cool and cloudy, where we could only see the bottom part of the Volcano. If you have a clear day and are in the area, then this trip is an absolute must -- the views would be the best of anywhere in the region. And I would recommend AlSur to bring you down the river. Review of: Half-Day Small-Group Rafting Experience in Petrohué River

review_text: We did this rafting trip on a beautiful sunny day when the water was pretty high. It was a TON of fun. It’s an adrenaline rush but in a very safe way. I would skip it if you are not able bodied because there is a lot of paddling involved and little bit of rock scampering at the end to exit the river. No experience is needed but you need to be in moderately good shape. It starts at 9:30 and finishes about 2:30, though you’re only on the River for about 1.5 hours, which felt good. Have a good breakfast on your own, you’ll need the energy and then at the end a light snack is provided. They provide a wet suits, jacket, helmet, life jacket, and booties. Wear a bathing suit under your clothes because you will be changing on the side of the road. Bring a towel and sunscreen. Don’t forget to lather the tops of your hands, that’s where my husband got burned. 4 instead of 5 because the bus to the river is a rough ride but from appearance they put more money into the river equipment and safety than the bus so I’m ok with that. Just an FYI. Totally worth it! Awesome experience! Thanks again Marcelo (our guide) for keeping us safe and happy!

review_text: For alpaca textiles, you have many vendors to choose - I enjoy Falcon Chile (near the entrance) because she deals with a variety of craftspeople and has very reasonable prices. For example, I bought a beautiful large scarf made of baby alpaca for 20.000P. I got an alpaca shawl at another shop, Cordillerana, for 45.000P, but it is a little more complex design and the shop is a fair trade shop for women who want to get training to preserve ancient crafts and make a living without leaving their children. Several lapis shops, pottery, carving. Interesting art and jewelry dealer at Patsali - art from recycled objects including forks and pots and pans, from very large scale to very small. Recommended. Food is fine (a couple restaurants), but unimpressive. Could have brought a sandwich and been just as happy. Re: weather. You'll be walking in and out of shops and have an awning over most of the sidewalk, but it's outdoors, so dress as such. The experience itself it not exceptional; go if you intend on buying something unique. Easy access from subway.

review_text: Be careful when booking......not what expected. The advertisement says you can have the option of a gourmet lunch at the winery, but this is not available. Very rushed and only 25 minutes allocated to the winery. Very disappointing tour with Stamps! Hello Mr. David and Mark From the moment you requested our tour guide Sebastian to take you to have lunch in Valparaiso we were not sure what you expected from this tour. After Sebastian gave the plan of the day to the group you asked where you were going to have lunch in Valparaiso. He was confused with the question because we do not offer lunch in Valparaiso in this tour which is a limited time frame because of the meeting time at the cruise ship. He called me at the office and I said that the option has always been to eat in Casablanca. After Sebastian's answer you seemed to be upset for the rest of the day while the rest of the group was enjoying the tour. In an attempt to make you feel good Sebastian decided to stop in Valparaiso at an Empanada restaurant so you could eat something because you seemed to be hungry and you ate empanadas there. After completing the whole Itinerary in Valparaiso with funiculars, walking around the main World Heritage Sites and an extra stop for empanadas (chilean meat pie) you left to Casablanca Valley. Before leaving the van at the winery Sebastian explained clearly over the microphone what the plan was for the winery, he said: Once we get into the building you will find the restrooms on your right, our tasting is set in the middle of the hall and on your left you will find the restaurant where you can eat after the tasting if you want. Sebastian realized that when you went to the restaurant you decided not to eat but you bought a extra glass of wine and you sat down to drink it. After the winery the van droped off the group safe at 3:30 pm at San Antonio port. From 10 people of the group 8 people were very glad with Sebastian and the tour that they chose which was focused in using the limited time frame with long distances of 200 km (125 miles) to visit the amazing city of Valparaiso. If we would stop in Valparaiso for lunch it will take at least 01:30 minutes eating and missing out on certain cultural stops. Personally I answer all your email where I never heard that you chose this tour thinking about lunch neither in Valparaiso nor Casablanca otherwise I would have offered you a different tour that we runned on this same day that was only Casablanca Valley. After the tour you sent us an 2email us very upset requesting a full refund of a tour that was complete with: - Pick up at the right time in your hotel. - Carry all your luggage - Tour 7 hours at all the places that the description offered. - Have a professional tour guide with wide experience guiding in large part of the country including Atacama desert and Patagonia. - Included Tasting - Drop you off safe and on time at San Antonio port to you take your cruise ship. But you insisted that the only thing you wanted was the full refund

review_text: The Bolivian Salt Flats have been on mine and my friends’ bucket list for some time and we were incredibly excited to do this three day tour across the desert to get there. From reviews we’d read of World White Travel it seemed like a safe tour company to travel from San Pedro de Atacama to Uyuni with. For some in our tour group this was the case, unfortunately though, not for us. On the first day of the tour the driver of our jeep forgot to bring our lunch with him. Thankfully, the people in the other jeeps scrounged together some of their own food for us to eat. After that hiccup everything was fine until our final night with the tour when we were told that we’d entered Bolivia illegally. Upon entering the country we had asked our driver when we would be getting an entry stamp in our passport, but he either didn’t understand the question, or didn’t want to tell us that he’d messed up. Ignoring the fact that our presence in the country was illegal, we set out early the next morning so as to see the sunrise over the salt flats. Unfortunately, when we arrived we were dismayed to discover that our driver had forgotten to pack gumboots for us. So while the people from the other jeeps in our tour frolicked about, taking stunning photos in the mirror-like surface of the water, our group tried to take in the view without getting hypothermia and losing a toe. Upon returning to Uyuni our driver pointed out the “embassy” we had to go to in order to get stamps in our passports. He then dropped us about four blocks away so we could walk there in the rain. At the “embassy” the man we spoke to attempted to charge my friends and I each 250 Bolivianos as some kind of ridiculous “late fee”, at which point we contacted the Uyuni branch of World White Travel. To their credit the lady who came and spoke to us was very nice and got us out of paying the nonsensical fine but we wasted about two hours of our day in that office. All in all my issue is not with the company itself but one of its incompetent employees. They should perhaps provide our driver a little more training.

review_text: We did the City Tour on day one. Felipe was a great tour guide, very knowledgeable and did not mind all our questions. His English was perfect. As we enjoyed the City Tour a lot, we also booked a tour to the Andes with Touristik the next day... a very different experience. The bus was fully loaded with people. The tour was in Spanisch and English. The tourguide's English was difficult to understand. After some time we stopped listening to her. Also, what we did not like at all: We were brought to a snow equipment rental store. The guide highly recommended to rent boots for 7000 pesos a couple. She made it sound like there is no other option. We showed her our outdoor shoes and boots and she said that we should still rent the boots from that shop as there is deep snow mud up in the Valle Nevado. That was simply a lie or at least a very unqualified statement. There was no mud at all and we would not even have needed outdoor boots. Decent shoes would have been enough. We complained about that. I do not mind spending money on tours, but I hate other people wasting my money. When we dropped the boots off at the rental shop their staff even confirmed that they pay Touristik a commission for bringing people there. This is just a silly rip off. I don't like to be fooled and this rating is the consequence. After the first very positive experience on the City Tour, I got very disappointed with the second tour to the Andes. Touristik is a very big tour operator and they seemed well organized. But I would not recommend anyway due to the fact that the second tour guide's English was terribly and that they ripped us off with the rental equipment (that we did not need). review_text: Though there was a lot left to be desired on the travel to the beach at Punihuil (a "river" crossing in our ultra-sub-super-compact rental), the day itself was one I will remember for the rest of my life. Despite a warning against the trip from a waiter in Ancud (he said it was too early to see any pens), we made the trip... a few weeks before the start of "Penguin season", as we were told. We were rewarded with dozens of penguin sightings, as well as a playful otter...animals I have only seen in zoos. Not only was the drive from Ancud especially rewarding with scenery, but was highlighted with 4$ King crab empanadas prior to the ~45min boat tour that cost ~$10-12 (USD). Raincoats were provided and needed due to the spray. The sea was a little on the rough side, so taking clear pics in-focus was challenging. Out of over 100 pics, I have about 4 good penguin shots and the tail of the otter. I would highly recommend this if you are going to be on Chiloe. I would recommend knee-high rubber boots to walk across the river unless you have a high-clearance car or truck (or a rental, heh). The crossing on the way back was no problem, so the "river" must be tidal dependent??? We went on Sept 20. Per the waiter, it is better to wait until October. We went to the first house thing for our tour, and had to wait between surf to load in the boat. I saw another group further down that had the opportunity for an elevated cart to climb in the boat all at once.

review_text: I found SORBAC’s site via reviews on trip advisor. After looking at their site’s potential tours to book and reading that they were all about the adventure, we decided to book 2.5 days worth of activities during our stay in the Atacama desert with them. If I had to sum up those days, it would have to be spectacular! Pablo responded promptly to my emails discussing potential itineraries, pricing etc. and was available every step of the way. Pedro and Fabian (both the managers there in San Pedro de Atacama were very responsive, easy going and accommodating. One tip, the best way to reach them is through WhatsApp or Facebook messenger, or call directly. Day one consisted of viewing a spectacular ‘moon-scape’ with sand dunes, a salt cave, and incredible vistas, a very nice and tasty lunch and sampling local fruit at Casa SORBAC, floating (with no effort) in a salt lagoon (bring your bathing suit and towel), jumping into a salt water hole in the desert and finishing the day with a sunset and snacks at a beautiful salt flat. Day two was spending a couple of hours sandboarding (think snowboarding but slower and your feet are your ski lift)...it was tiring but very fun...finished it off with another snack / sunset from a beautiful vista. Day three was visiting multiple places at a higher altitude including multiple lagoons at Tuyacto and Piedras Rojas (one note, due to other inconsiderate tourists the locals are not letting tourists go to the rocks themselves but the area and scenery are still magnificent). Then enjoying a delicious meal served by SORBAC on the side of a hill with an amazing vista. Then the back half of the day finishing with a couple of other spectacular lagoons and ending with flamingo viewing and a snack at Salar de Atacama. Some tips from our family: Try to be in at least ‘good’ physical fitness...SPA is already at 2500 meters and some of the tours are 4000+ meters. Dress in layers with the desert temps at different altitudes ranging from 75+ and sunny to ~50 and windy at altitude (Fahrenheit temps). Make sure to keep drinking water / fluids...this is the dryest non-polar area on earth. Last, a special shout out to the guides. Javie on the first day was very knowledgeable on the ecology, geography and geology of the area. On day 2 and 3, Rafael was simply outstanding. From giving information on the history, wildlife, vegetation, geology, to sharing his view on the culture, foods, and people in Chile, he was an amazing, easy going guide. ¡Muchas Gracias! for an awesome 3 days of experiences. Cliff Otte

review_text: If you're short of time in San Pedro de Atacama, in my opinion the tour to the El Tatio 'geysers' is the tour to leave out. It's one of the most expensive (we were first quoted 18,000 pesos for this tour, but in the end got a discount package of tour tours for 50,000 pesos), and it includes an additional 5,000 pesos as an entrance fee. You have to get out of bed at 3.30am, the road getting there is very bumpy in a lot of places, you are only at the place for slightly more than an hour, the breakfast provided is minimal, and the main attraction, the geysers, are less than a metre high! The thermal pool that you can swim in has squishy mud on the bottom of the pool and is not very warm, at about 28-32 degrees, so we did it for the experience, but it wasn’t really enjoyable. You do get to eat a goat’s cheese empanada and a llama-meat kebab (at your own expense) on the way back, and you see some ducks in a river and if you're lucky some vicuna and llamas on the side of the road. However, this tour could be so much better if the tour companies made a feature of other things as well as the geysers, as the geysers themselves are very disappointing. For example, we could have stopped at the llamas, or maybe we could have talked to a local llama farmer, instead of just passing by quickly in the bus without even stopping. Similarly, the guide that we had made no mention at all of the spectacular landscape, including huge cactuses and stony mountains, that we passed through on the way back to San Pedro.

review_text: Slightly off the beaten tourist track, this museum, which occupies three enormous halls in the former Military Academy, is worth an afternoon of your time. It tracks, in extraordinary detail, the history of the country from pre-Columbian times to the present day from the angle of the country's armed forces. There's the odd information board in English, but otherwise you'll need a certain level of Spanish. Maybe there's some way of getting commentary in English on your phone. I wouldn't know, I don't have one. Hall One starts with the Inca invaders from the north till around the time of independance, in the early 19th century. Hall Two will take you through the nineteenth century, including German colonisation around 1860 but centring on the War of the Pacific. Hall Three from around 1886 to the present day, with interesting interactive World War exhibits. Chile also has a slice of Antarctica, but not as much as it once had. I was completely alone the entire time, fortunately just missing an incredibly noisy school group who had the good grace to be just leaving Hall Three when I got there. I'll definitely go back, there's just too much information to absorb in one visit,, especially if your knowledge of South American history is as sketchy as mine.

review_text: This is an overdue review of the three days we spent with our guide Vivi. My SO and I are both passionate about wine, and it was the main focus of our trip to Chile. We did a lot of research into wine guides in Santiago, as they are as plentiful as the vineyards in the surrounding valleys, and are so happy that we went with Uncorked. We spent three days touring -- a private tour on our first day, and small group tours on the next day. Not only did we tour the Maipo and Casablanca Valleys, but we asked owner Jose to put together a tour of the Aconcagua Valley for us as well, since we were already planning on visiting their other primary destination, Colchagua. We visited the whole spectrum of wineries, from tiny La Recova, where the wine is fermented behind the owner's house in a shipping container, to huge producers like Errazuriz that make some of Chile's most iconic wine. In between the guided tours at each winery, Vivi educated us on Chilean wine history and the current state of production in the country. The included lunches were all fantastic, paired with equally fantastic wine (which often included a special glass or two given Uncorked's close relationship with many of the wineries). Vivi handled curveballs very well, and she and our driver were promptly on time each morning. The van was comfortable, and Jose even helped us secure some of the hard-to-find wines that we regretted not purchasing at the wineries. (Hint, if you visit La Recova, buy their rosé by the case!) In all, whether you're a wine newbie or experienced drinker, you can't go wrong taking a tour with Uncorked. Review of: Best Wine Tasting in Santiago

review_text: A group of seven of us started planning our Patagonia adventure seven months in advance, conducted research, and contacted Fantastico Sur to book our trip and refugios, knowing that they book up quickly and we were a large group. In mid-2017 they kept saying that they could not help us because their 2018 pricing wasn’t out yet for our trek over New Years. We called and email Patricia repeatedly with no response for months. When they took our money they told us that all the refugios had already been booked up, with the exception of one. We missed out on the refugios because of their lack of communication with our group that was spending nearly $8,000 on this trip. There was a four week period where 30 or so phone calls and five or so emails were not answered during business hours. Only when we publicly tweeted our discontent did we get an email returned. THEN, when we showed up in Puerto Natales to collect our vouchers for camping/food/transportation that we had already paid for at the agreed upon time, no one from the company was at the booth. We had to change our plans to return to the bus station to collect our vouchers only to be told they didn’t have them because Patricia was on vacation and that we’d have to come back the next day (the day of departure for the park) to pick them up. Luckily once we started the trip, we had a fantastic time and saw beautiful scenery, but Fantastico Sur was not so Fantastico. They caused our group a significant amount of stress and frustration. The company is run incredibly poorly with no customer service or follow through. They unfortunately have a monopoly on the W circuit, so there are few alternative options. I would suggest having very low expectations when working with this company.

review_text: If you find yourself in San Pedro de Atacama and don’t spend at least one day with Jorge, then you are missing a true jewel of the Atacama. My traveling partner and I, both mid-60s, spent 3 days with Jorge as our guide. Each day was amazing and better than the last. He adjusted to our capabilities as we traveled from 7,000 to almost 16,000ft. He and his business partner (wife) provided tasty lunch spreads while enjoying incredible private views. If you have only one day make sure to take the “El Tatio Geyser” tour. If you’ve never seen geysers then you will enjoy these. If you have they are still a nice experience, but the magic comes after. Traveling back, we suddenly go off road to a less traveled path that leads us to a spring lagoon with flamingos, Vicuna and more, where we enjoy a private breakfast. After that, there is an easy 2 mile hike down the valley following the spring fed stream. The views and wildlife are awesome and you get to enjoy this as if you are the only ones in the world. At the end is a hot springs which we got to enjoy by ourselves. This is something you shouldn’t miss. There could be no better end to our trip. I plan to send family and friends to visit Jorge and I hope to return myself. THANKS! Thank you Bryan, I will be happy to see you again and take you to another magical places in the Altiplano. Kindest regards,

review_text: I went on a 1 day kayak trip with Juan (tour guide and owner). We were picked up right from our hostel in Puerto Varas and taken on beautiful ride to where we would begin kayaking. We were the only people on the trip that day, but Juan was very professional and wanted to make sure we got the most out of our trip. He knows a lot about the area, and talked about the history as we drove. I would highly recommend this company, as Juan is very personable and kept us laughing all day. We saw beautiful views of the Osorno volcano, and had perfect weather. Juan provides you with everything you need for the trip - all the gear and a very generous lunch of sandwiches (2 each), cookies, chocolate, olives, drinks, and fruits. He took us to a woman's house on the mountain and we got to see her farm full of sheep, and had a picnic on the shore. The mountains are truly breathtaking. Juan was also a great photographer and took pictures of our trip to send to us afterwards. We were so excited to see some wildlife- birds, sea lions, a penguin, and even dolphins! Our trip wasn't too paddle-intensive, which was our decision, and we had a more of a relaxing day on the water. Juan really caters the trip to what the group wants, which is a benefit of small groups. Juan also gave us the option to go to the Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park, and the waterfalls there were absolutely stunning. This trip was like nothing we have done before and we will remember it forever! Thank you Juan for the great memories - we loved your trip!!

Sure, Chile's repression was due to the extreme fascist right, but extreme left commits the same barbaric acts. Either confine the museums goals to Chile, then, or, if you're going to pretend to have universal concerns, then show the heinous activities of the current terrorist nations on earth, the major ones having just been listed.

review_text: Once you make your way down the steep hill to the river, you are in for a treat at Los Pozones. There are six different pools built on the side of the river, each a different temperature, from icy cold to nice and hot but not too hot. The thermal baths in the Pucon area range from small, cement rooms to luxurious spa-like pools -- for us, Los Pozones was just right. It was casual, yet clean, serving mostly tourists but neither high-end nor all back-packers, and friendly people throughout. This was one of the few places where we had easy conversation with Chileans as we all enjoyed the waters. It was a perfect place to spend time after a long, hard day of trekking in the national park.

review_text: My husband and I spent 7 months travelling around South America and I have to say that this was one of the more memorable of our experiences but for all of the wrong reasons. For all those that have commented on the standard of their food, cabins and the fact that they were 'slumming it with the backpackers' I am not really sure what they expected from their trip. This is not a luxury cruise liner. It is a freight/cargo ship that has just happened to cash in on transporting naive tourists, under the impression they will experience an enlightening and cultural journey. It could not be further from this. To begin with, our journey was delayed for 4 days, which we spent in Puerto Natales willingly, as were looking forward to experiencing a boat trip for a change, as opposed to the frequent, long bus journeys we had up until now. We later discovered that the reason our boat had been delayed was because the captain of the boat we were supposed to get had steered the it into an island which had left a hole the size of a car in it's side. He was, consequently serving time in prison for reckless endangerment of life. Alarm bells should have rung for us at this point. Once on the boat, we were upgraded to a four man berth from a 12 bed dorm without extra charge [sorry to all those non-backpackers who paid considerably more than us but you were "done" I'm afraid]. The beds were reasonably comfortable for me being 5 foot 2, however my poor husband was pretty uncomfortable as his bed was several inches too short for him and his legs hung out the end. Food wise it was pretty dire (but abundant). Mainly mash potato with either dry beef, dry lamb, an occasional meatloaf and a few veggie options. Nothing really more to say regarding this, but we didn't really expect more. Our room was directly adjacent to the cargo area. This was the most distressing aspect of the trip for me as it held dozens of lorry loads of livestock, including cows, horses and calves. If I had known about this beforehand there is absolutely no way I would have travelled with the Navimag. I know there have been several comments regarding this already however I can not stress how upsetting it was to see animals in such horrendous conditions. They were so cramped together they were unable to turn around or sit/lie down for 5 days. Cows were giving birth on the boat, with their calves being trampled to death. It was horrific. The smell was also awful, made worse by a few days of bad weather, which lead to the bathroom facilities smelling of raw sewage. On these days, I would say that 75% of the passengers were seasick, and so you can only imagine the effect this smell had on how people were feeling. The scenery was lovely on 2 of the days where we travelled through some fjords, saw a beautiful glacier and were even lucky enough to see some Blue Whales and dolphins. For these reasons only I have awarded the trip one star. For all those considering this trip please reconsider, particularly if you suffer from motion/sea sickness or if you are an animal lover. Once on the boat you can not get off. I left never wanting to eat beef again. Furthermore, please don't think that if you pay more, your trip will be more pleasurable. It wont be. You may get a more spacious berth at night but everyone eats together [the food is pretty dull, canteen food], plays together [mostly cards to kill many hours of boredom], and puke together [with the inevitable seasickness that will strike]. Our trip was also prolonged by a day as the engine blew up and we had to continue our trip on low power for the rest of the journey. Definitely an experience never to be repeated and I would take the bus over the Navimag any day.

review_text: Ascending and/or descending the teleferico in Santiago is an experience everyone must do, even if afraid of heights! The vistas out the wrap-around windows are to die for. On clear days, the entire metropolis of the Chilean capital is visible amid the dramatic backdrop of the Andes. I showed up to the street-level teleferico platform without a ticket and was able to get one very quickly, assisted by a super friendly, English-speaking member of staff. She assured me my electric wheelchair could be accommodated in the car, which was great—I didn’t totally know upon visiting (I read contradicting info about accessibility). Perhaps due to my disability or the low winter season, I experienced no lines and simply rolled up into the car using a ramp already prepared by the crew. The whole operation was amazingly efficient and disabled-person-approved! I was anxious at first as the cable car began to move with the doors still open (and with slippery wheels, I imagined myself sliding out at 500 feet high, lol!). Thankfully, the doors automatically closed before the car started climbing. The modest jolting and rocking throughout the ride takes some getting used to, including myself, having only been on larger and smoother cable cars before; once I got familiar with it, though, it was extremely fun. review_text: There were lots of small geysers that went off just before sunrise and continued into the morning. Lots of steam in the cold high altitude morning. Not that much water, maybe about 6 feet high on the largest geyser at its highest point. Everyone gets here before sunrise to see the geysers at their peak, so it is quite crowded even that early. The geysers are cool and there are a lot of them. If you really don't like waking up that early though... I would consider skipping. There are bigger, cooler geysers elsewhere. We had rented a car for the trip and did drive up. Many people said the way was hard and dangerous but that could not be further from the truth. The road is paved the whole way with several exceptions. The first is just before the fork in the road near Guatin. The pavement ends and you cross two stream beds, which are big dips which a small car would not handle well, though it probably could be done. The pavement then picks up again. Note that both forks in the road here will go to El Tatio but the west fork through Guatin is the better road though it has more sharp curves. The other hard part is just after the entrance to the geysers. There are some muddy tracks in the road here which could catch an unsuspecting non-4WD car off guard. Watch for them and don't stop in them and you'll be fine. The road is also very curvy, which can be hard in the dark for some, though we did not find it so. We left at 4:45am and arrived at 6:15am. We could have left 15-30 min later and not missed anything but we did drive fairly fast.

review_text: We spent 6 days with Mistico exploring the Atacama highlands and desert with our 8 and 10 year old boys. We spent time with an Aymara family learning about llama/alpaca herding, swimming in fabulous geothermal pools, sandboarding and fat biking. The experience for our family was amazing. Billy is a biologist by training and gave us education on the ecosystem and environment that could be understood and appreciated by kids. He also came up with fun activities that he modified on the fly to suit the feedback from my children. Everywhere we went, the people that Billy introduced us to were lovely and delightful in their engagement of our family. If you are a family, I would highly recommend an adventure with Mistico but be aware of what you are signing up for - the Adobe hut accommodations are not plush but they are lovely. The food is what the locals eat, kids who are picky eaters might have a tough time, and the hiking is at 13K feet and above, but Billy is able to modify hikes and activities to suit the needs of the kids where necessary. Mistico also does day trips specific to hiking, fat biking, and sand boarding and has kid sized bikes if six days seems a bit much. Getting out to Atacama takes some effort, but with Mistico and Billy, you will get a fabulous, safe, and well planned adventure. We are already planning a trip to Peru with Billy for our next trip. review_text: If this review helps one person, it will be extremely valuable! There was so much confusion related to the booking process the day I visited (1/22/2023) It's very important to follow the process outlined on the official website of Socaire Chile to purchase tickets. First, you need to purchase a ticket in advance and only at the official website. Next you have to select a date and time to visit the site. Next, you need to arrive in the town of Solcaire at least 1 hour before your ticket time. You will get a paper ticket from the office in Socaire using the QR code of the ticket you purchased online. You must also provide your license plate number. There may be big line in Solcaire when you arrive so plan to arrive on time. Solcaire is 30 minutes from Lagunas Miscanti y Miniques if arriving from San Pedro Atacama. You cannot miss any of the steps above, or do them out of order, to gain entry. You must present your paper ticket at the gate of Lagunas Miscanti y Miniques. Your QR code will not gain you entry to the park without a paper ticket from Solcaire one hour in advance! The visit is amazing and well worth it!

review_text: My chef husband and I took two wine tours with Uncorked to start off our 2 week "wine and foodie trip" in Chile, and were very pleased. We did their tours of both large and small wineries in the Aconcagua and Maipo wine areas, and especially liked the first one in Aconcagua, with Patricia (ask for her- she's great!), as we were able to blend and bottle our own wine at one of the wineries. That was such a great (and delicious!) learning experience- and so much fun- that we Highly recommend it to anyone starting out on a Wine Trip in Chile! Private wine tours in Chile are not cheap, and I contacted several companies, all of which offered excellent sounding trips. I chose Uncorked based on their email correspondance with me and online reviews, although there were several others, including Santiago Adventures, that also seemed to have great wine trips. We didn't want to do private tours, and would have happily joined a small group, but as it was only the two of us, joining with others wasn't an option with any of the wine tour companies I contacted. The lunches at the wineries were excellent, as well, and we highly recommend eating at any of the wineries you go to. Most private wine tours will run at least $250.00/pp per day, but it is a whole day, and well worth it. As you do need reservations at most wineries, unless you speak Spanish it may be difficult to make your own reservations and get driving directions, and with a driver you are free to enjoy all the wine and not worry about driving home! Review of: Best Wine Tasting in Santiago

review_text: My wife and I recently completed the 7-day rafting trip with Earth River in Futaleufú, and it was the highlight of our month-long travels through Patagonia, which also included other popular destinations like El Chaltén, El Calafate, and Bariloche. Futaleufú is one of the most breathtakingly beautiful places we’ve ever seen — and the Earth River experience made it even more unforgettable. This trip is the perfect blend of adventure, nature, and comfort. Each day brought a new and exciting challenge — whether it was navigating world-class whitewater (rafting and kayaking), hiking to stunning waterfalls and lakes, or stepping outside our comfort zones in the best ways. The variety of activities kept things fresh, engaging, and rewarding. One of the biggest takeaways from our trip was Earth River’s commitment to safety. My wife had been nervous before the trip after watching rafting videos on YouTube, but once we arrived, those nerves were quickly put at ease. The guides are world-class professionals who train every participant thoroughly, walk you through each rapid in detail, and maintain an impressive system of support boats and backup plans. We felt safe the entire time — which allowed us to fully embrace the adventure. In addition to safety, the comfort and quality of the lodging exceeded expectations. Each night is spent in beautiful, thoughtfully designed accommodations, complete with delicious meals, evening campfires, and cozy beds. This was the perfect way to unwind after a day of adventure. And finally, it’s the people who make this trip truly special. Earth River is family-owned and operated, and that sense of care and connection is felt throughout the week. From Teal and Cade to Ty, Tommy, and the rest of the guiding crew, everyone we met was kind, passionate, and genuinely committed to making the experience unforgettable. If you’re considering this trip — do it. It’s a rare and powerful adventure, and we’re already hoping to return again someday.

review_text: I recently redid the W trek - its been 10 years since I last did it. Last time I was here it was the best thing I did in 6 months of travelling in SA. So coming back maybe my expectations were a bit too high or maybe I just notice things being 10 years older and feeling the bumps a bit more. The trail itself was a lot rougher than I remembered - you are walking along a lot of uneven rocks a lot of the time. The trail between Grande and Gray was very busy - 10 years ago I remember seeing some people but this time it just seemed like there were constantly other people with you. The trail up to the towers was even worse - I joked with my friend that you need Waze there to try and find a path past the crowds. We did the ice hike at Gray which was great but expensive ($160USD for 1-2 hours on the ice, 1 hour hike each way to get to the ice and a 20 min boat ride each way). The other thing to note is that the catamaran between Pudeto and Grande is now VERY busy - If you are doing a day hike I would definitely avoid it - we saw a group who had waited 3 hours to get on have to abandon their plans that day. We were meant to be on the 11am cat but due to crowds and some engine issues (the catamaran is getting old - pretty sure its the same from 10 years ago) we didnt board until 2.30pm - staff aboard dont care that you have spend lots of money to get there and only have very limited time in the park and they then waste half your day because their service doesn't cope with the current demand. Ultimately I think there will have to be changes to cope with the crowds - one thing could be improving the connections to Gray so that you can get there faster and cheaper to start the W there. Since currently lots of people start at Paine and walk to Gray then back again this would significantly reduce the traffic on this path. Finally it seems to be much more expensive than it used to be. I hope Chile will one day get rid of its discriminatory pricing (charging a different amount to foreigners) since developed countries dont really do this. I know that you are in a very remote location - but I just dont remember it being that expensive relatively speaking last time I was there. One other note, when paying the entrance fee make sure you have exact change - we saw them telling people they didnt have change despite having a huge wad of notes, and no they dont take cards - although the refugios do. Saying all that - you will see amazing mountains and scenery etc and get some great photos and I'm sure the popularity will continue to grow - just hopefully they begin to plan for it better so that the crowds can be managed.
