review_text: We booked from California the canopy tour via Ayakara tours. We took a taxi from our hotel in Puerto Varas, because Las Cascadas was like 50 min away. The place is located just on the side of the road. Because we arrived earlier, everything was closed, even the restaurant; so we explored the area. Across the street there was the lake, a nice beach with beautiful views. Our tour started on time, and our 2 guides helped us to secure our gears, then gave us an intro of canopy because we were familiar with the activity. Juan the driver/guide took us up to the hill to platform 1, and we could see a beautiful cattle and horses. Our guides explained in each platform what to do and what to expect, and reinforce security instructions; so we felt very secure and we could enjoy every circuit. The landscape was beautiful, even though it was overcast; we could see the forest, the lake and a little bit of the volcano. At the end, after almost 2 hrs, we felt so happy to completed the tour, and had the experience to be in the second longest canopy in South America. We have a 20 and a 12 years old daughters, and they had so much fun! Highly recommended! At the end; Juan the driver and guide (he was so kind and informative)helped us driving us to Las Cascadas ( waterfalls park) for a posterior hike; because we didn't plan it well and we thought we can have access easily to public buses to get to our next stop, so be sure to accommodate round trip transportation to this canopy tour. In the area, locals know about these public buses, that they have their schedule to pass at certain stops. Coming back to Puerto Varas from Las Cascadas it was a big journey, we took 2 buses arriving to Puerto Octay, and from there we took a taxi better to Puerto Varas. But still the journey was quite fantastic and the roads, landscaping are amazing and we always felt secure, because the locals are very kind.

review_text: My girlfriend and I did a 2 day hike in Huerquehue that ended at the Rio Blanco Termals (hot springs). The first part is along the Tres Lagos trail, during which you will see some very impressive forests of the Araucaria (Monkey Puzzle) trees, which was probably our favorite part. We then camped one night in the park and had a very short (about 4 hours not going too fast) second day that ended at a campsite with some very natural hot springs in a beautiful location. Camping in the park was expensive (15,000 CLP), but the hot springs were cheaper (just 7,000 CLP). Getting back from the hot springs was a little trickier; you could just walk back the way you came through the park, but we didn't have the food for the extra days and paid for a rather expensive transfer to a bus stop at Reigolil (really in the middle of nowhere) where we were able to catch a bus back to Pucon. The park itself was easy to access (there are frequent buses to/from Pucon), the trail was well marked and not too difficult, and the scenery was unique and well worth the trip. Many people do the trail to Cerro Sebastian, but I would recommend the trek to Rio Blanco, or at least the Tres Lagos trail, in order to soak up the beautiful Araucaria forests. Also a couple of nice waterfalls.

review_text: STOP and read before continuing: - Do you have any previous hiking experience? Walking 10km or more with a pack? - Do you have a basic level of fitness? - Do you have any experience with camping, setting up a tent, camp cooking or related activities? - Do you have an aspiration to be outside, climbing mountains and being in nature? If you answered no to any of the following questions it would be advised that as friendly, fun and rewarding as this trek can be it is by no means a 'walk in the park' and will present a different challenge to all of you, so be willing to accept this. CONTINUE... Hi all, I wanted to write this blog as I found in researching for hiking in Torres Del Paine (TdP) there was a lot of conflicting information and no clear definitive answer from anyone as to what to do and how to do it. So here is my bid to give you the best advice, guidance and information if you are thinking of undertaking the walk of a lifetime! Get excited! For your information I hiked TdP O track in late January/early February of 2016. My girlfriend and I did it over 8 days (7 nights), bringing all our gear with us along the way. I will break this into three sections; firstly, all the stuff you need to know before and getting into the park. Secondly, the actual trek notes and daily walks. And lastly general questions, checklists, advised stuff you do and don't need. Part I: Trek Preparation 1. How to get to TdP. We flew into El Calafate, ARG from Buenos Aires. We then took a bus from El Calafate to Puerto Natales, CHI. Puerto Natales is essentially the hub to TdP National Park and will be your home before and after your trek. From Puerto Natales you take a bus into the park. -Buses from El Calafate to Puerto Natales leave daily at 8:30am. These cannot be booked online, but rather on arriving to El Calafate go to the bus terminal in town and there are numerous bus companies that have a route to Puerto Natales. - This bus trip does cross the Argentine/Chilean border so you will need your passport and any other documents you would usually carry when leaving a country. - You do not need to pay any sort of reciprocity fee entering Chile (but will need to keep your receipt for Argentina if you are looking to return) thus don't be worried if you don't already have Chilean Pesos on you before leaving, you can get this in P.N. 2. What to do in Puerto Natales- storage, info, gear, food, bus. - A place to stay: Once in Puerto Natales find a place to stay for a night or two (I would advise allowing yourself 2 nights so you have an entire day to prepare and aren't rushed, remember you have a lot to get before leaving). There are plenty of hostels for reasonable prices most take online bookings, and cater for hikers so have luggage storage. I would strongly advise staying at Erratic Rock (unfortunately they don't take reservations online just on a first in, first served basis) beautiful homely hostel with friendly staff and great rooms and plenty of knowledge about TdP. - Gear/Info: I cannot recommend highly enough the free daily information session that Erratic Rock puts on each day at 3pm. They have all the info you need about the park whether you are experienced or have no experience at all and open question at the end of each session. This is held next door to Erratic Rock Hostel at a place called Base Camp (there are signs out the front for it). Gear, once you have gone to the info session plenty of places around town rent different sorts of gear, depending on what you need. It is all at a pretty similar price. Once again we got all our stuff at Erratic Rock (to keep it easy). Google "renting hiking gear in Puerto Natales" and a range of places will come up with all comparable prices. This includes: tent, backpacks, sleeping mats, sleeping bags, stoves, gas, mess kit, walking poles. They know what they are doing, and will help you along the way with whatever you may need. Trust them :) -Food: there are a couple of smaller grocers in P.N that have all your basic food stuff as well as one large Unimart which would have everything the others wouldn't have. FYI they don't use bags so bring a back pack or something to put all your supplies in. Also there is a guy that sells dried fruit and all kinds of nuts (great hiking food) he is on the road from Erratic Rock to the Unimart (fairly major street) and is definitely a recommendation to go and get a good amount of snacks from. -Bus to the Park: Ok you have all the info, all the gear,food and now just to get a bus to TdP park. We just walked up to the bus terminal you arrived from El Calafate in (5 minutes from town) and once again a range of different companies do daily trips out to the park between 7:30am-8:00am. Price = 7,500 CLP. There is a later option at 2:30pm but would advise to get the early one as you can get walking straight away. 3. Bus to TdP National Park So you get up early, jump on the bus with all your gear. All you need to know for this portion is the bus' first stop will be Laguna Armada. It is here that you will get off and pay the park entrance fee (Price 18000 CP). You also sign a form saying you will abide by the park rules, they will give you a map of the park and then you are free to take your pack and get hiking! The O trek starts at this stop, however, for general info it does stop at two other stops in the park depending if you want to start at a different point. Part II: The Trek Day 1: Trek to Camp Serón, approx 12km. Today is a good warm up. From Laguna you walk along a road/track over a bridge until you see a sign for a trail to Seròn. A relatively level and casual walk, you will pass through woodlands and open grass lands with beautiful views along the river. Today gives you a chance to warm up the legs, get used to the pack weight and get excited. It should take you approximately 4-5 hours arriving mid-afternoon at the camp. Here they have two cold showers, two bathrooms, washing water, and a small kiosk for snacks. Price is 6000 CLP. Plenty of room for tents. Day 2: Trek to Camp Dickson, approx 19km. Today can be a bit of a shock to the system, a few hill portions, and a fair few kms to get through while still getting used to the pack weight. Do not fear! You are in for some amazing views and a great day. Rise at around 7am, pack up and have breakfast for an 8am departure. The first hour is along the river in grassland then heads up hill over a pass to the back end portion of the park. This should take you approximately 5-6 hours and get you into camp around mid afternoon. A beautiful camp ground with a lake and glacier views, Dickson was one of my favourites. Here they have two warmish/cold showers, two toilets, washing water, and a small kiosk for snacks. Price is 6000CLP. Plenty of room for tents. Day 3: Trek to Los Perros, approx 10km. Today is a relatively easy day, so take your time, enjoy the views and try and rest your legs for tomorrow which will be a big day over the pass. You will hike through Forrest areas different to what you have seen before, heading slightly uphill. You have a mirador lookout back on Lago Dickson and a waterfall along the way. Crossing rivers, stones and forest you teach Mirador Britanico with a view of Glacier Los Perros. Take your time and enjoy the view, the camp site is only another 20minutes away. Once at camp get some sleep for your big day tomorrow. Not my favourite campsite, on dirt and forest terrain, chance of mosquitos and midgies. Camp has two toilets, two ice cold showers, washing water, cooking shed and small kiosk for snacks. Price is 6000 CLP. Limited room for tents but you shouldn't be too worried about finding space. Day 4: Trek to camp Grey (easy/bad weather option is to Trek Camp Paso), approx 23km or approx 12km (Camp Paso). Today is a big day! Rise at 5am and try and pack, grab a bite to eat and be on the road by 6am. You will heading uphill for the first 2.5-3hours. Starting through forest and then arriving at stones and rocky terrain be sure to check the weather is clear from here! If it isn't it is probably smarter to head back as you could get caught up the top, with stories of people taking what should be a 3 hour climb around 10 hours, this is silly hiking! Provided the weather is good, follow the orange track markers up 1200m of elevation, be sure to take in and enjoy the views! This was probably my most favourite view of the trek, absolutely stunning. Be careful of the strong winds at the top. On the descent you have a tough time on your knees and legs but stick to it and enjoy the view on the way back down. If you make it to Camp Paso by 12 midday you can decide if you want to push on to Grey camp (another 11km, approx 4.5-5 hours of intermediate terrain). We took this option so that we could have shorter days in the upcoming trek, it is really dependent on the weather and how your legs feel. If not, stay at Camp Paso (it is free) you have water from a stream, a cooking shed, a small amount of spaces but is not too busy. Toilet is a basic squat drop toilet and no shower. But it is free :). Deciding to push on to Grey, you will walk alongside the Glacier and have spectacular views and some fun suspension bridges. Grey camp is slightly more commercial as you are now on the W part of the trek so a different atmosphere of tourist groups and louder groups. Nonetheless always good fun. The camp has two women and two men hot showers (from 6pm to 9pm) and also two toilets in each, an indoor cooking area, kiosk for snacks, a good amount of room but some spots have reserved pre-set up tents and can get busy so try to get in early to ensure a good spot. Cost 6000 CLP. Day 5: Trek to Italiano, approx XXX Today you have a relatively simple walk ahead. Once again you will be skipping a camp (but if you are feeling exhausted feel free to have an easy day and simply stay at Paine Grande, it is a great camp, good cooking shed, good amenities as well (the more tourists, the better the camps). Leaving at a leisurely time around 8:00/9:00am heading mostly down hill you will reach Paine Grande in 3-4hours. You can pop into the camp site and make a hot lunch and pick up any supplies if you need. There is also a ranger station here where you can make a booking for Italiano camp (if you haven't already). We did it on the day as we weren't too sure about where we would stay, as it is a free camp it can book out so try and book if possible. From Paine Grande you have a leisurely walk along lakes and woodlands for approximately 2.5 hours when you cross the lake and reach the French Valley you will arrive at Italiano mid afternoon. If you are feeling good you can head up the valley that afternoon (a 2 hour track, or 4 hour return trip to a look out in the French Valley) however we were pretty exhausted so hung out by the beautiful lake and relaxed. Camp site has basic toilets 50 metres south of camp, no showers, you get your water for cooking and washing from the stream. Get a good nights rest for views tomorrow. Day 6: French Valley then trek to Los Cuernos, approx 17.5km (with valley), 7.5km (without). Stay motivated! Don't worry we found it tough around this point, but you are doing well! If you didn't do the valley yesterday, rise relatively early and leave your big pack at camp to head up the valley by 8am. Take a day pack with snacks/lunch, jacket and water. After 2 hours you reach the look out (unfortunately it was raining and cloudy for us) but I have heard there are spectacular views to enjoy. Return to Italiano, pick up your big pack and begin to Los Cuernos. After a leisurely walk along the mountainside and along the pebbled beaches you reach Los Cuernos after 2 hours. This is probably the busiest camp site, so try to get in early and find a good space. Once again there are the pre-reserved tents for the tourists so spots can be limited. They have warm showers from 6pm (4 for men and 4 for women), ample toilets, small indoor cooking area, tap water for washing, and kiosk for snacks. Price 8,500CLP Day 7: Trek to Torres, approximately XXX Today you will be freckling into the valley at the base of the Torrres look out. This camp site you should have booked prior to leaving at the CONAF centre in Puerto Natales (see Part III). Leave Los Cuernos around 8am and get a good amount of walking done before the track gets too busy. After 2-2.5hours you will reach a split trail take the trial labelled "shortcut to Chileano" it is pretty hard to miss, the other trail goes to Los Torres Hotel. From here the track heads gradually uphill towards Camp Chileano where after 2 hours you will be deep into the valley at the camp. Here take the opportunity to cook lunch and enjoy the views before a 1.5 hour hilly track towards Torres Camp. After going up and down small hills you will reach the camp. Set up your tent and with the time left in the afternoon head up the 45minute trail to the Torres lookout. This is what you have been waiting for! Hang out at the top and enjoy taking pictures and enjoying the Torres. Head down late afternoon and get a good nights sleep, as tomorrow you will head back up at sunrise (even better than seeing them by day). The camp has 2 toilets, no showers, a stream for cooking and washing and a basic cooking shed. On dirty and under forest but I liked this campsite. Day 8: Sunrise at Torres then Los Torres Hotel, approx 16km Check with the camp ranger the night before as to what time sunrise will be. Generally over summer this will be 5:30am-6:00am. Wake up approximately 1 to 1.5 hours before sunrise (for us it was a 4:15am wake) take with you your day pack, with breakfast, sleeping bag, warm clothes, camera and head torch. Hike up the track (hopefully because you did it the day before it will be easier and you should be able to make it up safely in just torch light). Italiano, Las Torres and Paso are all free. -How much money do I need? 18000CLP for park entrance and approximately an extra 60,000CLP for camping, kiosk snacks, wine, beer etc. -Should I book/prepay for sites? If not, I'm sure they can always find room for just one more tent. DO BOOK your night at Los Torres before leaving (do this at the CONAF office in Puerto Natales. While there are no bears; foxes, mice and Pumas have been seen in the park, so keep your food well buried inside your tent. -What about bugs? I would recommend bringing bug spray. Although not always around it is nice if there are mosquitos or midgies to have some good spray with deet in it. -Why do the circuit counter-clockwise? It makes you pack lighter for when you head over the pass, and trust me.... You don't want to walk up the pass the other way! -In case of emergency? Powder milk, soup sachets and instant noodles make great fillers and are light and easy. Hi all, I wanted to write this blog as I found in researching for hiking in Torres Del Paine (TdP) there was a lot of conflicting information and no clear definitive answer from anyone as to what to do and how to do it. So here is my bid to give you the best advice, guidance and information if you are thinking of undertaking the walk of a lifetime! Get excited! For your information I hiked TdP O track in late January/early February of 2016. My girlfriend and I did it over 8 days (7 nights), bringing all our gear with us along the way. I will break this into three sections; firstly, all the stuff you need to know before and getting into the park. Secondly, the actual trek notes and daily walks. And lastly general questions, checklists, advised stuff you do and don't need. Part I: Trek Preparation 1. How to get to TdP. We flew into El Calafate, ARG from Buenos Aires. We then took a bus from El Calafate to Puerto Natales, CHI. Puerto Natales is essentially the hub to TdP National Park and will be your home before and after your trek. From Puerto Natales you take a bus into the park. -Buses from El Calafate to Puerto Natales leave daily at 8:30am. These cannot be booked online, but rather on arriving to El Calafate go to the bus terminal in town and there are numerous bus companies that have a route to Puerto Natales. - This bus trip does cross the Argentine/Chilean border so you will need your passport and any other documents you would usually carry when leaving a country. - You do not need to pay any sort of reciprocity fee entering Chile (but will need to keep your receipt for Argentina if you are looking to return) thus don't be worried if you don't already have Chilean Pesos on you before leaving, you can get this in P.N. 2. What to do in Puerto Natales- storage, info, gear, food, bus. - A place to stay: Once in Puerto Natales find a place to stay for a night or two (I would advise allowing yourself 2 nights so you have an entire day to prepare and aren't rushed, remember you have a lot to get before leaving). There are plenty of hostels for reasonable prices most take online bookings, and cater for hikers so have luggage storage. I would strongly advise staying at Erratic Rock (unfortunately they don't take reservations online just on a first in, first served basis) beautiful homely hostel with friendly staff and great rooms and plenty of knowledge about TdP. - Gear/Info: I cannot recommend highly enough the free daily information session that Erratic Rock puts on each day at 3pm. They have all the info you need about the park whether you are experienced or have no experience at all and open question at the end of each session. This is held next door to Erratic Rock Hostel at a place called Base Camp (there are signs out the front for it). Gear, once you have gone to the info session plenty of places around town rent different sorts of gear, depending on what you need. It is all at a pretty similar price. Once again we got all our stuff at Erratic Rock (to keep it easy). Google "renting hiking gear in Puerto Natales" and a range of places will come up with all comparable prices. This includes: tent, backpacks, sleeping mats, sleeping bags, stoves, gas, mess kit, walking poles. They know what they are doing, and will help you along the way with whatever you may need. Trust them :) -Food: there are a couple of smaller grocers in P.N that have all your basic food stuff as well as one large Unimart which would have everything the others wouldn't have. FYI they don't use bags so bring a back pack or something to put all your supplies in. Also there is a guy that sells dried fruit and all kinds of nuts (great hiking food) he is on the road from Erratic Rock to the Unimart (fairly major street) and is definitely a recommendation to go and get a good amount of snacks from. -Bus to the Park: Ok you have all the info, all the gear,food and now just to get a bus to TdP park. We just walked up to the bus terminal you arrived from El Calafate in (5 minutes from town) and once again a range of different companies do daily trips out to the park between 7:30am-8:00am. Price = 7,500 CLP. There is a later option at 2:30pm but would advise to get the early one as you can get walking straight away. 3. Bus to TdP National Park So you get up early, jump on the bus with all your gear. All you need to know for this portion is the bus' first stop will be Laguna Armada. It is here that you will get off and pay the park entrance fee (Price 18000 CP). You also sign a form saying you will abide by the park rules, they will give you a map of the park and then you are free to take your pack and get hiking! The O trek starts at this stop, however, for general info it does stop at two other stops in the park depending if you want to start at a different point. Part II: The Trek Day 1: Trek to Camp Serón, approx 12km. Today is a good warm up. From Laguna you walk along a road/track over a bridge until you see a sign for a trail to Seròn. A relatively level and casual walk, you will pass through woodlands and open grass lands with beautiful views along the river. Today gives you a chance to warm up the legs, get used to the pack weight and get excited. It should take you approximately 4-5 hours arriving mid-afternoon at the camp. Here they have two cold showers, two bathrooms, washing water, and a small kiosk for snacks. Price is 6000 CLP. Plenty of room for tents. Day 2: Trek to Camp Dickson, approx 19km. Today can be a bit of a shock to the system, a few hill portions, and a fair few kms to get through while still getting used to the pack weight. Do not fear! You are in for some amazing views and a great day. Rise at around 7am, pack up and have breakfast for an 8am departure. The first hour is along the river in grassland then heads up hill over a pass to the back end portion of the park. review_text: It was misrepresented from the start. It was not a small group. There were 32. Valentina tried hard. It was difficult to hear her commentary while the bus was travelling but I think more due to the equipment she is given to use. It was a Spanish and English speaking tour when we understood it would be just English. The first stop in the so called wonderful wine region Casablanca was an absolute farce. It did nothing to promote that region if that is how they treat tourists. We stopped at a huge shed which sold clothing, a few ugly overpriced souvenirs, coffee that cost a lot but just came out of a machine. The wine tasting was at a counter in the store. At 9 in the morning I did not wish to taste but my friend did and said the wine was dreadful. The promised olives, crackers etc for tasting did not exist. I will be letting the Australian agent who booked it not to use this group again. We weren’t the only ones to feel they had been misled either. It was booked via Viator but the tour operator was MTO Tour Chile. MTO should be ashamed for embarrassing Chile by such a poor tour for tourists. I will be trying to put a complaint in with the tourist authority as well. The walk around Valparaíso was OK. I did note other guides talking about murals and buildings but we got nothing. Lunch at the selected restaurant was good but expensive. Review of: Full Day Group Tour - Viña Del Mar-Valparaiso -Casablanca -Reñaca Thank you for sharing your experience with us! We apologize for the inconveniences and we'll make sure it never happens again. MTO Tour Team

review_text: For only 2,000, we got a tour of an old submarine, now just a museum, and we stayed down there for a good half hour learning about torpedos, escape plans, radar, and how 70 men slept and ate down there. It was so cool to see all the small spaces and bunk beds, and there are even signs that still say "quiet-they are listening to us" in reference to the part of the crew responsible for the radar. We wore helmets because of the low-hanging apparatus and the portholes we had to crawl through which was helpful. Great little tour! The have tours every hour or so, and it's located at the end of the pier, with the ticket stand being a tiny little booth that you would miss. Look carefully!

review_text: I hesitate to tell you how beautiful this place is, because it is not at all yet protected in any way. When you visit, please leave it as you found it and refrain from taking any more rocks away! The variety and contrast of colors in the rocks and formations (leading into) this spectacular valley are surprising. After visiting tens of times with different geologists I learn more every time - this place is unique in the world! Not only its beauty is striking because of the constrasting colors and crazy shapes, but the fact that here there are ancient rocks formed deep inside the earth that we usually never even see on the earth´s surface, plutonic and hypabyssal beauties, makes it even more fascinating. Despite the fact that you will find extremely few guides who actually really DO understand its formation and provenance, it is a fabulous quiet and awe inspiring tour. An hour and a half drive from Sn Pedro. Combines easily with a wealth of other less visited sites (Rio Grande, Yerbas Buenas, Matancilla). Most tours will also take you for a quick stop at the Yerbas Buenas petroglyphs (ancient graffiti on ignimbrite blobs) in a huge landscape between deep canyons. Then you will drive into the Matancilla valley, soothing green and water trickling through a beautiful valley. I recommend taking your time in the ArcoIris valleys, rather than jamming in the petropglyphs, which really deserve your full attention on another separate excursion if you have the time (and a really good guide to give you teh low-down), Absolutely worth while. Remember, please help us keep it intact !

review_text: We planned a short trip to Chile first week of January, use as an opportunity to get a feel of travel in Chile as well as enjoy the warm weather of the southern hemisphere. I found Echo tours Chile online read the reviews and started corresponding with them about three months prior to the trip. WE are active people and wanted to do things that required some physicality and wanted to do a lot walking. They website offered these types of trips and we found their descriptions to accurately depict their trips. They were very responsive gave us tips on where to stay and suggested day trips to take. WE selected three, at the last minute we decided to change one to customized trip to the coast, they were very accommodating in the change and mad that trip special. We did three trips a walking trip in Santiago, A day hiking trip up in the Maipo Canyon and a trip to see the Humboldt penguins. Our guide was excellent, very adaptive to our experience level, physical level, our likes Etc. The guide was well verse in the areas we went, had lots of local knowledge, Had experience in mountaineering (not that we did any) wilderness First aid, fluent in English and truly focused and aware of what we enjoyed and wanted to accomplish. He was always prompt and we felt very safe in our adventure. Chile was AWESOME!!! I strongly recommend the company and the guide, if you are looking for the type of adventures and trips they cater to.

review_text: The Cerro San Cristobal provides the best view of Santiago. You get here by walking through Barrio Bellavista along the same street with "Patio Bellavista" until you reach the park with the Zoo (ask for directions if you get lost). Then you take Funicular(cable car) to what is almost the top and it cost 2000 pesos (U$4) for round-trip transportation. Once you get off, you still have more stairs to climb to reach the top. It is great exercise, a nice day-trip, and a fun experience. I would say it was the most fun I had in Santiago, Chile. Once you are at the top you can enjoy the view for as long as you want. There are snack shops, souvenirs, and places to sit and have a cold beverage. On a very hot sunny day I advise tourist to wear sunscreen because the sun is very strong at the top and there are not many shaded areas. I also do not recommend this site for people who are unable to walk up stairs. Have fun making it to the top of Santiago, Chile. Happy Travels!!!!

review_text: I took 3days/2nights tour to Uyuni with Cruz Andina. The trip was well-organized. Since the shuttle pick-up from the hostel, the driver did make sure that we were one of the first groups that arrived at Hito-Cajon -- the Chilean border checkpoint -- so that we were the first group to pass an immigration avoiding a long waiting lines. After we arrived at Bolivian side, the 4x4 car is waiting for us. It was in a nice condition. The sceneries were mesmerizing and really unforgettable. I read many reviews stating that no matter what companies you chose from SPdA, you will end up in different company when you arrived in Bolivia. This is not the case of Cruz Andina. They have offices in both SPdA and Uyuni. This is to guarantee you will be served with the best services from them. Cruz Andina may not be the cheapest tour company you could find. But, with the (reasonable) prices they quoted, this, at least can ensure you that you will have "qualified" travel companions in your car. With 6 passengers in one jeep, our group got perfectly blended with polite, professional, kindness and respectable members. This is one of the most important factors to have a perfect trip. I am not a racist guy; however, it is unavoidable to accept the fact that "prices could differentiate people". In last paragraph, I would like to honor our driver -- Marlton. He was an absolutely professional driver. He gave us clear information on each point we stopped. Not only that, he was a really cool DJ with his magical USBs that could take us back to 90s. lol He is also an experienced and creative photographer. We got many perfect photos from him. This trip should not have been this awesome without him. I really wish him all the best in this career.

review_text: We go to La Parva regularly, as the set up is the most kid-friendly (and adult friendly - with good options for mommies and daddies who want to ski black and double black diamonds) of the 4 resorts near Santiago. If you get there early, around 8:20-8:30, you stand a chance of getting a parking spot right near the ski school area which makes transporting kids, equipment and lunch stuff very easy. The ski school is good - they allow you to purchase a ticket for lower La Parva, so you don't have to waste money on a full ticket for small children who will never visit the peaks. My biggest issue is that the options for small children are limited - baby ski school is for the 4 and 5 year olds (who are not "babies", so the name angers my 4 year old who is a good skier) and is really more like daycare, with more than half the time spent indoors and messing around in the snow, sin skis. If you think this is a waste of cash, you are right, but the only other choice is a private lesson, which is outrageously costly (and the only option available for kids under 4 years). The reality is that all the resorts have this issue - they stick to age restrictions for the various kids classes like it it LAW. Food at La Parva (as with all resorts) is very expensive - like 4 times the price of the equivalent in Santiago. Bring everything you intend to eat / drink unless you are open to spending $25 USD on a hamburger, $4 for a Coke or $10 for a hot chocolate. The lift tickets are as expensive as many places in North America and Europe that have far better infrastructure (ski resorts in Chile rarely have high speed lifts and gondalas) so be prepared to pay. title: Family friendly ski resort close to Santiago
review_text_preprocessed: We go to La Parva regularly, as the set up is the most kid-friendly (and adult friendly - with good options for mommies and daddies who want to ski black and double black diamonds) of the 4 resorts near Santiago. If you get there early, around 8:20-8:30, you stand a chance of getting a parking spot right near the ski school area which makes transporting kids, equipment and lunch stuff very easy. The ski school is good - they allow you to purchase a ticket for lower La Parva, so you don't have to waste money on a full ticket for small children who will never visit the peaks. My biggest issue is that the options for small children are limited - baby ski school is for the 4 and 5 year olds (who are not "babies", so the name angers my 4 year old who is a good skier) and is really more like daycare, with more than half the time spent indoors and messing around in the snow, sin skis. If you think this is a waste of cash, you are right, but the only other choice is a private lesson, which is outrageously costly (and the only option available for kids under 4 years). The reality is that all the resorts have this issue - they stick to age restrictions for the various kids classes like it it LAW. Food at La Parva (as with all resorts) is very expensive - like 4 times the price of the equivalent in Santiago. Bring everything you intend to eat / drink unless you are open to spending $25 USD on a hamburger, $4 for a Coke or $10 for a hot chocolate. The lift tickets are as expensive as many places in North America and Europe that have far better infrastructure (ski resorts in Chile rarely have high speed lifts and gondalas) so be prepared to pay. I'm convinced that the prices are geared to Brazilians... but are inaccessible for most Chileans, which is unfortunate.

We arrived in Santiago almost at 23:00, all tired and exhausted from the trip, and our transfer took 1h30 to arrive, probably because they had forgotten us. The guides Daiana and Felipe were extremely rude and uneducated. Felipe took us to Valparaíso and Viña del Mar, but made his "tour" without allowing us to stop to take pictures. If, by chance, any of us stopped to take a picture, he got angry. The tour, which was supposed to end at 18:00, ended at 15:00. She did not allow us to eat in the van, even knowing that the tour would last all day and that the journey to the mountain was long. We left at 4:30 in the morning without coffee, and that day Zerando's house was closed, so we didn't have breakfast. Daiana was rude with the colleagues inside the van, humiliating them and speaking extremely rude. On the way back to Brazil, the transfer came with two cars, but we were 9 people, each with two bags and backpacks. They wanted to plug us all in two cars, in our day-to-day walking in Santiago we used 3 Uber cars, it was impossible 9 people in two cars and with baggage. I DO NOT RECOMMEND ZERANDO CHILE. review_text: I started chatting with Santiago Adventures after booking my Antarctic expedition. I had a few days in Chile en route to and from the port, so I thought I'd make the most of my time in South America. In stepped Santiago Adventures, with an entire itinerary of activities. Unfortunately, I had to cancel some tours, due to last-minute work requirements, but they were more than understanding about it. The tours I was able to keep were perfection! First, a gourmet food tour of Central Market, to include a cooking lesson from the El Galleon executive chef. I learned how to flick the pan to flip food during saute-ing, and once our demo dish was done, the staff brought out an enormous platter of seafood for our group to finish. We were devastated to have to waste so much amazing food, but we just going could not eat anymore after the demo, the pisco sours, and wine wine wine! Speaking of wine... tour #2 was a heli-wine tour of the Casablanca and San Antonio valleys. Loma Larga is now my favorite winery. The heli-wine tour ended with lunch at Matetic. Our helicopter pilot? Oh, only the OWNERS of Loma Larga - wow!! If you want first class, private tours in Chile, go with Santiago Adventures. Oh, and I nearly forgot... Manuel took such good care of me that when I started sniffling and sneezing, thanks to a cold I picked up in Antarctica, he went to the chemist and came back with some meds so I could enjoy my afternoon of wine tasting! How amazing is that???

review_text: I took this tour yesterday. It included wine tasting on the return journey which was a relaxing non pressured visit to a fine vineyard. The journey by comfortable van took a little time on hotel pickups in Santiago for six guests but we still reached Valparaiso by ten am even allowing for a coffee / bathroom stop on the way. The visit to the working port / fish market was a highlight of the tour for me. We were also able to see a large group of sea lions who come into the harbour regularly. This was followed by a walking tour on one of the hills forming part of the city. There are some very interesting buildings, painted in beautiful colours, and views are enchanting. The tour involves climbing quite a large number of stairs and I doubt that this part of the trip could facilitate wheelchair access. Lunch then followed in a local restaurant which was very good, especially the local seafood, but it should be noted that lunch and drinks are not included in the tour price. In the afternoon we had a nice tour of the nearby coastal resort of Vina del Mar, a more modern city. The guide Jaimie speaks first class English and he and the driver were exceptionally good at their jobs and friendly too. It was a really enjoyable day out. Review of: Valparaiso Port and Vina del Mar Full-Day Tour from Santiago

review_text: During our time in Chile we have taken both Valparaiso tours, the Vina del Mar tour, the Santiago afternoon tour and shortly the San Pedro de Atacama as well, all with the same company after good experiences in Valparaiso. The Santiago afternoon tour is a good thing to do on arrival - you get a really good feel for the city centre and the guide points out a lot of things you can then go and do during your time there. You also gain a good knowledge of the history of the city and in the Santiago tour there's also a very honest history of the problems during the dictatorship years. review_text: A long awaited bucket list experience for both my husband and me was a trip to Chile. For years, we remained focused on this goal and had plenty of time to plan it right. Among the surprisingly pleasant and wonderful experiences we had was our tour of the Concha y Toro winery. As adventurous as we are, we did our research to figure out how to get there from our hotel in Santiago. We learned about the bus we had to take to get to the subway system, bought our tickets, and close to an hour later, we arrived there on a late morning in March. We had to ask the locals how far to walk there from the subway station, and luckily it was not far. The first impression of this magnificent winery is of awe. The sheer size of the vineyard is colossal. The scenery equally gorgeous, and the buildings and vila quite magnificent. We were actually surprised that they allow visitors get so close to the vines. We actually picked a few grapes from the vines to taste them. We booked a private wine tasting session and we're giggly with excitement. The experience did not disappoint. We must have tried no fewer than 10 different wines. Our expert sommelier was excellent, he took our taste buds and senses on a an exquisite journey, which confirmed why we like Concha y Toro wines so much. We particularly enjoyed the tour of the cellars, the Casillero del Diable cellars. How awesome that was! Our only complaint relat s to the overly expensive food and souvenirs in their souvenir shop. We would have loved to have brought gifts home with us, but the prices are just prohibitive. It was very disappointing. For a prestigious winery like this one, we had expectations for something better than what they offer. We felt the food was only ok, nothing great, and certainly not impressive. Bad bread with unimpressive charcuterie items brought disappointment to an otherwise lovely experience. Staff was hospitable but cold though. Yet, I highly recommend a visit here. Enjoy it, take your time and try all the wines!! It's always best to go there in the summer to enjoy the magnificent views.

review_text: We went there with a tour operated by Flamingo tours. They picked us up at 4:30 because you can see the fumaroles better the colder it is and the coldest hour of the day usually is around sunrise. We had breakfast (bread, ham&cheese, tea and coffee) there and then went to see the geysers. The geyser field is one of the highest and biggest in the world but there definitely are more spectacular ones. You can see lots of fumaroles and water bubbling in holes but (at least when we were there) there's not water splashing out of the ground like in other places. There's also a natural pool with about 40°C where you can go in. The guide told us though that you shouldn't stay in there too long because the hot water might enhance the chances that you get high altitude sickness. Tips: - eat light the day before and don't drink alcohol (~4.300m high) - bring lots of warm clothes since the temperature drops to about -7°C

review_text: My husband and I both really enjoyed the Cejar Lagoon tour. We visited 3 lagoons, including one on the salt flats to watch the sunset. The vehicle was really amazing and comfortable. We had Dan as our tour guide and he was friendly and knowledgeable. He spoke good English. It felt a little awkward being the only English speaking couple on a Portuguese speaking tour but I guess that's just the luck of the draw. Booking and paying in full in advance was easy and I was grateful for this option which most other companies don't offer. We were criticised a little by the receptionist for not having large coats (we only had big jumpers with us for this afternoon tour). I see where she was coming from but it did worry me unnecessarily as we were plenty warm enough on this tour (perhaps the difference between coming from the UK and South America). It would have been good to leave slightly earlier so there could be slightly more time to swim in the lagoon - we only really had time to get changed and walk down then it was time to come back. Don't wear sunscreen, just take some to put on after the lagoon if you need it as they make you shower first if you have sunscreen on and it's really cold. We had really nice snacks and a pisco sour at the end which was appreciated before the long drive back. Overall, a great tour with amazing scenery.

review_text: I decided to take this walking tour because my hostel suggested it. It wasn´t good at all, and now I´ve wasted my only day in Valparaiso. First, the tours are supposed to be in English. A number of Spanish speakers were on it and seemed fine knowing it was in English, and then some French girls arrived who spoke NO English and made a sound of frustration when the guide started speaking in English. So the guide offered to speak mostly in English but translate into Spanish every now and then. From the start he translated completely, and within an hour he was speaking primarily in Spanish and then giving much much shorter summaries in English. It was extremely frustrating since there is another tour that is offered by another company at the same time, and if I had known I would have gone there instead. In addition, the guide, while very nice, was extremely lacking energy. This is my third free city tour and both of my previous guides (in other cities) were AWESOME. They had so much energy and enthusiasm. This guide was so so nice but had absolutely no energy. Also, other tours I´ve been on include recommendations for local places to eat, drink, etc. This tour had none of that. Overall it was like a boring history class, where a nice professor drones on and half of the time sounds like he´s speaking another language (except this time he was). Definitely would not recommend- just follow the map and do it yourself. At least then you can stop and get food or a drink along the way. Note: while this is a free tour, they make it clear from the start that they expect 5,000 peso ($10) tips PER PERSON at the end, unless you can´t afford it. This was also off-putting since the other two tours I´ve been on mention tips but never tell you how much to tip. Also, when it says it leaves at 3pm, that means 3:20pm. review_text: I went along with my partner and a couple of friends (ages 24-29) for a wedding to Santiago. We all were traveling with a limited budget, and only one of us knew how to ski. Nevertheless, the bride recommended visiting Valle Nevado and we thought the easiest way would be to go on a tour. Turistik was our first option, but they had no more places. Given that it was 8:30 pm on the day before we wanted to go, and we had no other days in Santiago our choices were limited. The only other tour office open at Patio Bellavista was Enotour. Their tour did cost 3000CLP extra, but it included a wine tasting and a free bottle of wine. We went for it, and it was a waste of time and money. The actual time visiting the snow (ahem ski courses where there is not much to do, nor guided visit) was around 1 and a half hours. The whole tour lasted 9 hours. Our original idea was to take some nice pictures with the Andes and play a little bit in the snow. It was difficult to find spots to do this in a ski resort. There were just short stretches where the courses ended. If you do not want to spend much, do some research beforehand, or you'll be paying at least another 20,000CLP for expensive and very regular food and snow gear you don't need. The wine tasting was not worth it. Wines were average, and the tasting was done in the middle of a very noisy restaurant. If there is something I do recognise is that our guide, Valentina, was always very nice and helpful. We had a flight to take, and she called another sprinter to pick us and take us get our bags instead of going through the city dropping off the rest of the people. Thank you for sharing your experience with us, it help us to continue improving our service, unfortunatly we can not manage the prices on the mountain during the ski season, the one that we stop for lunch and tasting wine is the cheapest one. The tour that you take was the shared one, with people from other hotels, thats why we need to follow the set route, the private option you can spend all the time you want on the ski center that you choose, but we trully thank your comment, because it give us more encouragement to work even harder. we hope to have the opportunity to make your experience unique warm regards

review_text: After horse riding in multiple countries this was the unsafest ride ride for beginners we have experienced. My Husband and son are beginners but I'm experienced rider with more than 35 years riding experience (Including racing on thoroughbreds and trot racing) as well as a qualified vet. My husband and son where as mentioned are not experienced riders and the horse my husband was given (Gaucho) which was not a horse I would recommend a beginner. The horse lost its footing on the narrow track up the mountain and was luck not to fall down the mountain and then later on without commanding the horse to go faster the horse suddenly started to fast trot. The only way Juan can control his horses is by using bits not normally used for normal horse rides and prohibited spurs in the horse world (most spikes I had ever seen). Both Juan and support guides horses were not in complete control all of the time. The support guide and Juan were also very rude when I requested a better horse to ride. As the horse they had chosen me as I would like to experience a good ride and the horse had breathing difficulties when standing. The ride we did as mentioned at one point the trail uses a very narrow and close to the edge of mountain track which if not experienced in our opinion would not be suitable for a beginners and kids. The return going down is via a sand dune which luckily my son and husband had the option to walk down rather than ride. This was a good choice as Juan when trying to take my sons horse down had difficulty with the horse refusing to go down the dune at first. More issues were encountered during the ride.

review_text: Absolutely amazing experience. We visited the lagoons and the thermal springs on the first day. Some of the lagoons had frozen over completely which was stunning while others, such as the red lagoon, still had flamingos, vicunas and llamas all around their perimeter. On the second day, we visited the arbol de piedra and some more lagoons before stopping at a salt hostel. The salt hostel was lovely, with private rooms and showes, just what was needed after two days of travelling! On the last day, we visited the Uyuni salt flat, Isla Incahuasi and the train cemetery. The salt flat is stunning! There is no other place like it, the salt appears to go on forever. It was truly a once in a lifetime experience getting to see it. Additionally, Vladi, our driver, told us interesting facts about each place that we visited as well as helped us out with photo ideas in the salt flats! He was a great guide and we would highly recommend travelling with World White Travel.

review_text: Bigfoot gave us incorrect information which stranded us in the park over night. Management refused to acknowledge, apologize for or rectify their mistake. Prior to our trip, we were in contact with Bigfoot to ask if different travel plans were possible. After a number of emails, we called their office. Over the phone, we were told that we could do an afternoon ice hike and then take the Grey III ferry. (We were told specifically which navigation to book). We said great and booked the ice trek. The trek was very pleasant. We enjoyed ourselves and after completing the trek we asked directions to the ferry landing. It was then that our guides told us that the last ferry of the day had already departed and there was no way to leave the park. As you can imagine, this was incredibly stressful. We had to arrange emergency lodging in the park. What was even more stressful was the our guides told us that they could not contact the main Bigfoot office. Suddenly we realized that if an accident had happened on the ice, we would have been in terrible danger. A guide company that cannot contact their main offices is not sufficiently prepared for emergencies. (To their credit, the guides themselves explained what happened to the nearest refugio, which helped us in getting space to sleep for the night) When we contacted management after the fact, they denied any responsibility. We are experienced travelers on all 6 continents. This was the first experience that caused one of us to cry from stress and worry while on vacation. Between office staff that share incorrect information, to guide staff that cannot contact the main office, to management that does not address complaints, I do not recommend Bigfoot.

review_text: As with the other lakes in Torres del Paine, this one has beautiful clear blue water. It is most notable for the deposits of calcium carbonate around the rim, lending it an unusual white rim which looks like a sandy beach from a distance. You can take a long hike, partly on unmarked trails (covered by remains of the fire of a few years ago) or you can take a short walk from the trailhead at the other end. I believe the trail is called Lacal-Sarmiento, but I am not sure of the spelling of the first of these names. It is worth seeing this lake and it is easy and quick to do from the trailhead.

review_text: My partner and I trekked the "W" and the"O" circuit. The conditions (rain, wind, occasional snow) make both a challenge, but the "O" is not a trek for the inexperienced or unfit hiker. The toughest day includes a 25 kilometer hike over streams, moraines of loose stone, and endless mud; it traversed a mountain pass and nearly 4000 feet of ascent and descent. The camping varies in comfort alone both trails, with comfortable refugees at either end with good restaurants and showers and a mixed bag of places along the trail. Without a doubt, this trek was the most challenging of my life, but also the most rewarding. The views, proximity of the glaciers, adrenaline-driving cliffside trails, and stunning terrain are not to be missed. Get fit and do the "O". Otherwise, take the catamaran to Grande Paine, stay in the refugio, and wait for the rain to clear to do a day hike.

review_text: Juan, our guide, picked me up on time before picking up another couple. So we had a small group of 3, easy conversation, and Juan gave us a little history and highlights as we went. I have been on several wine tours on a few continents and was pleased with seeing the small to medium sized businesses instead of huge producers. The first one gave us a very good tour of production facility and the tasting was in an actual cellar. This was the first time I had seen and tasted wine fermented in huge clay jars, an old Egyptian method. The second winery was newer and offered just a tasting of two wines and two types of cheese, but it was in a beautiful open patio surrounded by a garden. Very nice and relaxing, and the guide took her time explaining and answering questions. We then went for lunch at a small family owned Italian restaurant where we all bought our own lunch, which the four of us enjoyed together in the nice outdoor seating area. The third stop we walked around vineyards checking out different grapes before going through the production and underground storage areas, which had been rebuilt since a devastating 8.9 earthquake. We proceeded outside to a table and stood as we sampled six different wines. There were no sales presentations, just a nice introduction to Chilean wine. Juan dropped the other couple off at the airport in Santiago before taking me to my hotel. Door to door was 9 hours, but very pleasant. Review of: Maipo Valley Wine Tour with 4 vineyards from Santiago.

review_text: We went to Huerquehue National Park hoping to drive around a bit and walk on some short trails. We stopped at the ranger station to purchase our tickets, and the guard told us where to drive and what we could do in terms of walking short, easy treks of about 1 hour, and what to see. We asked questions and took a photo of the map on the wall, since there was no trail map printed that we could take with us. Ranger also told us to stop and ask ahead in the other ranger stops. We saw none. Because it was low season, the guard was nice enough to charge all three of us local Chilean fees (only one is a resident). We stopped first at the beach on the left, to use bathroom facilities, where there is a parking lot and walk down to the lake. Very nice. Went back to the car and drove straight as we were told. We arrived at a point where the car coudn’t get through due to a small stream of water, and with a sign that read No cars except for the refugio. Asked around and were told there was no were else to drive, just a trail up to the lake on the left, where people coming back from it told us they had walked for over an hour, that it wasn’t an easy trail, and got back tired before ever reaching the lake. There was lots of construction of modern facilities in that area, maybe a hotel or a nice refuge. We decided to leave. While we could have stopped again at the ranger’s entrance hut and asked, we didn’t feel like doing all that drive back again. I suggest for anyone going looking for a similar, short experience walking on easy trails, to try to find a trail map on line and have the ranger mark it for you. Driving is only possible for a mile or two but not further, at least it wasn’t during low season.

review_text: Countryside is very pretty and clean after Santiago. Wineries are smart, well run and fun. Wines themselves are not nearly as impressive as anticipated (or said to be). Even the whites ( nominally the stars here ) lacked the complexity anticipated given the hot days and cool/cold nights that should be outstanding for SB production. Nice high end lunches (ubiquitous in the central region of Chile) and an interesting one time experience, but the valley itself a bit underwhelming. Price to value ratio for wines sampled here is poor. Not bad wine but...not bad. Very little that is special. Price to value ratio for nice lunches at wineries can be very good as food itself, and some of the cuisine, is very good quality. Like much of Chile, it is best to politely ask for a sip to assess, then buy a bottle to accompany lunch...much better value than the formal tastings, tours etc. Food, esp seafood, outstanding as anticipated. Casablanca (town) itself is "interesting" as an example of a different side of Chile. Not poor but certainly a long way from middle class. Interesting for one night (we had two) -- it might be best to stay one night or just keep going after sampling the wineries. We do recommend two local attractions. Nearby ( ~ 25km) Lago Penuelas is like a small provincial park with some nice forest, good walks, excellent picnicing by a lake, some alpacas and lots of birds. A very pleasant way to spend a few hours or most of a day relaxing in a natural (not wild) environment if you bring a picnic and bottle of wine. Near Vina, the Jardin Botanico Nacional is outstanding. It's a bit further but well worth the trip. Check online reviews at TA.

review_text: Our group travelled to Patagonia in November and completed the 7 day W-trek. We were so very lucky to have Felipe and Pablo as our guides. Time bends a little when a geologist explains how mountains and terrain form over millions of years. Felipe is a geologist and was able to articulate the formation of Torres del Paine, which made our experience even richer. Felipe and Pablo were very knowledgeable about the flora and fauna as well. Hiking during spring, we were lucky to see so many wildflowers in bloom and Felipe and Pablo were able to identify them and speak specifically on how the various flowers and plants survive in the harsh environment. Felipe and Pablo adjusted to our pace and encouraged us when we were challenged on the hikes. They made us feel secure and safe. They have great energy and warmth. They spoke to us about Chilean culture and gave us tips for the next stage of our trip, where they wouldn't be with us, in Argentina. review_text: This cultural center is locally referred to as the GAM, and was one of the highlights of our trip through Chile. For anyone pursuing art galleries or Chilean artesans while in Santiago, this should be at the top of the list. In pursuit of an art gallery zone in Santiago, we came across this new modern building on the edge of Lastarria. There was a long line of youngsters outside waiting to purchase Lade Gaga concert tickets, while inside were a couple of amazing exhibitions. The exhibitions rotate every six months or so, and while we were there we saw a UNESCO artisan exhibit of indigenous Chilean crafts, a photography exhibit, and an architecture exhibition of about 50 recent modern Chilean projects. This one building provided an amazing vista of Chilean arts; past and present. During the month, we noted that the GAM was hosting music, dance, and theater performances as well. This is a gem that Santiago and Chile should be proud of. I must see in Santiago for culture junkies!!

review_text: This is a must do in the Chilean Andes. I had originally booked for a trek to Cajon del Maipo which got cancelled due to heavy snowfall in the valley. The agency Ando Andes was quick to help with accommodating me in the horseback Andes tour. Our tour guide Gonzalo was fabulous. Great knowledge about the region and with a witty sense of humor. He also became the paparazzi for us, so we could manage my horse and take in the scenery while he took the pictures. Started at about 11:30 from the base of the cerro and the total journey was about 3.5 hours. Up and down. Then treated to some great lunch. Chicken-ham sandwiches, chilean wine, fresh cheese, raisins and peanuts. I didn't need to have dinner that night! Caution: Be sure to sit on the horses correctly, else you may get pain in your back, thighs. Keep yourself wooled, it gets cold up in the montanas. Don't carry your valuables, passport, etc up on the mountains. Thank you for a great review. You are right about 'be sure to sit correctly' but correctly on these well-behaved horse means relaxed, not stiff and self-conscious. The first time I went on a long ride on one of them, my early days in Chile, I tried to ride as I had learnt in England and got the most violent cramp. I looked at the guide and saw that he was riding in a completely relaxed position, no heels down or toes turned out, no straight back and head held high - just comfortable and almost floppy but held together inside, ready to react if it became necessary. You obviously got it right. Thanks alot.

The church is somewhat dark (much like most European cathedrals) and large. It is very old and has interesting several side altars to various saints. My wife and I attended a Sunday mass at 7 pm (1900 hours Chilean time). It is an interesting place to visit and is the church of the Archbishop of Santiago (who may be a Cardinal). Mass times for most of the churches in Santiago are listed in some of the daily papers. Although the papers are in Spanish, you can easily determine the names of the various churches and the mass times shown.

review_text: We went to the Valle de Luna two ways. Firstly we hired bikes (3000 Pesos each for 6 hours) and headed off. It's 4 to 5km from town to the ticket office at the entrance to the park. This section apart from the last few hundred meters is all on made road and not too difficult. Entrance to the park is 2250 Pesos each. The road into the park is unmade and from the entrance gets steep in places and very corrugated for long sections. We got to the Cayon (5km into the park) when it got too difficult for my wife and we headed back to town. We got back in time to get a tour to the valley, which cost us 7000 Pesos each and was well worth it. We went to the Cayon, Tres Marias, stopped at a couple of other spots for photos and finally to Piedra de Coyote (the highlight). The tours cost between 7000 to 10000 Pesos depending on the company and your bargaining skills. Tours run from either 2.00 or 3.00pm to around 6.30 to 7.00pm.

review_text: I was quite impressed by the level of depth in the exhibits at this museum. They have pieces from cultures that I was familiar with, but many of these were new and interesting, unlike the ones I had seen before. I also like how it covers all Meso-American cultures from Mexico all the way to the southern tip of South America, giving you an opportunity to really contrast some of the styles of art that existed. Lots of modern technology and lighting as well, particularly in the textile room with electronic drawers and automatic lighting to preserve the artifacts for longer. My only lament was that the Inca exhibits seemed a little sparse are were overly focused on the Chilean aspect of them without considering other areas such as Peru or Ecuador. I recognize that the museum logically would have more Chilean artifacts to work with, but if you're going to put up Aztec and Maya items I think it would be profound to really draw attention the massive empire the Incas had built.

review_text: My mother and I took the Cajón del Maipo tour and we are over the moon on how great of an experience this was. They picked us off at our hotel for this tour, which was greatly appreciated. We did a few stops on the way to the volcanic pool. First we had the chance to eat a breakfast in one of the old trains that used to make the service towards the cajón. We even got the chance to drive the train which was very fun. We then stopped in route to get equipment for the tour, which was a big plus for us because we did not bring all our hiking gear with us. We then passed through a ghost town on our way to the cajón. The springs were out of this world: imagine swimming in volcanic springs with a condor flying over your head, at 2500m altitude. On the way back the volcanic springs, we stopped at a local place to eat a picnic and drink chilean wine. Our guides were always on top of everything. Jesus was a jokester, but always making sure everyone was feeling included and had fun. Paolo, the other guide, was super helpful and made sure everything was always alright and we were feeling well. We could not have asked for better guides, they knew their chilean history and geography very well and were very warm and careful. For the whole tour the group felt like family, even through the language barrier. Jesus always translated everything from English, to Spanish, to Portuguese. Paolo even took pictures of everyone while we visited to send to us afterwords. We highly recommend this tour, it is one of the best tour I ever took in all my travels around the world.

Review of: Inca Lagoon in Andes Mountain Range - Visit Local Vineyard with Tasting included Good day, we thank your feedback. - According to Wine Tasting. We do not take a tour at the winery. We prepare a beautiful table for our clients to enjoy. - 3 Different wines are offered Chardonnay , Carmenere and Syrah. Its more than good for tasting. LUNCH - Its a restaurante in a hotel portillo with the best view of the Inca Lagoon. We make sure that our guide suggest options. The restaurante gives a very important impression . Its clients own expense meaning that in the first stop starting the tour people can buy snacks , bottled water etc. For clients to feel free to decide to have lunch at the restaurante. The menu has the different alternatives and prices as well. LLAMAS - This is a very nice local farm located at the foot of the andes mountains. There are few llamas that you can interact with, feed them and pictures witch these are very friendly. We are here no more than 20 -30 min. - This is a very important stop ending the tour for Rest rooms. We do not consider its a joke in respect of our local owners and people. After this stop the trip back to Santiago takes 1 hour 30 min approx. Meaning that this is the place we have to offer our clients rest room stop before heading back to the city. Very important not forget we are in the middle of the andes. Where this tour we enjoy nature and greatfull to have places where we can stop. And enjoy the presence of local people. Once again we thank your personal feedback. This allows for us to clear many of your questions or doubts before booking this trip.

review_text: Lake Chapo is a unique natural treasure in Chile, only 40 minutes from Puerto Montt (1 hour approximately by public transport). It is surrounded by the Alerce Andino Park and the Llanquihue Reserve. Making it a special place, where you can explore one of the few places in the world with protected temperate rain forests. The lake overlooks Calbuco Volcano and is surrounded by mountains with native forest. On weekends, there are cycling, kayaking and hiking activities with local guides and there is a café where you can access the network of artisans, entrepreneurs and cultural activities of the place. The Llanquihue Reserve is a 15-minute drive from the lake, and is a unique space to see the remains of the latest eruption of the Calbuco Volcano in 2015. It is an ideal trail for the family to do; it has a panoramic view towards the lake, and a direct waterfall of the volcano, it is also a trail where you can see flora and endemic funga, as well as bird watching. If you want to climb up to the volcano shelter, you should bring adequate clothing, basic supplies, and I recommend climbing with a guide or group, and carry a telephone with coverage or radio.

review_text: We were fortunate that a window of good weather appeared during our stay in pucon to take on the volcano ( was one of our key objectives for our trip to South America !) Aguaventura allowed our sons aged 13 and 15 to climb ( covered by insurance - not all agencies do ). They were very clear in their instructions the night before and stressed was important not to lag behind and get caught in a slow group if you were keen to make it to the top. The guide to trekker ratio was 3 to 1 which was excellent. The gear was clean and the staff were patient with the fit out. The trek is very difficult - even in perfect conditions. My husband and son (15 yr) were two out of four of our group to make it to the top in perfectly blue skies and 0 winds. My husband is extremely fit and found it to be one of the hardest treks he's ever done. The guides were great and our group ended up as three separate groups which each made it to their own capability level. My son and I were happy to take in the views 'half way' up and chat to other group members back in the cafeteria while waiting. Do take the ski lift as it saves you time and increases your chances of making to the top. The groups tend to turn around at 2.30pm (in September) to ensure you make it back in a timely fashion. Do not underestimate the effort required to make it to the top - so give yourself every chance. Would definitely recommend these guys.

review_text: My husband was in Santiago on business and we decided I would join him as neither of us had traveled extensively in South America. Because my husband was working during the week we decided to hire Hector to show us around Santiago and surrounding areas on Saturday and Sunday. This was a great decision since our time was limited and we love to get a true insider's view of areas we travel to. Hector was delightful, kind, knowledgeable and seemed to pick up quickly on the exact kind of tour my husband and I would enjoy most. (i.e. we want local flavor, not the typical tourist or shopping related spots.) Because Hector was born and raised in the Santiago area, but also studied in NYC for several years, he was exceptionally knowledgeable and passionate about his beautiful country and his English was excellent. One of the things we loved most about Hector was watching him interact with the other local people throughout our drives/tour. He is simply a kind and good person and other people respond to his genuine positivity and respect for everyone we encountered during our travels. Hector does not take incentives from restaurants or other establishments so he really does take you to the places he feels are the best fit for the experience you are looking for. (This is part of why we wanted to be sure to tip him beyond his charge, as he is not making kickbacks from promoting other establishments.) In fact, one of the highlights of our trip out to the coast, was stopping at a simple tiny farming home belonging to a lady who is rumored to make the best empanadas in Chile! It was true!!! Hector knows her through friends and Rosita makes a small number of empanadas on the weekends only to help her with medical bills for her daughter. It was such a lovely experience to visit with her in her neat little home and enjoy her delicious empanadas and a cold glass of Coke. Hector even had us ride a city bus in Valparaiso so we could feel like locals. (He grew up in Valparaiso so he was especially friendly with everyone there.) We've traveled pretty extensively and our experience with Hector was one of the very best we have had. It was just so genuine and he is a lovely person who we felt honored to spend 2 lovely days with.

This region sure is stunning and shows Chile’s Andes mountains at its best. Seba is a lot of fun and a very professional and experienced guide so you can’t go wrong with him ! Whether you already have mountaineering experience or not, he makes sure everything is going well & safe for you, provides good quality technical gear, etc. If you’re planning on visiting Santiago or around, and love adventures and mountains, send him a message and go explore Maipo’s region for yourself ! You’ll thank me later.

review_text: If you want to the best views of Santiago, this is the place to go. It is accessible by road, cable car, Funicular (not working) and on foot. I was hoping to use the Funicular but it was closed. A replacement bus was offered but I decided to make the climb. The climb is worth it but not easy. Even young climbers in their teens and early twenties were feeling exhausted and stopping frequently. The city council has provided frequent benches and water fountains on the climbing route. The ascent took about 50 minutes but the views are great. There is a shrine and the stature of the Virgin faces the old town with her back to the modern financial district. At the top, you will find toilets, places to eat and free WiFi. The journey down is faster but you need to watch our step on the unsealed and rocky path.

review_text: Brutal honesty time: I was having a rough stay in Santiago. There was an earthquake cluster, my dog was bit by a street dog, and I witness a brutal mugging. I had 0 interest in even leaving my rental apartment, and then I saw the reviews for this tour and thought, I literally have nothing to lose. The tour itself was AMAZING. It honestly made me like Santiago. There I said it. She turned around my entire stay here. I opted for a Saturday tour in English @ 10:00am and was greeted by Valentina. She immediately gave us the rundown / tour details and provided us with a map of Santiago. By the time the tour started, there were over 15 people in the group. Everyone was insanely friendly, and we all had a great time getting to know each other as we walked through the city cites. The tour itself lasted just over 4 hours and covered the history of the major sites, and the current political and social climate. The information Valentina provided was super palatable. She made the info memorable, so I feel like I not only learned something, but retained the information too. She's also super funny, and we spent a chunk of the tour laughing. She's fantastic at answering specific questions too. I could not recommend this tour enough. If you love Santiago, you'll love it more. If you're struggling and are frazzled from 83 earthquakes in a row, give this tour a shot. It'll change your entire perspective! Thank you Valentina!

review_text: Vina Casa Marin was our favourite place to stay in our tour of Chilean Vineyards. The guest house is situated in the middle of the vineyards, at least a couple of kilometres from any other building. It is on the top of the hill, which affords a wonderful view of the vineyard, valley and the ocean in the distance. And that's not the best part. That was Maria, who, for a very reasonable price, will cook a wonderful Chilean dinner for you, at the guest house. And then she comes back in the morning to make you a terrific breakfast. The house has 2 large bedrooms, with king beds in each, 2 seperate washrooms with showers in each, a large living room, an eating area, a kitchen and a nice deck with a hammock and a large sitting area. Casa Marin is also a winery, and has tours and tastings by Christine, who is very knowledgeable about wine, it's flavours and how it is made. And the Casa Marin wine is excellent. I would highly recommend Casa Marin, both as a place to stay, and to sample their wine. We are really pleased to read that your stay was good and that you enjoyed the Casa Marin experience. We hope to receive you again! Kindly, Hospitality Team.

review_text: We went on a day trip that took us south of San Petro de Atacama. We traveled through high desert at elevations up to 14,000ft, which is an adventure in itself. Depending on the location there could be no vegetation or low tufted grasss. Our route traveled along a huge salt field that stretched for over 100 kilometers. We saw lots of vicuña as well as a chilean Rhea, large rodent type animals, and finally flamingos. The flamingos were eating the brine shrimp that thrived in the very salty lagoon. This was a perfect place for a lunch stop although the wind can be very strong at times. There was the water of the lagoon, the flamingos and a type of black & white goose, as well as the volcanoes in the background. Very picturesque.

review_text: My wife and I were visiting friends in Santiago and needed something to do the one day they both had to work. We found Mick through our friends there and set up a trip to a vineyard and up in to the Andes mountains to Embalse de Yeso. We had such a great time! Mick was an outstanding guide! He took us to Aquitania vineyard where my wife and I got a private tour and tasting. After our fill of wine we jumped back in the truck and drove into the mountains. I wanted to do a little fishing so he made sure and brought some fishing gear, since I didn't travel with any. We didn't have any luck fishing but the view of the mountains reflecting off of the lake made up for it! He even brought a couple of stand up paddle boards for us to try out (though both my wife and I decided it was a little too cold and windy for us). Overall I would highly recommend Ride De Vuelta if you are looking for tours in and around Santiago. They offer a variety of tours and can customize them to accommodate you. And last, but definitely not least, Mick is an outstanding dude and it was a pleasure to spend the day with him. I look forward to going back to see what else Chile has to offer!
