review_text: I’m writing this review to make people aware of my experience as a cautionary tale to prevent tourists from becoming victims of a crime. Let me start by saying I am an airline worker based in the USA, and as such I have traveled extensively for over 27 years. I initiated my journey by car in Villarica, Chile crossing to Argentina. Upon arrival at the Argentinian crossing the guard was been nice and tried to speak English to the one English speaking only person in the car all other 4 were bilingual been Spanish the mother tongue. The officer asked if we were returning the same way a few times then proceeded to ask if we had something to declare all these at the first stop he speaking from his shelter to us in the car. We declared 3 cartons of cigarettes. We were told to proceed and leave the car open outside so they can inspect it and were told to go inside with our passports. We did everything got on our way arrived in San Martin and to our surprise the backpack where I had the cigarettes, together with other items like my airline badge, sida badge, car keys, beats headphones ,work phone was gone. I know it was there upon arrival at the Argentinean side as we have taken our passports (two US passports), from there. We went back we got no answers. So please take a picture of the items in your trunk before you arrived at the Argentinian check point and make sure you check your trunk and items before leaving. The backpack was a little open so they saw the cigarettes and that’s why I think they took the whole thing, and evidently no one will distrust the authorities specially customs agents stealing from tourists but I think they were confident that people won’t noticed until they are far from the border. I wish they would’ve taken the cigarrera only as it is a nightmare to replace the airport badge. Coming back to Chile via Cardenal Samoré was a completely different experience the process is to have the owner and occupants of the car present when they open the trunk for the search. Officer in Chile were very professional and the car search very transparent.

review_text: My girlfriend and I had a couple of days to spend in Santiago after coming back from Easter Island before heading back to Europe. We would realy like to see Valparaiso before leaving Chile and we found out that booking a day tour with Ecochile would be the perfect way to get to do this. Their website is very organized and easy to manouver. You book your tour through their very good onliune booking system. We booked and payed for a group tour, but on the morning of the actual day of departure we were picked up in a privet SUV by the greatest guide. We hit the road down to Cassablanca Valley, and started the day of by eating breakfast in a local driveby place which was realy bissy and had a nice atmosphere to it. Then we drove to our first destination which was the organic vinery of Emiliana. there we had a grat guided tour were we learned a lot about organic wine production. Then we had a wine tasting before heading down to Valparaiso. This strange city is a must see for everyone. Beautifull old arcitecture mixed together with new urban culture and a lot of musicians and artist make up this great city. The entire day was a great experience and our guide was realy nice and informative. It felt like we were on a roadtrip together with a friend. Sadly I dont remember your name because it is almost a year ago and you only got my contact information because you said you would get in touch, which you never did. So if you remeber the strange Norwegian couple that you drove down to Valparaiso in the end of January 2014 drop us a shout out. Thank you so much to the entire Ecochile team for giving us this great ending to our tour of Peru, Easter Island and Chile.

review_text: After meeting the 3:00 PM Tours 4 Tips guides in front of the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, our very large group was divided into smaller groups but our group was still too large. During our brisk walk, Oscar imparted a lot of information about the political, social and cultural history of Santiago and Chile with some personal commentary about the political situation in other countries. Unfortunately we missed pertinent information about certain sites because: 1. the group was too large; the guide's voice was drowned out by so much city noise. (this is where a wireless tour guide audio system would have greatly enhanced the tour) 2. while his English fluency is awesome,we found it difficult to understand his heavy accent at times. Near the end of the tour, Oscar took us on a short metro subway (our own expense) where our tour ended in the Lastarria neighborhood; Oscar gave us several good recommendations for restaurants and even one for an ice cream shop. Hi J A, Thanks so much for your feedback--it really means a lot to us and is very useful in helping us improve. I’m glad that you felt that Oscar knew a lot and was able to give you good information. At the same time, it sounds like there were a few, non-ideal issues with the tour. With respect to group size and not being able to hear the guide, it’s a combination of a few things. Every once in a while, the groups get large. It’s high season right now, so that sometimes is a difficult problem. We are always examining ways to make the tours more intimate and personalized, so we are very much aware of the problem with group sizes. Concerning the guide not being loud enough and his accent--I agree, those are definitely issues, and it’s good that you brought them to our attention. Those are also problems that we will surely look into. It's such a shame that this happened because our guides are all incredibly smart and know so much! But how will they be able to impart that amazing info if they can't be heard? We are a small, tourism startup with a firm belief in customer satisfaction; we don’t want your tour to simply be good, we want it to be enriching and unforgettable. I have to thank you for being honest in your feedback so we can continue working hard to make sure our tours are as incredible as they can be. Safe travels, Peter

review_text: Found this to be an excellent tour with Ignacio who walked us through every step in the wine making process. Have not ever seen the actual bottling of wine so this was interesting. At the end of the tour, (only four in our group) we got to taste three wines, two of which we purchased. Tour lasted about 1 1/2 hours. Just a few facts - 12,000 bottles are filled per hour, 80M per year with 60% exported. Plant is operational 24 hours a day from Monday to Saturday. Oak casks are purchased from America and France at a cost of $700 to $1,000, the more expensive being from France as the trees are older. They are only used three times and are then sold to smaller wineries. Waste products from the grapes, skins and pulp are returned to the vineyard as fertilizer. review_text: Before writing this review I went back to their web site to make sure I hadn't missed something about this tour and was shocked to find all the stellar reviews of this organization. We must have caught them on a bad day. We have found food tours to be a great way to sample and gain knowledge about the local food scene and have been on many in different parts of the world. We took the half day food tour and it was far and away the worst tour of its kind we have ever been on. To start, it was more walking than food sampling. We started at the Santiago fish and produce markets but did not enter those buildings, instead beginning a half mile journey to a hot dog stand. We ate a hot dog drowning in toppings. At the time I had no idea that would be the food highlight of the tour. We next walked to a small restaurant where we had a beer and two (each) of the same wafer sized Chilean appetizers. We finished at a wine bar for a flight of wine with no food. So to repeat, the food tour was a hot dog and two wafer sized appetizers per person. For $95? We had arrived for the tour hungry as we anticipated a lot of food samples. We ate immediately after the tour because we were still hungry. Our guide was a nice enough guy but he knew almost nothing about food. This tour is absolutely not worth the money it cost. I'm not sure what all the other reviewers of FoodyChile experienced but our tour was terrible and I could not recommend this tour if you are looking for an experience tasting the local cuisine of Chile. Thank you for your review, and sorry to hear that you had such a horrible time. That is not the idea by any means, and a stark contrast to the feedback we are accustomed to receiving. Just for clarity: you took the afternoon food & cultural walk, purchasing our small group special. The price reflects not just the food, but the guide and our overhead costs as a business, and keeping in mind that these are small groups, normally between 2-4 people. As far as the food, it includes a juice, then the hot dog, then a tapa style dish along with a craft beer, and finishes with a flight of three wines. We have always been concerned to offer just the right amount of food. In the end it is a mix of tasting, walking and talking. Getting the right mix so that you can still get in your dinner reservation at one of Santiago’s restaurants, usually a highlight for our customers, is always a challenge, and the nearly unanimous feedback we have received from customers on this tour is that it is just enough. After speaking with the guide who led the tour, we are a bit perplexed as to why you found it “terrible”. Maybe the fact that you had to wait an extra 10 minutes or so while another couple showed up weighed in on that, and set things off to a bad start. It was a hot day, and yes there it is a walking tour as it says in the description on our webpage where you booked the tour. The hot dogs do have lots of condiments, that is the style here in Chile, actually there are many places where it is even more extreme. But in the end the idea is to show the local food just as it is consumed by residents. The final stop we generally do without food, but the guide is instructed, and in this case did ask, if you feel you want some more samples. According to him, you passed because you already had a reservation at the same wine bar, and were actually planning to eat afterwards from the start. And it would be good to know exactly why you say the guide “knows nothing about food”. He has years of hospitality experience and has been doing tours with us since we started four years ago, and with repeat customer praise both for his knowledge on food, Chilean culture and history, and also his ability to adapt to the different tastes of our different customers. According to him the group as a whole discussed food throughout the tour, so it would be good to know exactly what causes you to feel this way. I can only think that this is largely a result of much different expectations. I am going to review the description and adjust to avoid these results in the future. Our apologies it did not go as you had envisioned. And we do encourage customers to send a quick email if they want to discuss the elements of any of our activities, and consider a private tour if you want something with more flexibility and tailored to specific requests, needs or tastes.

review_text: Incredible! Three floors. Start on 2. Go to -1. Then to 1 where temporary exhibits are shown. The 2nd floor has amazing works from Pre-Columbian America, from Mexico to the Straits of Magellan. Inca, Aztec, Toltec, Olmec, Maya, Nazca, name it--they got it. The first gallery you enter is the Masterpieces, and they're not kidding. But, not necessarily the most interesting items in their collection. Just depends on what strikes your fancy, Outside of this gallery, on 2 which covers the Americas and -1 which focusses on Chile, you might encounter: A collection of ceramic coqueros from various cultures. Coqueros? Ah, that would be coke addicts, specifically coca leaf chewers. The decapitators. 'Nuff said. Genuine Inca quipu. The Inca were like a New World version of Romans except for a 100% lack of Virgils, Tacituses, Augustine's and Marcus Aureliuses, for the simple reason that the Inca never had an reading or writing (arithmetic they had). Instead they had quipu, knotted strings whose meaning changed based on the number, type, color and position of knots. But quipu was not a written language: it was more of an aide memoire, to support spoken messages. Once everyone who had heard the spoken message died, the "reading" of the quipu died with them. But for whatever it's worth, among this museum's collection of quipu is one that's got over 15,000 pieces of data on it. Americans had mummies 700 years older that the earliest known Egyptian mummy: there's one on 2 and several more on -1. Textiles--fabulous textiles. One is three-dimensional: the nose sticks out from the face. Incredible colors and patterns! On -1 you get some impressive glimpses of the Mapuche culture of Southern Chile. The Incas tried their hand at conquering the Mapuche; they lost. The Spanish sent in troops throughout the colonial period; they lost. The Mapuche are still there, on their ancestral land, doing very well, thank you. Oh, somewhere or other they have an entire display case devoted to shamanistic psychodelic-mystical kits. We used to just call it paraphernalia, and to tell you the truth I didn't see a single pack of Zig-Zags in the case! . Seriously, Olmec, Maya, Nasca, you name it--this museum has an incredible with great curatorship and very good interpretations and explanations of the collection in both Spanish and English. Plan to spend an entire morning or afternoon. This is an outstanding collection, but as always, the more you put in, the more you get out.

review_text: Yes, there are more comfortable busses, and cheaper ways to go to San Pedro de Atacama. But this is a very original way, and it leads you to places you wouldn't be able to reach with public transport. For me the best was the boat trip to see whales, dolphins, penguins and sea lions, and the stops in the desert. If you want, they book accommodation for you, and it's always acceptable low budget places. They also stop at supermarkets to allow for self-catering. Groups are not larger than 15, that makes good travel company. We had an excellent driver, Pedro, who was also very knowledgeable about everything from history to mineralogy, and a friendly and entertaining guide, Matteo. We had a lot of fun together. We chose to go only to San Pedro and then stay there some days (the two-nights stay Pachamama offers is far too short), and then flew back to Santiago - that way we could view the desert from the air, which was wow.

review_text: My husband and I did the four-day fjord trip this past fall. I hate writing this review, but we didn't have a great experience, and I want to be honest. While there were definitely good things about our trip with Yak, if I could go back and choose not to go, I would. Thus, my two star rating. When you go out paddling, the first thing you do is flip your kayak. You’re freezing and soaking wet and you stay that way all day. (It didn’t help that my husband got sick with fever for two of the days.) While the scenery is stunning, it’s hard to enjoy when you’re absolutely freezing and hardly moving. You’re in the ocean, not a fast-flowing river. You see pretty much the same thing you see from the camp site. And the camp site….your campsite two of the nights is on a farm, next to a farm house, sheep, barns, etc. You’re in someone’s yard. You eat your meals on those nights in the house. While I would have preferred real camping, the two women that live in the house and host dinner are awesome! They are so cute and hospitable. Since we weren’t enjoying paddling, we asked Juan if we could try to rent a local fishing boat so we could see more of the landscape and fjords than we would be able to in a kayak. We did have to pay extra for it, but it was worth it. Juan was generally a likable, funny guy, but when we asked to change our itinerary, he seems a little bit offended. It got awkward. From our experience and the cost of this trip, I would not personally recommend Yak Expediciones. I know many others have had great experiences, so please take that into account as well. Hola , I really appreciate your feedback and we will work to improve the experience of our future participants. As the owner of the company and your trip leader this time , once i I read your comments , I felt very surprised as we have been runnning trips in this area since 1998 , with more than 10-12 trips a year , for almost 15 years and most of our participants return very happy with their experience with us , as you can confirm reading the other Tripadvisor comments. - Expensive ? a) The whole trip (4 days , All Inclusive, transportation to a remote area, ferries , insurance, guide, paddling instruction, all the food, paddling gear , tent, hotsprings, wine, hike to a National Park, etc.. ) was run… just for the 2 of them, like a …. private trip. They new the cost in advance , the característics of the trip (trekking in a National Park an seakayaking the Patagonia fjords) , what was included, and it´s requirements in advance. We also had a pre-trip meeting the day before the trips starts , where every detail was clearly explained and answered all the questions. We always encourage our potential clients to check ou Facebook page where we publish most of our trips so they can have a better idea of what to expect….to avoid surprises. https://www.facebook.com/yak.expediciones?ref=tn_tnmn#!/media/set/?set=a.10151556515364244.1073741831.826984243&type=1 b) ….until " they decided " not to continue… the program was being run according to what we offer . As soon as I knew their decisión not to conitune paddling more , inmediately I try to offer an alternative plan and it was to visit a different area of the fjords , far from where we were , but it will be need to rent a boat ( not included in the program they choose ) . It is not easy to do this kind of things in the middle of the fjords(telehones doesnt exist) but luckily i have a good network of local friends and was solved very fast , not loosing time , offering them a very good option to navigate and explore " more of the area " . Of course the price I obtain from my local friend was extremely cheap. - Wet ? -The weather conditions we had were average (some days of very good sun and some fays of some kind of rain) as you can see in the photos in YAK EXPEDICIONES Facebook. -We sent previously a detailed "gear list" so with that gear they can feel confortable in our conditions (but it seems was not considered seriously). - we sent in advance , an many times, a link to the weather forecast (it also appears in the program of ther trip) …to avoid surprises and to come prepared - we lend them 2 wetsuits at "no extra charge" (they were not included) so they can enjoy more the "Northern Patagonia Fjords". I have to borrow them from a friend If you choose to visit Patagonia, you have to be properly prepared for the conditions of the area (weather, changing conditions , limitations ,..) but mainly with apositive attitude always for unexpected situations. For us safety is very important so , at no extra charge , all our participants " are taught and participate in a practice " where they learn some paddling and rescue strokes in the sea (wet-exit and assited rescues). In this case they flip only once (with wetsuits) and inmediately we keep paddling. We had only sun that day. - Many emails where sent to her "before" the trip starts asking if she has any questions , insist to read carefully the "program" she choose , read the "conditions section" , where appears a section about "what we expect of our participants" , and to "come properly prepared for the rain" as " they choose " to do activities in PATAGONIA" (where normally can rain even in summer , and where facilities are very limited). - Some days "before" the trip starts , even thought it was clearly specified in the program that exist a practice day in the sea , I sent her an email insiting that " we will have a practice day , and we willl flip on purpose , meaning that everything will be wet, and that´s why we ask for 2 fleece jackets" . After the practice we normally paddle to an island where were we enjoy some hotsprings and also was an option to carry a bag with dry gear if they want. About the campsite : As you can see in our Facebook page , their trip photos shows a campsite in the local family property , with a a spectacular view of the fjords , in a clear and dry ground, instead of camping in the beach , exposed over the rocks. If we eat in the house was to make more intense the inteaction with the local culture having the possibility to see how is the life in this part of the world (and have a bathroom inside , protected from the rain, if it rains). It is important to consider that this trip was " choosen by them " after reading it´s detailed description. It clearly specifies that this trip wants to show not only a nice landscape but also "how this people leaves in this remote locations...without make-up…an authentic experience". It says in the link of the program , in black letters : Our trips not only will take you through an inspiring scenery , but you will go home with fond memories of the time you spend with the local fishing pioneers families (colonos) in their own surroundings and how they live , plus first hand experience of the local fishing industry. Also says: DAY 1: In the afternoon we will setup our campsite in front of the sea , in the property of a family of "colonos" (pioneers of this area) having the opportunity to see and feel how people of this remote locations live. Another example that we always wanted to help that they have a great experiece was that even their flight was delayed the first day , we re-organize our timetable so it can fit with their new availability. Also the last day (day 4) we change our driving route back and did a hike to see some Alerce trees , that were not included in the original program, as was their final decisión for day 1 to change the original program and not to do a hike the first day to a National Reserve in order to paddle more. After looking the photos taken during their trip , that anyone can see in our Facebook page , you can see that they where properly dress for the activity with the gear we supply and lend , that the campsite at the local family had a spectacular view of the fjords , in a flat and dry ground , but mainly it seems that they had a good experience (at least him).

review_text: This ' navigation' starts with a half hour walk from the car park to the beach where the boat docks. The main goal is to see the glacier at the other end of the lake, although the boat is also used as a ferry for people who want to go waling or camping at the far end of the lake. Unfortunately, the weather was miserable with persistent rain and low cloud. The cabin of the boat is reasonable and a drinks voucher is given to you, to use on the trip. The interesting thing about the voyage is the number of mini-icebergs floating on the lake, some of which we were given close-up views. It took about half an hour to get close to the glacier and we spent a long time looking at it from every conceivable angle that the boat could safely negotiate. Photography was difficult due to the awful conditions, the greatest challenge being to keep the lens dry. I am sure that it would be great in pleasant weather.

review_text: The Santiago subway system is a great way to explore the city and very inexpensive. We stayed in hotel Solace right next to the Metro stop p. de valdivia and we took the Metro each day we skiied to Escualer militare then walked a few blocks to 'ski total' here we rented skis and took the van to the slopes. We visited in late August 2016 at the time chilean pesos 650clp =$1 us. The metro runs every few minutes, which is good because at rush hour, when we traveled, you might not get on the first train be prepared to be a 'New Yorker' and hustle your way in to the train, it was packed like sardines each way and with a back pack and ski boots, quite a squeeze! At the Metro you can buy a ticket for a one way trip (660clp one way, 770clp during rush hour) which you slip into the gate like a slot machine to let you through, or better still buy a BIP card. We used the manned agents to buy a BIP but there are machines, though a little confusing of you don't speak Spanish. The card costs 1500clp to buy, then you load it with the amount you need (note the minimum load is 1000clp) you use the card to pass the gates so we used one card for two people and scanned it twice. review_text: With only being in Santiago for a few days my wife and I thought this tour would be a great way to see parts of Santiago we might not visit on our own. It also appealed as it wasnt your typical museum/government building style of tour (they offer this in the afternoon tour). As the name suggests the tour is free and if you were happy with the guide you can tip him at the end. We were not disappointed. After a short overview of the city and some of its history we went out to the fish market and La Vega central which were absolutely buzzing. A real insight into how the people of Santiago live. We visited the cemetery which seems to be a day out for locals. After the tour we had a drink called Terramoto which was local wine mixed with pineapple ice cream. We were happy with the tour so gave the guide a nice tip at the end. We then went back to La Vega central for lunch in the market. This is not something many tourists get to do so was an amazing experience and made better by the guide Carlos joining us. We would definitely recommend the tour to anyone visiting the city for a short time.

review_text: My hotel arranged this for me last minute, so I shouldn't have expected much. I was told the tour would be in English. It was actually a tourist trap where we were repeatedly encouraged to buy things. No explanation of anything, just shop. Off to Vina del Mar. Next stop - 30 minutes at an empty stadium in a park. No information, no signs. But good thing we were there for half an hour. Same thing at a beach, and then lunch at an overpriced restaurant. It was about 5 hours before we got to Valparaiso and even then, it was more time in the bus. At the end of the day, the bus was comfortable and it was an easy way to get to Valpo. But I wouldn't recommend this to anyone who actually wants to learn something.

review_text: HIGHLY RECOMMEND! This was an incredibly enjoyable tour with Valeska. Her command of the three languages (English, Spanish and Portuguese) and the fluidity in which she kept all of us apprised and informed no matter which language we understood. Her pacing was ideal and since the tour company keeps the group small up to 15 people, it was quite easygoing. It was also perfect for keeping tabs on everyone. The wine tasting was simple and either you like the white and/or red wine or you didn’t. I personally found them a bit too strong and oaky, but not to worry, you can still enjoy this portion of the tour by visiting the docile llamas and the roosters, hens and its chicks. The drive to get to the locations are long, but Valeska keeps it light with interactive banter and animated personality. We were also kept apprised of where to meet and when in case we wander away from the group or get caught up in the scenery. The vehicle is a Mercedes-Benz Sprinter van. Please note that the seats are packed very close; airplane seat spacing seems like a step up with spacing comparatively. For those who are taller, the seats at the end of some of the rows have no seat obstructing leg room and the first row of passenger seats have a little more leg room. I’m only 5’ but my knees touched the back of the seat in front of me. Wiggling down the row was a bit awkward and annoying, but the seats are comfortable. We saw so many colorful murals of various types and Valeska provided us background on some of the styles and murals which was fascinating to learn. Numerous vantage points for panoramic view of the city and the ocean. Valeska also makes a strong concerted effort to play cameraman for anyone in the group to ask! review_text: I am an expat who has been living for 15 years in Chile. I often take clients of my winery on the Tours 4 Tips walking tour of Valparaiso where I live but recently I did the Santiago walking tour for the first time with my girlfriend. From the get go it was very well organised with the arrival of our two Wallies at 9:45am. The group was separated into English and Spanish speakers (we jumped in with the latter group) and we left at 10am on the dot. Our Wally took us around some interesting sites in downtown Santiago with an excellent explanation at each stop. We then hit Mercado Central (the main seafood market) and then continued on to La Vega (the main fruit and veggie market). The guides did a great job of explaining the different areas of the market together with how to buy from the vendors. Finishing the tour of the market we were treated to a gigantic sopaipilla (deep fried pumpkin bread) before we jumped on the subway to Santiago's main cemetary. Our guide then gave us a fascinating tour of the more interesting tombs accompanied by a very good explanation of some of the more peculiar traditions of the Chileans when it comes to asking the dead to grant miracles. Finishing the tour we retired to a nearby restaurant where we were treated to a local cocktail, the infamous "terremoto". Overall a great experience and in spite of all my years in Chile where was still abundant interesting information which made it a fully worthwhile experience. Next time I'm in the capital I will most definitely make time to do the afternoon tour!!! Mr. Ruprekt2015, thanks for your extended prose on how our team show off what we love most, the locals, Chileans, the culture. It is hard to impress a 15 year old expat (you are probably older than that), so those words alone stand out as a seal of approval that we are headed down the right road. Saludos a ti, Grant, Abrazos desde Santiago, Peter

review_text: Read the reviews and curiosity got the best of us: we chose a Sunday to visit on our last week in Santiago. Take the metro and get off at the franklin stop- just follow the crowd and yellow brick road of vendors at the start of market with stuff laid out on blankets for sale. You will love the market if you are a flea market enthusiast, if you wanted to know where all the metal signs, posters or flip phones have landed. If you are looking for high dollar items and fancy settings, you will be disappointed. I enjoyed the outdoor vendors and bartering for price. There are large warehouses with hundreds of stalls selling items in addition to the outside vendors. This continues for several blocks. One warehouse on Placer advertises antiques and 16 restaurants. We went in for coffee and elected to order food. The name of the place is Donde Chile. We ordered a churrasco italian style sandwich. Delicious- enough for 2 people and wonderful service including large cups for coffee and tea.

review_text: I fell in love with this lake. It's breathtakingly beautiful. You've got the Osorno Volcano on one side, dark green trees covering the steep mountains on the other, and turquoise blue waters in the center. Bring your camera. And your lunch. A picnic on the sand by the lake is therapeutic. I did a solo hike on the Isolation Trail whose entrance is just a short walk from the lake. As a relatively novice hiker, it was challenging for me, but I thoroughly enjoyed it. I was there during the off season, so I hardly ran into anybody on the trail. I probably took 200+ photos - it's quite a photogenic walk with snow-capped Osorno to the west and Todos Los Santos to the east. It's not recommended to do the entire trail if it's cloudy or foggy, but there's a shorter version you can do that doesn't climb up towards the volcano. The last bus back to Puerto Varas leaves at 6pm from the lake.

review_text: We rented bikes to get to Laguna Cejar, for the views and for the floating! It is about 18km from San Pedro on a road that can at times be very rough. However, it's mostly flat and not too difficult. My girlfriend and I are in decent shape, but we don't bike much and the altitude in San Pedro was affecting us a bit (I know it's not that high up there, but still more than we're used to), but we still did the ride in just a little more than an hour. Go early to avoid the crowds and tours. Speaking of which, I don't know how much the tours cost, but they are probably not worth it; we watched one tour arrive, get herded to the lagoon, change, spend about 10 minutes in the water, and then get herded back. Definitely better to get there yourself, either in car (have 4 wheel drive) or on bike. There are actually 3 lagoons in the area. Laguna Cejar and one other (can't remember the name) aren't for swimming, but the other is. We were lucky enough to see a couple of flamingos as well. The "swimming" (floating) was a ton of fun! You don't even have to tread water; try as hard as you can to sink, and you just bob around, with your full shoulders out of the water. Cold, but hey, it's a desert so it feels kind of nice. As some have mentioned, the entry is a bit pricey at 15,000 CLP, but the facilities are really nice and they have showers to rinse the salt off after swimming (you'll definitely want to). Also, it is run by the indigenous community, so you're helping to support something worthwhile.

review_text: This hike in Chilean Patagonia is justifiably famous. The mountains of Torres del Paine are dramatically beautiful. The camp sites and Refugios make the multi-day hike quite comfortable if your knees and ankles are in good shape. The altitude is low – less than 5000’ – so that is not a factor. We used EcoLodge as our starting point, and then as a base for three nights at the end. We hiked east to west, ending at Lago Grey. We then had a boat ride to the glacier face and then back to a point where our bus could pick us up for the return to Eco Lodge. We then had 3 more nights there, with one of two days for the hike up Ascension Valley. This is the most dramatic part of the W hike, and having two days available for it improves the odds of seeing it clear of clouds. The group that went the first day had good weather and excellent views, those of us who went the second day found the valley filled with cloud and winds strong enough to have me hunkered down and grabbing rocks to hold on to at times. We had to turn back that day. For the 3 day hike from EcoLodge to Lago Grey, we just carried the items we needed during the day, and our items needed at night were ferried for us each day to meet us at the refugios. That certainly kept our packs light, but it does limit your options. My wife and I backpack each year, but did not do that here. The refugios provide a bed, shower and meals, but are pretty basic. You can drink water from the streams here, a real treat. Our trip was organized through a company called Adventure Life, who set up lodgings and our excellent guide, Diego Aldrete. I don’t usually hike with a guide, but he was great – identifying peaks, telling about the climbing history in the area, identifying some of the birds, plants, trees. He also taped people’s feet if they were developing hot spots. Between the rocky terrain and the fierce, gusty wind, hiking poles are a big help here. I hiked in low top stiff hiking shoes with gaiters (to keep out water AND pebbles and dirt). I recommend a stiff sole, as you will be stepping on lots of irregular rocks. WARNING about horses. some in our group tried to do the horses for the day, going up Ascencio Valley. They were to be there at 9:00 for 9:30 departure. They left more than an hour late, and in fact were too slow to get to the wonderful view at the top. I would avoid the horses if you want to get to the dramatic view. The drive from Torres del Paine in Chile to El Calafate or El Chalten in Argentina takes most of a day, but is quite do-able. You are not actually crossing the Andes on that drive, as Torres del Paine has the flat grassland just to the east of you. Drive east and north through relatively flat country and you are in Argentina. There may be public buses. We had a van hired for our group.

review_text: I originally planned on using Turistik for one day tour (Valparaiso and Vina del Mar) and booked this a couple of weeks prior to leaving for my holiday. At the airport waiting to board my flight I thought perhaps I'd be better to arrange an airport transfer for my arrival into Santiago rather than battle with a taxi and my lack of Spanish. So booked an airport transfer quite last minute, and got confirmation straight away. On arrival at the airport, I headed to the desk and was helped straight away, and as my flight had been delayed, my originally planned (tips only) walking tour of the city was going to leave before I got to my hotel, so I booked the hop-on-hop-off bus tour for that afternoon as well. Got all the information and made payment quickly, and the man assisting me took me out to the kerbside and helped me find the minivan I needed to get to, and I was on my way to the hotel. The driver didn't speak English, but I was able to simply hand him the hotel confirmation which had the address on it, and it all went into the GPS - no problems! review_text: Our group of 9 travelers (55-70 years old) spent two days with Chile Nativo while in Patagonia. I am glad we did these activities, they gave us much more of an idea of how the local ranchers live and a more intimate view of the animals that live in Patagonia. I would highly recommend Chile Nativo to anyone wanting a tour that respects the land and the animals of this unique ecosystem.

review_text: We had a great time at Punta Choros; some directions are below because it can be confusing. The drive after you leave Ruta 5 is a VERY bumpy dirt road, so keep that in mind when taking a car. You want to head towards the water (there is a pier on Google Maps, this is where you want to go). There will be plenty of signs leading you to the penguins. Once inside the fenced-off area on the water, go to the Tickets booth (Billetos) on the right (to the left of the bathrooms (Banos)). Here you will purchase tickets for the boat *only* (we found this out the hard way). They were 10,000CLP per person. Then, you must go to the CONAF (this is essentially the national park service) area; these are reddish wood cabins to your left once you enter the fenced-off area (past a bunch of vendor/food stalls). Here you will buy entrance tickets to the park: 6000CLP for non-Chilean adults, 3000 CLP for Chilean adults. Make sure to get these two different tickets! Then go to the pier and wait at the land-end (this part is a bit confusing). Someone will collect your boat tickets (we had little tiles with the name of the boat and a number) and you will board a small boat, roughly 10 people. The boat will take you across the water to Isla Choros and travel around the island (you may get splashed a bit). The guide pointed out various animals (though all in Spanish), and we saw a dolphin, penguins, sea lions, pelicans, and various other types of birds. Then the boat takes you to Isla Damas, where you can disembark – this is where they will take your ticket for CONAF. We had about 45 minutes to explore the island (make sure you confirm the return time with your guide). There is a mirador (lookout point) which takes about 5 minutes to climb up to, and a trail around that island that takes about 40 minutes to walk. We saw a lot of nesting seagulls and some seagull chicks, and some other birds, but no penguins here. Then you get back on the boat and return to Punta Choros. All in all, a fun trip! I would brush up on your basic Spanish phrases, as we didn't talk to anyone who spoke English.

review_text: If god created the world in 7 days, he would have spent at 3-4 days creating Lauca. The magic on the way there and once you get to the lake is majestic. We booked the 1 day tour from Arica and paid 20,000 Pesos. We picked the right agency too because the bus had a toilet and it paid off as our altitude-affected friends had the opportunity to go there once the altitude overwhelmed them. One of the first stops we made was near a historical church in Poconchile. There, you will find vendors selling their crafts. Go straight up to them and slide 500 pesos in their shorts and walk away with the famous coca leaf. When you get on the bus, chew on it to release the juices which will aid you on the 4500 meter above sea level journey. If you've had altitude sickness like myself and want to avoid it at all costs. Try to avoid - cheese, yogurt, milk, coffee, a big breakfast & alcohol. Most of the people suffered at least a headache so take precautions as we start driving off from 500m to 4500m until we get to the lake. The wildlife is amazing... We also went past hieroglyphs, the magnetic field road, the one baby a year rabbit, alpacas, vicunas, condor, the national deer etc. Highly Recommended!

Marcelo was a great support with empathy and good vibes, he gave us ideas and organized our schedule by day and time, giving advice on each tour. Our second and third tour was to the Puritama Hot Springs where Juan, knowledgeable about the path, guided us with precision and tranquility giving directions allowing us to enjoy the pools. I will always remember his love for that greenish chirihue that perched on the car, at night we took the astronomical tour. They picked us up at 11 at night, Manuel our guide showed his love for astronomy, showing us the constellations and suggesting an app on the tour group's WhatsApp to learn more about the movement of the stars. Also, the photography that I worked on for 3 days is majestic (he is an astrophotographer!) Also grateful for Carla and the preparation of the cocktail in the middle of the cold desert. Seeing the stars with their support is a great memory, even though the cold of June was felt by some people, with their warmth they made me and my friend go to sleep thinking about the stars. The fourth Tour we went Trekking under the Puritama Hot Springs, Saraha our guide went to look for us with a smile to accompany us to the fall of the hot springs, thanks to her we saw vizcachas for the first time on the tour and she took great care of the group, especially those of us who had problems with walking among the rocks. She was even prepared with material to find new animals. We were looking forward to seeing Loa toads, but it is not Sarah's fault but rather the mining industry's fault that we are not able to see as many of them as before. The fifth Tour was to the Ruta de los Salares with Andre and Cesar at 7 am, with both of them we discovered Vicuñas, Guanacos, more Chinchillas and birds that lived more than 3000 meters above the sea. Breakfast was perfect to have energy for the morning and be prepared for the wind and lunch too. Finally, the red stones tour at 6 in the morning. Pedro the guide and Victor made this magical experience with all their energy in the middle of the madrigada while they made us excited by the appearance of the sun on the Licancabur hill. We managed to see Suris (something that is very difficult), Andean donkeys and Famencos. It is a beautiful and long tour, but it was shortened by the good vibes of both. Pedro put his signature on this tour by helping to make videos for the tourists, raising their energy and introducing us to Macarron, an adorable dog where we had lunch. His eyes lit up talking about the region and its beauty. Honestly, we closed the trip of a week with this trip. The whole experience was magical, really all the guides made the name of the agency make sense: Connection with the Atacama region.

I will always remember his love for that greenish chirihue that perched on the car, at night we took the astronomical tour. They picked us up at 11 at night, Manuel our guide showed his love for astronomy, showing us the constellations and suggesting an app on the tour group's WhatsApp to learn more about the movement of the stars. Also, the photography that I worked on for 3 days is majestic (he is an astrophotographer!) Also grateful for Carla and the preparation of the cocktail in the middle of the cold desert. Seeing the stars with their support is a great memory, even though the cold of June was felt by some people, with their warmth they made me and my friend go to sleep thinking about the stars. The fourth Tour we went Trekking under the Puritama Hot Springs, Saraha our guide went to look for us with a smile to accompany us to the fall of the hot springs, thanks to her we saw vizcachas for the first time on the tour and she took great care of the group, especially those of us who had problems with walking among the rocks. She was even prepared with material to find new animals. We were looking forward to seeing Loa toads, but it is not Sarah's fault but rather the mining industry's fault that we are not able to see as many of them as before. The fifth Tour was to the Ruta de los Salares with Andre and Cesar at 7 am, with both of them we discovered Vicuñas, Guanacos, more Chinchillas and birds that lived more than 3000 meters above the sea. Breakfast was perfect to have energy for the morning and be prepared for the wind and lunch too. Finally, the red stones tour at 6 in the morning. Pedro the guide and Victor made this magical experience with all their energy in the middle of the madrigada while they made us excited by the appearance of the sun on the Licancabur hill. We managed to see Suris (something that is very difficult), Andean donkeys and Famencos. It is a beautiful and long tour, but it was shortened by the good vibes of both. Pedro put his signature on this tour by helping to make videos for the tourists, raising their energy and introducing us to Macarron, an adorable dog where we had lunch. His eyes lit up talking about the region and its beauty. Honestly, we closed the trip of a week with this trip. The whole experience was magical, really all the guides made the name of the agency make sense: Connection with the Atacama region.

review_text: I spent 5 days in this amazing park but will definitely try to get back again to spend more time. I did the "W" hike and had a great time. The range seems like something out of a Tolkein novel. I kept expecting to see and elf in the forests or a dwarf pop out of the mountain. The hike itself isn't very difficult. Like any outdoors trip, you want to know what you are doing, but this one is accessible to just about anyone who is physically able to carry their own gear for 4-5 days. The trip can easily be broken up into ~15 km days, leaving the bulk of your gear at lower elevations. However if you've done much trecking before, you'll enjoy camping up the valleys at Campiamento Britanico and Campiamento Torres. This time I did it solo and met many great people at the campgrounds. However next time I'm bringing someone with me and doing the full circuit.

review_text: Going surfing with Yoyo was one of the best things I did on my backpacking trip through South America. With him you will get so much more than just a normal surfing lesson, he shows you what the real surfing life is like. He's a great, experienced guy that knows a lot about surfing. On my first day of surfing Yoyo came to our hostel and picked me and some friends up in his surfing van. We spent the whole day at the beach, learned how to surf, sunbathed and we had an amazing barbeque. It was just perfect! I had never tried to surf before. But Yoyo made me feel really comfortable on the board and in the water so thanks to him I learned how to surf and connect with the ocean. The spot where he teaches how to surf is perfect for beginners. The waves are small and in Arica the sun is always shining. Another great thing about the spot is that while in the water you'll be able to take a close look on the big sea turtles swiming around just next to you! review_text: This is an unusual museum, jammed into a corner of an industrial estate on the edge of Punta Arenas just off Ruta 9. Several historical vessels, associated with the region and with historical figures like Magellan, Darwin and Shackleton, have been recreated at full scale and visitors can explore them freely. Clambering onto these cramped and fragile decks a stone's throw from the Magellan Straits really brings history to life. The museum is a work in progress with HMS Beagle accessible but still under construction. English-language audio commentary was available only for the centrepiece, the Nao Victoria. Shackleton's modified, ocean-going lifeboat has to be seen for his feats to be believed. The entry fee was a bargain and included a hot drink. Overall, I'd love to see this museum survive and thrive. Thanks for visiting the museum, effectively for 3.5 years we have built the HMS Beagle, it is the first replica escale 1: 1 worldwide, and we hope to complete it in 1.5 years more, thanks for your kind words , give me courage to continue this personal challenge.

review_text: I booked two tours with Flamingo: the Laguna Cejar & El Tatio Geyers. At first we we're skeptical of the Laguna tour as the park enterance fee was steep ($17000 CLP) on top of the tour fee. However, our guide Kevin and team knocked it out of the park! My girlfriend and I were the only English speakers on the tour that day and our Spanish is okay but not good enough for long scientific explanations. Kevin took us aside whenever he could and explained his whole speel over again to us in english and was very enthusiastic the whole time. One thing I would recommend on this tour is to be prepared to get in the water! There is a sunken salt pool halfway through that you had to jump into which was fun... Also made for great action shots. The Laguna itself afterwards was also super fun to float around in. The sunset probably took the cake as it was absolutely breath-taking. 5/5 for sure (maybe not recommend if you didn't get in the water though) The next morning we did the El Tatio Geyers. Our guide was amazing and even took us off course at one point for a 20 min hike of a beautiful waterfall. Her English was great, just as our other tour. The Geyers were neat (very cold outside though ..-10C) and the thermal springs were rewarding. Breakfast surpassed my expectations as well. Baguette, cheese, jam, salami, eggs, coffee, and tea. For these two tours, the prices are exactly the same as all the other companies we price checked and they did an excellent job overall! So I would recommend checking them out. Pro tip: Always ask for what their rock bottom price are if you pay cash!

review_text: We're an active, retired couple who arrived in Arica on Oceania's Sirena for one day in late November 2017. Arica has a sunny and warm desert climate so we were looking for a fun outdoor activity instead of the usual ship's bus tours. We contacted Alejandro, the owner of Norte Outdoor, by email, several months in advance to reserve a kayak tour. He responded immediately to our many questions and we arranged to meet him at the cruise terminal immediately after our ship docked (09:00). Kayak tours are only available in mornings because that's when the sea is reliably calm. David is just learning English so he brought along his colleague, Francisco, who translated everything for us. Both of these young men have business degrees and are consultants to small business owners. They are smart, reliable, and personable, --- and love outdoor sports. Norte Outdoor is a fairly new business venture for them and they are working hard to find ways to attract North American tourists in addition to their usual Latin American customers. Alejandro and Francisco met us at the cruise terminal at the exact time we requested. They drove us to a small, sheltered beach where it was easy to launch the kayaks. The kayaks, paddles, and life jackets were all in excellent condition. We received adequate instruction on how to use the kayaks. There was good emphasis on safety throughout the tour. We were surprised at how comfortable it was to sit in their vinyl kayaks. We paddled west for an hour and talked to Francisco about geography, history, economics, and culture on the way. Our first stop (off shore) was at two small islands which were inhabited by sea lions, ---- one huge male on each island, accompanied by dozens of females. Next, we visited another small island to see pelicans and other sea birds. The island was white because it was covered in guano. Lastly, we paddled by some of the Anzota caves. Our tour was supposed to be just kayaking for two hours. However, when we got back to the launching beach, Alejandro said he would take us into the Anzota caves. Most of these caves are huge, and interconnected, and were inhabited by local Indian tribes centuries ago. The Chilean government is in the process of developing them as a major tourist attraction. We spent almost an hour walking along the beach and into two of the caves. We had a fabulous morning. It was fun, informative, and very good exercise. Alejandro and Franciso were very generous with their time. They took photos of us and will be sending them to us by email. They exceeded our expectations. (And the tour cost about 20% of the cost of any of the ship's tours.) If you're looking for an alternative to the usual ship's bus tours, we would highly recommend Norte Outdoor's kayak tour. review_text: Valpo is known for cultural position within Chile and therein you find rooted one of Chile's two Noble Winners, Pablo Neruda. To visit this wonderful city he loved so very much and not spend some time at La Sebastiana, his Valpo home of choice, is to have deprived yourself of an essential connection to this special city on the Pacific Ocean. The Museum House (Casa Museo) consist of some 5 floors and the entire complex has been restored and now offered portable translations in several languages, a small restuarant is also on site but the true Gift is is moving about each floor and placing yourself back in the time of this wonderful gift to humanity. Strongly recommended.

review_text: The service provided by Patricio Jr was exceptional from the moment he proposed a 2.5-day itinerary for a group of 4 of us. He ensured that we cover all the beautiful landscapes of Atacama, flora and fauna, experience sunrise, sunset, moonrise and he is happy to share his photography tips, as well as taking photos for us. We loved the tranquility of Chaxa lagoon, a national reserve for the flamingos. Patricio planned it well by being the first to arrive in the morning where flamingos are more concentrated and water are calm, creating mirror images for amazing photo opportunities. Patricio prepared delicious breakfasts nicely set up in beautiful landscapes and provided hot coffee/tea for cold & windy days. I am amazed at how much Atacama can offer in terms of landscapes – saltflats, lagoons, mountain ranges, volcanoes, craters, ice geyser, etc and the landscape and vegetation changes above 4000m (Andes mountains with blue skies). The moonrise and astrophotography are unique experiences. Patricio has special apps that provide timing of moonrise and milkyway and the best location for those. We had a spectacular moonrise, but not quite the right timing for milkyway, which I will return for it, given the opportunity. I have gained quite a lot of photography tips from Patricio and he is ever willing to impart his knowledge. Highly recommended! Review of: Private Atacama Photo tours

review_text: My experience with FlaviaBia was incredible! We went to Atacama and Uyuni. In Atacama we did Valley of the Moon, Hidden Lagoons, Astronomical Tour, Pedras Rojas and Lagoas Altiplanicas and Geiser del Tatio. In Uyuni we did the 4 days and 3 nights tour. I chose to go with FlaviaBia because I wanted a reliable agency for the tours, especially the one to Uyuni and I had seen several positive opinions about it on social media. Best choice I made. The tours are organized with great care and affection (my husband and I had dietary restrictions that they took care of at all times, at every meal). The food prepared by FlaviaBia is wonderful (the best food I ate on the entire trip), both in Atacama and Uyuni. The guides are all amazing. We went on tours with Ramon, Edu, Mora, Kaique, Rodrigo and Moisés. They explain everything very well and are always concerned about us. On high altitude trips, they are concerned with checking whether we are well and how we are adapting. In fact, this was one of the fears I had and one of the reasons for signing with a reliable agency. They carry emergency equipment and always support us. Our altitude adaptation was also very well done with the gradual increase in heights up to Uyuni. In Uyuni, FlaviaBia organizes all the details, hotel with spa in Salar and dinner included, snacks on tours like in Atacama and the last hotel, which has a different infrastructure from the others (because it is in the middle of the desert at 4,600m altitude) also They looked after us very well, including a very delicious dinner. Everything is very well explained by them. Oh, and the guides help take incredible photos on the tours too! Anyway, I highly recommend FlaviaBia and I think it's really worth going with them. We are even thinking about going to Patagonia now :)

review_text: Being quite honest, the only nice thing was the service during the sale, very well carried out by the desk worker in the basement of the Costanera, who explained to me about every detail. After that, everything went wrong. Starting with the war in search of clothes at Rental, without the slightest organization and guidance. After that, the climb was excessively time-consuming (the only factor for which Turistik is not guilty) and, in the end, we arrived in a Farellones without electricity and therefore no lift (therefore no access to the restaurant and any covered area for small breaks), no food in all sales (which need energy for preparation), no water (which needs energy to be pumped), no ticketing system, and with a typical super crowd of the worst experiences one can imagine. Definitely, that day the park should have even opened. Worse, no Turistik employee was willing to give a satisfactory solution to the case, they just said they could do nothing, because it was not their fault. Practical result: a family, in the snow, with poorly chosen costumes, without the ability to buy food, without the ability to use the bathroom, without a roof to shelter and without access to attractions by super crowd. There was no fun, only suffering. The end was overwhelming: the guide, with a rehearsed excitement, asked us on the bus on the way back if the experience had been unforgettable. I'd rather be quiet. review_text: Three of us cycled around the vineyards with our guide. She knew her stuff and was informative and answered all our questions. Our guide cycled in front and another guide behind us and when we were on the road the van drove slowly behind us, so felt quite safe at all times. The wine tasting of Q wine was great, the vineyard owner Mario was very entertaining. Personally I liked that wine so much I'd go so far to say it was the best red I had in 8 weeks in South America. Afterwards we went to lunch in a great little restaurant and the food was plentiful with different brands of wine but still really good. The trip is quite expensive - but when I looked into doing a wine tour, I found them all to be very expensive. We were there in June 2011 and paid $120 each but have to say, it was a really enjoyable day out and I would recommend this tour.

review_text: I hesitated for a long time between W and O - I had to time for both. In the end option for O has been the best decision as I simply wanted some peace and quiet in the nature. Views vary every day - from the fields to forests to alpine terrains back to the lakes and forests. You do feel alone on the O part which is great and almost scary since there is no signal. But there are always people 10 min in front of you and behind. You get to admire the nature (that's why you came, right), glaciers and lakes, you see lots of wildlife. O is also hardcore. The John Gardner pass is no joke and I live in the Alps. The wind is so strong it bounces you off your feet (gigantic backpack doesn't help with the balance). Conditions are truly harsh and there can be a lot of mud!!!! I absolutely didn't expect that. Try making your way up in the forest after it's rained for 12 hours and you find yourself slipping in the mud holding to the branches for balance. Descent from the pass is even worse - it's super slippery, muddy and there are only few installations for safety. Retrospectively, I find it crazy. There was one person from the camp who was injured due to the slide and had to stop at Paine Grande (which was still 8+ hours walking from the pass). When you join the W, the contrast is striking - somehow there are handrails on the bridges, metal plates of wood trunks to prevent slipping etc - very much double standards! and, of course, massive crowds of people, even in crocs! Still overall, a fantastic experience. Good gear and attitude are necessary to enjoy it.

review_text: We booked the Valparaiso & Vina Del Mar day trip through our hotel. Price was good for a day trip $36.000peso. We got picked up at 8:15am and drop to the meeting point where we changed buses and more people joined. This tour was full with 48people in total. The normal drive was about an hour and half however there was roadworks and we had to detour so the trip took a bit longer to get to Valparaiso. There was a toilet stop midway. The scenery was nice on the way there, it was amazing leaving Santiago area going through a tunnel and coming out the other end of the tunnel in Valparaiso area and the weather was just so different. I loved Valparaiso, it’s very different to Santiago. Lots of murals/ graffiti on the buildings/ walls and very colorful houses. We first stopped at the top of the hill in Valparaiso and walked down as a group with our guide Paula giving us information about Valparaiso. Then we had lunch at a restaurant by the port that. We had a bit of time to look around after lunch before we got back on the bus and headed to Vina Del Mar. Vina Del Mar is a beachy area. We saw a castle and ship shaped restaurant along the way. We stopped at the clock made out of flowers and the beach for a short time. We then headed to this park which I didn’t hear the history about it. It was a short stop so you couldn’t walk far. Then it was on the way back to Santiago with a toilet stop and back to meeting point where you got on different buses to take you to your hotel or if you wanted they could drop you off at certain shopping centre. Overall I did enjoy the day, it was long but I loved Valparaiso. The vibe is different and just love the colorful houses. Our guide Paula gave great information all the way through. She spoke in both Spanish and English. Our driver Arimis was very friendly. Notes/ recommendations * As a big group it was hard to hear Paula when we were out walking and she was giving us information. There were lots of environmental noises too. The guides should wear some kind of microphone/ speaker on them?! *i wouldn’t recommend the restaurant they suggested. It’s about $16,000 pesos (you get 10% discount) the buffet wasn’t worth that price. It’s a small buffet area and they serve you the food. There’s not much options to choose from. The desserts didn’t look appetizing. Some dishes got cold easily like my fish (and I was one of the first ones to get the food). The beef was really salty. When you have 48 people dining there the food runs out quickly and they don’t seem to replenish I went for seconds and there wasn’t much left. There’s a lady that also stands outside the toilet and she shakes her pockets full of coins hinting tips when you come out. You can choose al la carte from this restaurant however it’s in Spanish so unless you know how to read Spanish you wouldn’t really know what you’re ordering. There’s no pictures on the menu. Now there are other cafes around but I’m not sure whether they have English menus * I don’t think the last stop at Vina Del Mar to the park was necessary as everyone was tired and most didn’t get off the bus. It was a short stop too so you couldn’t wonder in there for a long time. I would’ve liked to stop at a spot where I could’ve taken photos of the castle and the ship shaped restaurant. Overall I’d recommend doing this tour for something different. I really enjoyed Valparaiso. The vibe was great. Dear Zudi, we are very happy to read your comment. We appreciate that you have taken the time to share your experience with the rest of the travelers. Thank you for highlighting the work of our team and for commenting on how unfavorable the service at the restaurant recommended during the tour was. We will take into account each of its details to continue offering a quality sercvice to all our visitors. We wish you a happy return home!

review_text: We ended a cruise on December 24 in Valparaiso and had booked a tour through Perro based on reviews I'd read on TripAdvisor. Our guide was Pedro and our driver was Monica, who turned out to be the mother of the owner of Perro! We can't praise enough the quality of the service they provided us. They'd asked for photos of us before we arrived, so they could spot us. Sure enough, as we passed through the crowded and hectic cruise port, there was Pedro, waving a Perro sign at us! My wife and I are not great walkers at this stage in our lives and Pedro adapted by taking us on walks lasting no more than 20 minutes. Then Monica would show up with the car and take us to the next delightful site. Of all the ports we visited on our cruise (Ft Lauderdale through the Panama Canal and on to Valparaiso), Valparaiso was the most interesting, probably enhanced by the quality of the tour we received. I could live in Viña del Mar, a Miami Beach-like resort town. We had the best empanadas we've ever had in our lives for lunch. At the end of the tour, they drove us to our hotel in Santiago and arranged for another driver to take us to the airport the next morning, which was Christmas. Perro Tour is a great company to deal with. My highest recommendation. Thank you for you recommendation Ken! We are so happy to know that your experience with us was great and that Valparaíso was the port that interested you the most during your cruise. Both Pedro and Mónica have good memories of you! Thank you for choosing Perro Tour!

review_text: I’ve seen the Andes, I’ve been close to the Andes. I’ve never been in the Andes in this way before. The Andes have been the backdrop of my horizon for as long as I can remember. I lived the first 19 years of my life in Santiago and the majestic mountains we can see from anywhere have always been one of my favorite parts of living in this special place. But Ignacio knows no limits to how far you can make it, and he takes you far beyond what you would expect. There’s something indescribable about being at the foot of the valley, on virgin snow, thousands of miles above sea level, and see these massive mountains towering over you. It really puts life and it’s scale into perspective, and it’s sure to leave an impression on you for a good while. The trip was fun and secure, the food thoughtful and delicious (a genuine Chilean food experience!) and the hot springs truly magical. Ignacio is hilarious, kind, very knowledgeable and very clearly shows a deep love for The Andes and everything they have to offer. As a Chilean, this was an experience I will remember for the rest of my life. If you’re coming to Santiago and love Mountains, Hot Springs and a good time, do not hesitate to take this tour. I promise it will be an experience you will never forget 😉 Review of: Santiago: Cajón del Maipo, Hot Springs, Waterfall & Chilean BBQ

I had only heard about it from TripAdvisor, as it has opened recently so it was not featured in the travel guide. review_text: My friend and I joined the one way tour from San Pedro de Atacama to Uyuni. We are english speakers and were lucky enough to have Mighal, our driver, who was AMAZING - and tried his very best to speak to us in English, and we could also learn Spanish from him. Along the way we found it common that the drivers didnt speak any english so we really did get lucky! He was very very safe and at no point was i concerned about our safety. We did go unprepared, it was SO cold the first 2 days, on the first night we got additional sleeping bags though which was good - make sure you ask for that when you book. You do go to 5000m on the first day, and slept at 4300m - everyone from the tour got completely nailed and all had insomnia and bad headaches that night, so take altitude sickness tablets. Mighal was very accommodating and explained that we were dropping in altitude which was good! The food was pretty good considering we were in the desert. Mighal made our lunches for us everyday. Cannot recommend enough, and it does come down to the 4x4, the driver, the people, the accommodation *which was basic* and the food. Make sure you take at least 5l of water with you, and toilet paper - essential!

review_text: I did two tours with these guys. Humberstone was great and the lack of an English speaking guide was not a problem because the place speaks for itself and there is loads of information in English. The all day tour to Isluga etc was also good - great scenery, animal and bird life (and virtually no other tourists) but I expected more information on the geography, fauna, life of the indigenous people etc. Found myself asking questions all day, the replies to which were a bit ‘thin’. This wasn’t just an English translation problem, the guide also gave little information in Spanish. All in all I probably found out more from my Rough Guide than from the human guide. I would also have expected more information along the route about where we were going, timings, advance indication about the location of toilets etc. Tips: make sure you take really warm clothing and a waterproof jacket. It’s cold up there at 4,000 metres! Take some snacks - it’s a long time from the start of the tour (a 4.30am pick-up in my case) til the minimal breakfast appears.

review_text: Santiago might be a nice city, but NEVER, EVER go there on Sunday. End even worse: sunday afternoon. Honestly, I have been to various places including Latin America but such "I do not give a s.t" attitude is rarely to be found. We were just passing by with one afternoon/night in Santiago on a way to conference in Valparaiso. I did not have high expectations: just to go to the city centre, sit for a dinner in a nice restaurant and have a glass of wine or beer. Apparently, this is not possible in a 7-million metropolis on Sunday evening. The city is just closed - nothing works. There are no currency exchange kiosks operating, you cannot buy a metro pass with a card (cash only!). LTE internet does not work either, so forget about using uber as there is virtually no internet connection around. After 30 minutes of unsuccesful tries we have finally ordered an uber from hotel and arrived on Plaza de Armas. Place full of people, dancing, having fun... great. But... not a single bar/restaurant open! Not a single place to sit, apart of McDonalds, KFC and Burger King. We ended up in McDonalds and got back to hotel - spending 10 dollars to withdraw money from ATM as there was no other way to go back with metro (no wi-fi nor LTE in the city centre, so you cannot get uber, and with dollars/euro you cannot buy anything). Even in hotel (Best Western!) there was no bar open, the only drink avaliable was coca-cola/fanta from fridge. Summing up: you need to have chilean currency in advance (of course, every country trades worldwide famous chilean peso), you need to buy alcohol in advance (this is not Quatar nor Saudi Arabia for God's sake!) and bring your laptop with Netflix as this is the only enterteainment you can get in Santiago on sunday evening.

A colectivo is a yellow taxi that goes to a specific city and it will take on people until it's full and then go. We paid 1500clp per person and it's an hours drive - bargain! They leave from near the bus terminal. However, once in Casablanca which is a small village, we couldn't find anywhere to rent bikes, so the taxi driver offered to drive us from vineyard to vineyard for 10.000 clp per hour. As we were 3 ppl this didnt seem to bad - around 3 pounds per person per hour. He took us to one he recommended called Casas del bosque and it indeed turned out to be a great experience!! The tour was in English and the guide was very thorough with the entire tour and ready to answer any questions. He was fun and tried to engage everyone. The tasting itself was amazing, we all got seated by a big dinner table and tried 4 different wines - 2 white and 2 red. Everything about the wines were explained along with teaching us the right techniques of holding, smelling, drinking and opening a wine. The tour was 15.000clp. We ended up only visiting Casas del bosque as the tour was really good and almost 2hrs long.

review_text: I used Uncorked for 2 wine tours based on recommendations from a friend who lived in Chile for a time. All I can say was that it was an excellent decision and the experience from first inquiry through booking and the actual tour was top-notch! Jose Miguel (the email contact) was very responsive and answered questions thoroughly, while Ayelen (the guide) and Jessica (the driver) were a great team. Ayelen's knowledge of wine and its history in Chile was remarkable, while Jessica got us everywhere we needed to be quickly and safely. Highly recommend both Casablanca and Colchagua tours as a nice contrast of the "young", coastal experience with tasty whites and rose vs. the "experienced", established vineyards with reds aplenty. Clos Apalta was notable for the architecture and design (think Dr. Evil's lair), while Recova was as quaint a spot as you will find in the world and could've slept in the shady cushioned chair on the terrace during a warm day. Looking forward to my next trip to Chile and wine tour with Uncorked!

review_text: I've used metro & light rail systems all over the world and the Metro de Santiago is a quick way to get around the city, but not that simple for a first time user, especially if you don't speak Spanish. All the signs are in Spanish and most of the ticket sellers only spoke Spanish. If you are intending to use the Metro a lot, you can buy a rechargeable card (the card machines are bilingual), but if you only want to make 1 or 2 trips, you can also buy single trip tickets. The ticket counters are confusingly sign-posted as card recharge counters though, rather than ticket counters. The tickets are quite cheap and the trains are regular and fast. We used them outside of peak times, but they were always full of people and some were uncomfortably full. Overall a good way to get around, especially once you get the hang of buying tickets!

review_text: Professionally run, fun tours, great bilingual guides, and nice, new vans. Overall experience was comparable to, or better than, other tours I've been on provided at luxury all-inclusive resorts in Chile. We booked 2 tours, both were fantastic: Piedras Rojas - an all day tour that included Lagunas Altiplanicas and the Salar de Atacama. Geisers del Tatio - a half day tour that also included the Chaxa Salar. We had the same guide for both tours, Felipe, who was very professional, charming and had great energy. He was very knowledgeable about the geology, wildlife, plants and history of the area, and took care in sharing the information in an entertaining way which enriched our experience of the beautiful locations we visited. He planned things so we visited sites at less busy times, and he also took us to special spots off the beaten track. It was awesome to be able to enjoy the natural beauty in peace. His English was excellent - we had one tour with only English speakers and the other was bilingual where he took the time to explain everything in both English and Spanish. He was very attentive of everyone in the group, checking in with people several times a day making sure they felt well, were having a good time or checking if they had any questions. The groups were relatively small - 8 people on one tour and 10 on the other. We had two different drivers and both were excellent, especially Patricio, which is very important since you are driving through dirt roads and rough terrain a lot of the time. Guide and driver made a great team often working together to spot animals, interesting plants or other sites. The Mercedes vans seemed new and were very clean - they must be deep cleaned every day. Seat belts at every seat, good air conditioning, pleasant/fun music during long drives. All this is very important as you're driving long distances to each destination. As far as the tours themselves, our favorite was Piedras Rojas, where we also visited two Altiplanic Lagoons and the Salar. Each destination on this trip had dramatic and different scenery. We would go on short walks/hikes at every stop. We saw many different animals throughout the day. Vicuñas, fox, flamingos, ostrich and vizcacha (rabbit squirrels!) It was a lot of fun. The Geysers tour was fun too, though personally I found the main Geysers everyone visits to be the least impressive part. He took us to one Geyser off the beaten path that was incredible. The rest of the tour was beautiful, driving through spectacular terrain with expansive views, again lots of wildlife mainly vicuña and flamingos. My one criticism, and this is completely subjective, is that I didn't enjoy the stops at the local towns. I understand these are to provide cultural context and so you can see the local communities. But there is basically nothing remarkable about these towns. I think they know this and that's why the stops are short, like 20 mins. But I could have done without them altogether. A piece of advice is to bring lots of warm layers for both these tours! You won’t regret it. They are not kidding when they say it’s cold at higher altitudes. We thought we were prepared and brought layers - fleece, down jackets and wool hats. But wished we had brought thermal underwear, gloves and warmer socks. The temperature and weather changes dramatically at each location depending on altitude and time of day. Finally, we booked in advance via email and paid in cash once we arrived in San Pedro de Atacama for a 20% discount. Recommend booking in advance as popular tours were sold out.
