review_text: As an avid skier, Portillo has been on my bucket list for a long time. The hotel, the amenities, the staff and the food are all top notch. Especially the food and the dining room staff. Be prepared to be spoiled. And I'm not just talking about the 3 course lunch and dinners. I'm talking about Enrique in the boot storage, who always seemed to know when I would arrive and the very attentive ski check staff. This is the ultimate ski in and ski out resort. The only downside to Portillo is the limited terrain for beginner and intermediate skiers. There is very little. As a matter of fact, if you ski mainly blues and greens, you can cover the whole resort in a half of a day. Since most people stay at Portillo for a week, it might night be worth it, if you are not an expert skier. The other draw back is the location, right next to a major road between Argentina and Chile. I had the impression that this was a remote, quiet location. There semi trailer truck traffic is non stop. One of the lifts even carries you over the road and the traffic. The amenities of the hotel and the attention the guests receive is amazing. For myself, that overshadowed the limited terrain that we encountered.

review_text: Ian Farmer and the staff of Turismo Rio Exporadores guided our family of 3 adults on an unforgettable 2-day trip in late April to Laguna San Rafael. We had rented a car from Traeger out of Balmaceda airport. (see my rant about Traeger below). Bottom line, we didn't arrive into Puerto Tranquilo until after midnight, but Ian's staff waited for us! Early the following morning we set out, and following Ian's very detailed instructions, we drove to the end of the road where he met us, transferred to other side of the river by small boat (bridge under construction), then further down the road in Ian's van to the dock. We were provided waterproof/floatation coveralls and vests, then headed out in their big Zodiac boat. They had plenty of hot chocolate/tea/coffee and snacks for the ride through gorgeous scenery. The weather was very nice and wind/tide agreeable, so after we arrived to the Laguna and navigating through the icebergs, we were able to land near the campsite where we had a nice lunch. We then hiked up to the glacier overlook. The sound of the glacier cracking and watching chunks of ice calving into the water was amazing. After the hike back to camp, we enjoyed a satisfying hot dinner with wine and slept very well. After breakfast the following morning, we packed up and took the Zodiac up to near the face of the glacier - we were the only boat there and everyone sat in quiet awe for a long time with plenty of photo ops. Then we headed back up river, had lunch and were back at our vehicle in the late afternoon. We had just enough time to hike up to the Exploradores Glacier overlook on the way back to Puerto Tranquilo. I can't say enough about Ian and his super accomodating staff. Perhaps in part because he also provides guide services to glaciologists and biologists studying the glacier environs, Ian was a wealth of information which was wonderfully insightful and really added to the overall experience. Regarding Traeger: One of the tires of the vehicle provided to us at the airport was nearly flat. The Traeger representative took it somewhere to add air, but we were not comfortable driving on the Carreterra Austral for hours without the tire properly inspected, so we had no alternative but to drive up to Traeger's shop in Coyaique. They repaired the tire (which had a nail in it!) They offered no apologies, no coffee or even a drink of water for our inconvenience, much less a gas credit. When we left their shop, we asked Rolf at Traeger to call Ian to let him know about our delay, but he didn't. We had to drive several hours after dark. I can't imagine what would have happened if we had taken that vehicle (as originally provided by Traeger) all the way down to Puerto Tranquilo. On those road conditions, we would surely have had to change the tire, at night, and keep driving without a spare and possibly become stranded. Traeger apparently has little concern for the convenience, much less safety, of their customers. We had originally booked cruise with Skorpios, but thankfully they cancelled in time for us to make other arrangements. While the cruise would have been luxurious, all of us agreed that having the more intimate experience and additional time at Laguna San Rafael was absolutely the best possible scenario.

review_text: What an amazing house and it's inconceivable that all of the furnishings and decor are original and weren't destroyed in any of the conflicts in the city. Everything about it (except the exterior) is completely over-the-top. Everything about it is like the 'cottages' in Newport, Rhode Island. We got there for the 10am tour and were told to come back, so we went to the Museo Historico y Miliatar de Chile to pass the time until the tour and that was a wonderful place to see, so it all worked out. We had a private tour and the guide was excellent. She kept apologizing for her English, but it was fabulous and we kept complimenting her on her knowledge and delivery. What an interesting place to see.

review_text: In Torres del Paine National Park we take a nice walk to the Cuernos viewpoint, the closest possible location to fully admire the mountains. The sun has since removed a lot of clouds, but unfortunately the highest mountain peaks are still hidden behind some mist. Too bad, but the visibility today is anyway better than yesterday. At the beginning of the hike we get a nice view of the Salto Grande waterfall, which plunges into the depths with enormous force. The splashing water creates a picturesque rainbow in the sunlight. Beautiful! Furthermore, today there is also a lot of wind and at some points of the walk we are almost literally blown away. At times it is quite a task to keep going and to get ahead. Always nice such a fight against the natural elements. During the walk we have an almost continuous view of the three horns of the Paine mountain massif and we also pass several times beautiful turquoise colored lakes. The sun makes it a real spectacle. We also come across a group of guanacos that are less shy this time and, unlike previous occasions, are willing to pose for the photo. Cool!

review_text: More than a great museum, this place it's a reminder of an era that left its mark on Chile. You could be there all day because how extensive it is and all the different media they use to get you closer to the events. If you liked the city, the country and the chilean people, visit the museum for a better understanding on who they are and how they managed to overcome adversity. ProTip: The museum is right on top of Quinta Normal subway station, so don't worry on getting lost. I also reccomend the multimedia room at the top floor if you like to see various documentaries.

review_text: My boyfriend and I were visiting Santiago for 3 days and looking to book a day tour to visit the Casablanca Valley to visit the wineries. We trusted the positive reviews on TripAdvisor and went with Love It Santiago. It was the best decision we could have made! We had a great time and would highly recommend them! A few things to note: - The booking process was super easy through their website. They responded promptly, and Anneliese (who was our guide) immediately engaged with us to plan our tour. - She designed the tour based on our likes/dislikes. We’ve been on a lot of wine tours before, so we didn’t want to do the educational at each place, instead we wanted to focus on tastings and enjoying the beautiful scenery and weather. Anneliese planned a tour accordingly. - Anneliese was very professional and friendly. It was a pleasure to spend the day with her. It was like spending the day with a friend. She’s very knowledgeable about history, politics and culture in general. Her english is perfect. - She let us nap in silence during the car ride home from the vineyards :) Highlights: - Indomita winery. They have big couches outside on a terrace that overlooks the entire valley and this is where you sit for the wine tastings. The wines were excellent and we had a delicious cheese and meat plate that was paired with the wines as well. It was wonderful to just sit, relax and take in the view here! - Emiliana winery. This is the one winery our guide recommended that we take the tour of. She said it was unique because it’s an organic winery and they teach you about the unique processes they use. She was totally right and we really loved it! This winery was our favorite because the property is beautiful, they have many animals roaming around (alpacas, guinea fowl, chickens) and the wines are excellent. Overall, we had a wonderful time, Anneliese was a great guide and it was well worth the price!

review_text: The whole experience is amazing and majestic. The whole tour is inside Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park. It departs at 08.00 with a bus trip, which is accompanied by the voice of Guillermo, a didactic and humorous guide, who takes the time to explain not only the history of the places visited, but also the people who compose it. First you will travel to the Petrohué Saltos, where you have to pay a $2,600 pesos ticket for Chileans. There are approximately 30 minutes to admire the jumps, take pictures, visit the souvenir shops on site, and taste the delicious kuchens in the cafeteria. After this the bus leaves on its way to a port, to take a catamaran on the way to Villa Peulla, which will travel for about two hours along Lake All Saints. Deorbitant passages, green mountains embrace the path of the emerald-colored lake, one can go outside and enjoy the caresses of the wind while filling the lungs with air so pure that it is nowhere else to be found. The catamaran features comfortable seating, clean bathrooms and a cafeteria that, while relatively expensive, has a great range of food, drinks, and drinks. During the tour there is no internet signal, so it is advisable to take a book, or download a podcast to listen while admiring the landscapes. Upon arriving at Villa Peulla, one is struck by the unusual landscape. Large green hills surrounded by the emerald lake, many wetlands, animals and, if you are lucky with the weather, a beautiful sky. Either walking or on buses that are there you arrive at Hotel Natura, where you will find the only negative point of the tour, lunch, which is not included, costs $24,000 pesos (without drinks) for a meal that is not up to the rest of the place. Apart from that, the landscapes are simply indescribably beautiful. In Peulla you can choose to walk, or pay for a 4x4 tour, horseback riding, trekking, or various adventure tourism tours (all at an extra cost on admission). Personally I opted for the 4x4, which took us to the heart of the island, walking its paths, crossing lakes, to leave us on a small barge that takes us to navigate an inner lake, where when they reach the center, they turn off the engine of the boat to connect with the serenity of nature. It is approximately 4 and a half hours that one has to enjoy Peulla, at the end, the same catamaran and bus will take care of leaving you at the starting point of the morning, at approximately 19.00 hours. One can’t wait to spend more time in Peulla or Vicente Rozales Park, but the tour is an excellent introduction for those who want to get into Chilean Patagonia. Review of: Puerto Varas: Full Day - Peulla navigation

review_text: Easter island-If fit definitely choose the 5 day hiking trip. we had a knowledgeable Polynesian guide, who slowly revealed the history. On arrival we went on a half day hike, starting in a forest but on rounding the hill top a beautiful volcano crater was revealed, along with the story of bird man. The hike along the north coast was amazing as the guide pointed out ancient artefacts revealing the rise and fall of the population. I should point out on most the walks we were completely alone with our guide with no other tourists around, I think that being taken on the roads in a bus would not give the same experience at all. Two tips-we stayed at the Tiare Pacific, a very nice small, hotel near the airport, but as it did not cook supper there was a long walk to find the best restaurants which are by the harbour. We had been offered an upgrade but there was a big price difference, if I had realised the geography I would have considered it to get nearer the restaurants. We also declined the polynesian supper/dancing night as supper was not served until 9pm and we were hungry! Ask for a super at Tahaa sunset instead-fantastic. Attacama-6 day hike--Another amazing experience, our guide Marianna and driver Daniel, took us to the right places at the right times for lighting. Once again we were mainly walking on our own in fantastic variable scenery with our guide. The driver drove 120km on one occasion to pick us up the other end! The walks varied from a deserted rocky gorge, to a walk through wetlands, pampas grass and deserted villages, opening in the Rio grande valley. We also experienced a scramble down a gorge with huge cacti and our own private geyser walk as the sun rose over the andes. Lake District--Another WOW-based in 3 centres we admired the lakes and volcanoes staying at an ecolodge and ending in a beautiful hotel overlooking the lake in Puerto varas. We were lucky to do a walk in the latter by the side of Osorno volcano, once again our driver dropped us at the top and picked us up at the bottom, all others had to walk up a down. There were volcanoes all around and completely deserted areas with mountains all the way to the argentinian border.

review_text: This starts as a "free" walking tour of the main tourist sites in downtown Santiago. You get a choice of guides who speak English, Spanish or Portuguese. We followed an easy walking route with a group of 10 and guide Ana from Florianopolis in Brazil. She gave a great explanation about each place visited and allowed for the group to stroll or take photos as each of us desired. The highlight was the local markets on the northern side of the river with the last 2 stops at the Central Market and La Piojera bar where we all had a drink, Terremoto, and many of us ended up staying longer and then went for a local hot dog, called Italiano Completo. Ana was a delight to listen to and organised the group well, letting us sample empanandas and a tray of various local fruits at the market. A long walk, 3 - 3.5 hours but well worth it with plenty of stops including a free clean toilet break. We all had a great time and the group got on very well together as a result. Easily recommended to anyone prepared to walk around the city and learn some more of the history and interesting facts than you ordinarily get on some tours. The English- and Spanish-speaking guides appeared to be just as enjoyable as the Portuguese one. Although billed as a free tour, of course after such a a good time, it is good to leave a tip of some sort considering the time and dedication of the guide. However, this is completely voluntary. Glad you took our tour! and happy you enjoyed it!

She gave a great explanation about each place visited and allowed for the group to stroll or take photos as each of us desired. The highlight was the local markets on the northern side of the river with the last 2 stops at the Central Market and La Piojera bar where we all had a drink, Terremoto, and many of us ended up staying longer and then went for a local hot dog, called Italiano Completo. Ana was a delight to listen to and organised the group well, letting us sample empanandas and a tray of various local fruits at the market. A long walk, 3 - 3.5 hours but well worth it with plenty of stops including a free clean toilet break. We all had a great time and the group got on very well together as a result. Easily recommended to anyone prepared to walk around the city and learn some more of the history and interesting facts than you ordinarily get on some tours. The English- and Spanish-speaking guides appeared to be just as enjoyable as the Portuguese one. Although billed as a free tour, of course after such a a good time, it is good to leave a tip of some sort considering the time and dedication of the guide. However, this is completely voluntary. Glad you took our tour! and happy you enjoyed it!

review_text: The village and factory were build to subtract and treat salpeter, and is thus located near the place where the stone containing saltpeter was found, in the middle of the desert. Once the natural saltpeter industry collapsed, due to synthetic fertilisers, the town was deserted, as its only reason for existence stopped. Since then the town has slowly decayed, although more recently the decay has been stopped, and some parts are partially renovated. It is thus a mining town preserved, although the housing for the miners themselves have collapsed and disappeared. But the other housing, the hotel, theatre, grocery store where they had to pay with fichas, as they weren't paid in money, but fiches that could only be spent in the town stores owned by the mine company. Also the factory buildings largely remain. Very well worth a few hours strolling through, in the part near the entrance typical objects used in the town are on display, and there is a decent amount of information also in English.

review_text: Just visited he Mamalluca Observatory last September. We took a tour from our hotel in La Serena at a cost of $25.00/person and it was well worth it. A group of enthusiastic astronomers explain to you the history of the solar system, how planets and stars are formed and how we keep finding more and more galaxys. Then you go to the main telescope to take a quick look at some constellations. Then the goups go to their assign astronomer personal telescope and spend a good hour + seeing different stars all well explained. They answer all your questions and you will see the brightest, most beautiful nightsight of the sky of your life. The tours start at 10:00PM but you have like a 1 hour drive to the town of Vicuna and then a 20 minute drive to the oservatory. The road to it is just dirt so be prepared to have an exciting experience getting there. They only take tours and they charge you the same if you go to their office in Vicuna than if they pick you up at your hotel and drive you back, a good 2 hours in total. They pick up us at 7:30PM and were back at 1:00AM.

review_text: I took the 72 hours cruise from Puerto Montt to Puerto Natales. Was it overpriced? Compared to the hotels and restaurants and land transport in Southern Chile it probably was. But it was certainly not as overpriced as the Fantastico Sur refugios in Torres del Paine. The scenery was excellent. But the food was of college cafeteria quality. The tourist manager, Mauricio, was enthusiastic and friendly. He keeps you posted about the schedule - there was a morning briefing everyday about what you could expect to see and when the ship will pass them. There were also talks about the geography and wild life of the region. The ferry was old, but the crew worked very hard to keep things clean. I stayed in the "big dorm" (essentially the corridors), got a reasonably comfortable bed with curtains and a locker next to the bed. The price is different for the north bound and south bound voyages because the scenery is slightly different (depends on where the sailing goes at night) so do check the itinerary. If you have a binocular, bring it. We saw several whale sprays at a distance. And by the way, if 72 hours is too long for you or if Patagonia is too far, you can consider the 16-hour Inside Passage voyage offered by BC ferries in summer between Prince Rupert and Port Hardy. It is basically a lighter version, minus the glacier, of this Puerto Montt - Puerto Natales cruise. The scenery is very similar - the boat sails in narrow channels with mountains on both sides. And if you are not unlucky you can see a whale or two.

review_text: I assume most people read the terrible reviews first as I do on trip advisor, however that is not the only reason I have rated Navimag as such. After reading other reviews, I had low expectations of this ferry. I was pleasantly surprised in some areas and disappointed in others. This ferry ride is not a cruise, you should not expect it so. It does not stop or slow down to admire special scenery or wildlife. It only stops in Puerto Eden for a short time at 6am (from south to north); you don't get off. Percy is the onboard naturalist who delivers interesting lectures and joins you on deck pointing out sights and wildlife. The scenery is stunning and untouched, but bear in mind it rains 7000-10000mm a year, meaning there are few clear sunny days. Most of the wildlife we saw were sea birds; Albatros, Petrals, Terns, Ducks, etc. We saw some Peal dolphins. Percy said they often see Orca and other whales, however we were unlucky. Navimag, like most of south america, is hideously unorganised. I sent them at least 20 emails before the trip requesting tickets, etc. They answerred 2, unhelpfully, and ignored the rest. Upon checking in on the day of boarding, they had put us in a different cabin from what we had booked. It turned out ok with a 4 bunk cabin for 2 of us, plenty of room. They told us to be at the bus station in Puerto Natales before 20:30 to catch a bus and board the ferry. The bus was delayed and delayed, we eventually left at 23:00. After boarding and putting our packs in the cabin, they did a safety briefing starting at midnight. The cabins are pretty good, heaps of curtains, working heaters, lockers, and mostly comfortable bedding. The heaters in the rooms are the only ones that work on the ship. The common areas are warm enough purely from the heat humans generate, but you still need a jumper and hope no one leaves a door open. We tried turning on a heater in the dining room, it made a horrid sound and was obviously broken. Unfortunately heat is also lacking in the showers. I had 3 icy cold showers and 2 that could have been tepid. I don't know if it just felt warmer as I was getting colder under it. Most other reviews are truthful. There is no alcohol on board due to some drunk chilean truck drivers setting their mattresses on fire at 3am in July 2014. The food is edible, but not great, I recomend taking many snacks. Coffee is available for breakfast, and you can purchase it throughout the day at the pub. There are some playing cards and a few board games in the pub you can borrow. The toilets/showers do smell strongly of disinfectant mixed with urine. It seems the cooking staff don face masks and hair nets, more for annonymity than hygene. If like me, you don't mind living rough, have low expectaions, and don't mind the price, you will enjoy this ferry. My main disappointment was the cold showers, for $605USD per passenger, I would have expected better.

review_text: I went to visit the Damas island in a tour. The tours leaves from Punta Choros. The ride cost CLP$15000 around US$15-16 per person. Punta Choros is about 100 km north La Serena, the ride is around one and half hour. Need to go north using route 5 and then take a secondary road. The road are in good condition but the speed limit in the secondary road is 70km/h (40mph) because some foxes and other animals cross the road. When arriving to Punta Choros, drive to the end and find the pier. You can park inside the pier for around $3. Then you have to buy a ticket to go in the boat for $15. The boat has a guide that tells you all about the penguins and the island, but it’s in spanish. The complete ride takes about 1 and a half hours. Usually you are not allowed to step in the islands, just go around in the boat. There very limited quotas for visiting the island each day. So you need to arrive very early if you want to disembark in one of them. Also you need to pay an additional fee to national parks services of around $7. Anyway, the tour is very beautiful you can watch the sea wolfs and the penguins. If you are lucky also sometimes you can watch the whales.

review_text: El Puesto, based in Puerto Rio Tranquilo were the main people involved in our first ever trek over ice. The start point is a refuge located about an hour's drive (or a little more!) to the northwest of Puerto Rio Tranquilo. The staff at the refuge are lovely and will painstakingly explain how to fit on your crampons and protective gaiters! You then carry these to the edge of the ice, as well as your box lunch and clothing layers. They even provide a small backpack if you don't have one yourself! The major issue with this glacier is that you have about 90 minutes of trekking over rocky moraine in order to reach the ice. This is physically satisfying but not very productive when compared to the Viedma or Perito Moreno glacier which have an access time of maybe 30 minutes or even less. The whole point is to do glacier walking with crampons, surely! We did about 3 hours on the ice and were brought to really great features like ice caves, arches and rivers by the very informative guides. The Exploradores is not the whitest or bluest ice in view of the lateral and central moraine burden. It is pretty flat, however, and you get to covering a good deal of ice territory! At the end of the ice trekking, I'm afraid it's back to the the very rough scramble over rocky moraine to get back to the refuge - on pretty near the same itinerary as the outward leg. I found this boring. However, the enthusiasm of the guide makes us rate this as 4-star plus in terms of satisfaction. Well done El Puesto! We are just under 70 years old and were up for this trek. I would caution that you do need a decent level of fitness and robustness for the trek. Solid walking shoes are an advantage and back-up clothing layers essential to stabilise the temperature variations conjured up by sunshine and a cutting wind! Highly recommended.

review_text: We signed up online (super easy), and they emailed us right away with instructions. We were outside of their pick-up zone, so we walked about 15 minutes from our apartment to the city center. They showed up right on time with a nice big van. We drove a few hours out into the wilderness. They took us out to a very nice Chilean style breakfast, which FYI is not an American style breakfast, so if you're the type that eats eggs and bacon in the morning, do that before they pick you up. Javier was our guide and he is the absolute cutest nicest guy ever, and he knows a lot about nature, being a guide, wilderness survival, all kinds of stuff. I really enjoyed him. It's important to note that the hike is NOT a joke. It is a real life out-in-the-wild hike. It took a long time, and it was hard. Don't come if you've never hiked in your life. DO come if you want to see a beautiful, wild, epic mountain range. It was beyond worth it. If you're as white as me, put sunblock everywhere haha. The elements are intense up there. The glacier was just dumbfoundingly beautiful. Then afterwards, we went to some rejuvenating hot springs. Everyone had gotten pretty close by this point, so we all went in together and had a great time. It was the nicest feeling to be in those natural hot springs, with that lovely view, and it was well-earned after that hike. In the end, they (Javier and the driver) stopped in a meadow and made us the most lovely picnic. We feasted and drank wine and laughed and hugged and it was pretty much my favorite thing I did in Chile. I highly recommend it.

review_text: When you travel it is important to be flexible because things will go wrong. This is especially hard to accept when you are caught up in the moment and emotions running high with thoughts like "I've spent so much money", "I'm only here for 2 days" etc. However, when it does happen on a trip of a lifetime you just have to roll with it and that is exactly what we did and had a fantastic time. We had a 4 days customized trip planned out for us by Matias and Tomas from Andes Explora. They were fantastic to work with and actually called me in the US to review our plans and provided recommendation. Unfortunately, on Day 3 we had a several hiccups that happened that prevented us from hiking up to the hanging Glacier In El Morado. This was disappointing as the weather was perfect and our time was limited but Andes Explora team did everything they could to make it up to us and made our trip memorable. We ended up hiking up to the glacier on day 4 and while the weather was dreadful we had the best time and made it to the the glacier in the middle of a snow storm! One thing I would highly recommend if you are planning to hike up to the glacier, start the trip early. For some reason Andes Explora starts the trip between 12noon and 1pm. We would rather have started the hike between 10am-11am and be back in Santiago by 5pm vs. 8pm. Thank you Tomas, Matias and Daniel for taking such good care of us! Thanks for your review Alicia. We glad you had a fantastic and memorable time with our company. Sometimes outdoor trips are very challenging with bad weather so I appreciate your positive attitude and adventure spirit. All of our full day trips starts around 7:30 to 9:00 AM (from Santiago or Puerto Varas) depending on the pick up address. You were in a tailor made trip out of the city in san Jose de Maipo town. We picked up the first group around 8 AM as usual and yours of course later because your address was on the run to our main destination far from the first pick up address. Keep that adventure spirit alive, and hope to see you again in new trips in the Chilean Andes. Matías and Tomas

review_text: This medium/difficult hiking trail is about 14 miles total out (7) and back (7) and skirts the east side of the extinct Mt. Osorno volcano. Plus, if you want more hiking and have the time, there is an additional 3-4 mile loop you can take that splits off from from the main trail. There are three milestones along the trail, including a mirador (vista point) at the second one. On this visit we hiked about 8 miles, reaching two milestones. We walked across two very wide lava channels and had panoramic views of Lago Todos los Santos and Mt. Osorno volcano, as well as a number of more-distant mountains, etc. We never reached the end of the trail, as the heat of the day and the steeper parts of the trail took their toll, so bring plenty of water. Note that this trail is on mostly sand and volcanic ash surfaces, which is both dusty and much like walking through very soft dry sand on a beach. The park didn't charge admission when we visited. There is a free parking lot (slightly past a paid lot where there are vendors trying to get you to participate in their kayaking or boating activities) that is closer to the trail entrance. There is a black-sand beach near the parking lot if you want a swim or kayak break with your hike. Note that the road is gravel and rather slow going from just past the Petrohue falls all the way to its end at Lago Todos los Santos.

review_text: My plan was to take a trip to Miapo and the lagoon but changed my mind at the last min. How can I say no to a hike in the Chilean Andes? The terrain is rocky and a moderate slope. I would not recommend this for a first time hiker but if you have done a few hikes you should be good for this one. It is only 5k and the guide (Gonzalo) breaks it into very manageable chunks. Gonzalo is very knowledgable about the area and will even break out his fauna book to answer any questions. It is also sweet that he takes photos and sends them to you free of charge. I disliked that we were next to a plaster mine and a hydroelectric plant, so I didn't feel as much like wilderness as I would have liked. That is not the companies fault. While I love being picked up from my hotel, traipsing Santiago with heavy traffic for 2 hours to pick up everyone got a bit irritating. It would be nice if an additional vehicle was used and a central meet up planned. That hour could be used better (lagoon?). My friend,How are you? review_text: At 5620 metres (higher than Everest base camp which is 5360 meters) this is one of the highest mountains in the world that inexperienced folks can ‘climb’ . Having read a bit about it we thought we should give it a go as it would likely be the highest any of us would ever get as we are not climbers and rarely visit counties with such high mountains. According to google maps it was a simple 36km drive from San Pedro De Atacama on the route 27 followed by an 11km drive on a dirt road to get to the spot where you start the climb, near a set of observatories. We had a decent 4wd vehicle with low range gearing and had warm clothing (ski jacket, gloves) and plenty of water and snacks as per advice we had read so were feeling confident. The first challenge was to find the turnoff onto the dirt road to the right off the route 27; it’s not marked AT ALL so you really have to watch out for it by checking your odometer and going slowly - you can see the road snaking up the mountain so this is a clue. Once we got onto it it seemed pretty easy apart from some initial soft sand and rocks but a after a few km gets quite gnarly - very steep with deep ruts and nasty sharp rocks just waiting to slash a tire; not the place to try to change a wheel!,used low range 2nd or 3rd gear much of the way. I had some 4wd experience so knew what I was doing but this is not a place for first time 4wdrivers . Next challenge is to find the spot where to park , it’s not marked and we drove past and had to back track after realizing we had gone too far. The parking spot is just beyond the observatory but we would not have seen it were it not for another car leaving. Then we were the only ones there. You can see the summit to the left of a valley which has a number of trails up it to the summit. You start at 5200 meters . We checked each other for signs of altitude sickness and made sure we were hydrated and set off. It’s really tiring and easy to get out of breath even though it’s not too steep and not too uneven at first. Got into a rhythm of walking 20 -30 steps and then stopping to catch breath. Even at this pace the total distance to the top of 2km took only 2.5 hours. Gets very loose halfway up and you have to keep an eye on direction (keep to the left when in doubt) else you can end up climbing the wrong peak ! The view from the top was worth the exhaustion and dull headache from altitude, magnificent! Windy and cold at the top so did not linger for too long. We were the only people on the entire mountain! The descent was much quicker, less than 1 hour but you need to watch it on the loose shale. Our headaches started getting better as we got back to the car where we rested before starting the slow drive back down, once again you need low range gearing so you can ‘idle’ down using engine braking. All in all an experience well worth having including bagging a 5620 meter mountain!

review_text: The whole thing started good, they picked us up on time at hotel, then they transferred us to the parking lot of a mall to sort the people to the different tours they offer and board the bus. This is where it started going downhill. The people who reserved online were on the list, but only one person and not their families. They apologized for the mistake, assigned another guide, called a van and we had to wait some 45 minutes for it to arrive. I thought, ok no problem at least they got it covered. The drive to Valparaiso lasts maybe 2 hours, however we had to make a stop so the driver and guide could get breakfast. We stopped on an overpriced and very run down place, the only thing that we thought was typical handouts. After half an hour we continued our journey, once there the "guide" rushed in less than two hours through everything there was to see and just made some comments here and there like "look at this" and "look and that" and the few explanations he gave along the trip seemed very made up. Then we continued to Vina del Mar and got delivered to a restaurant where this company seems to always bring the tours, here we spend over 2,5 hours. We were hungry and ordered something, but if you are not eating anything you are pretty much stucked there for this time. At the end we rushed through Vina del Mar and got back in the hotel way too early. If we could do it again, we would get a cab or a bus to Valparaiso, do the free walking tour and then explore on our own, since it felt very rushed and that we missed out on some attractions. review_text: We were doing a drive from Puerto Varas to Petrohue and along the coast of Lago Llanquihue. It came time for lunch and we came upon Canopy Chile. The sign said that they had a restaurant so I went in to check out the menu. They said that they had only a fixed price meal and told me the options for each course. The price was quite reasonable and I relayed the food choices to my traveling companions. We decided that it sounded fine and were seated at a table by the fireplace, overlooking the lake. Our orders were taken quickly and we were served warm bread with several different spreads. Our wine by the glass was served in 187.5 ml bottles. (I believe it was around 2500 pesos.) I had a large salad with plenty of variety. My main course was a small strip steak, probably 6-7 oz. and a very large serving of potatoes. The steak was tender, flavorful and cooked medium rare as ordered. All-in-all a good, generous meal at a reasonable price.

review_text: We went here on a whim on our way to Cerro San Cristobal and were glad we did! It's on the side of the hill so there are lots of hilly paths and you can kind of get lost - in a fun way - but I wouldn't recommend this zoo to people with mobility issues. Also, there's a little bit of English on some of the signage, but don't expect much. They had a nice selection of animals, some big cats, a nice big Jurassic Parkish aviary with lots of peacocks, and a good number of reptiles, but for me the highlight was the red pandas! I had only ever seen photos and videos of these guys and they seemed too cute to be anything but mythical. But they exist and are just as cute in person! Even painfully cute when sleeping! Even cuter than my dog, and I'm not at all objective about my dog. So go check out the red pandas!

review_text: Hugely disappointed with the service for Atacama Connection. I came to book a trip to the Puritama springs with them based on a recommendation from Whipala (just down the road) as they did not have a tour on the requested date. I checked with the the evening before if they had availability, to which they said yes, and could give me an estimated group size. I was told I could come back the next day to confirm, which I did. I checked again if there was still availability and asked how big the group was. They said 6 people. Half an hour later when we met for departure, they told me there were not enough people so they arranged for me to go with a different tour agency. First off, AC did not have the courtesy to tell me that the timing was different either -so I met AC 15 min earlier, and got to the next agency shortly after.... and waited idly for half an hour ish... no one told me I was early. I was just asked to wait. Anyway, Group size was ok, but service left much to be desired. For one, the tour guide/driver only spoke Spanish (and I did not). And the transportation was very uncomfortable (very dusty and squeezey minivan - when the driver switched on the ac, everyone was either breathing through their shirts or trying to desperately close the vent because sand was coming out). What is worse is that I was paying a premium vs. what Whipala had quoted me (15,000 CLP vs Whipala 12,000 BEFORE 20% discount). In any case, I will leave the other agency’s name out of this since they’re not at fault. We still got there and back safely, and since this was the Puritama springs tour, there wasn’t that much requirement for an English-speaking tour guide. What I am upset about is how I was completely misled by AE. Whipala was upfront with me that they did not have a tour running the day, but could recommend me another agency or arrange for me with another agency (if I agreed to it). Atacama expeditions on the other hand blatantly misled me into believing they had a tour running on the day itself and quote me the current group size, when in actual fact, had zero participants. TLDR: misleading and expensive. I wouldn’t go back.

review_text: My husband and I had a great time with Caro, learning all about Chilean cuisine, making some ourselves and then getting to eat the results. The class starts with a tour through the public market, a place where I could have stayed all day looking at all the wonderful stalls. Caro knew where to get the best produce, meat and fish from. When you return to the kitchen, you dive into cooking right away. Our class split into 3 groups and each group made a key component to our final meal. Once all the cooking was complete - Caro taught us to make two different kinds of pisco sours, the traditional type and a delicious ginger version as well. Then it was time to feast!! Great Chilean wines were paired with the meal. We came away very happy and well feed. Plus we got a copy of all our recipes (plus some extras!) in our emails to try at home. Absolutely recommend!

review_text: Our tour and lunch at the Clos Apalta winery was great with both things turning out to be that little bit special. The winery produces only small volumes of wine unlike its big ‘brother’ - Lapastolle - which is a major commercial producer. The jewel in the crown is the Clos Apalta wine which is a blend of Carménère, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon which, based on our tasting, is undoubtedly a fine wine. It is expensive!, The winery itself is also something special being built over 6 floors, five of which are under ground, the whole of the production of the wine being done systematically across these floors. An amazing tour and as my wife said, it would make a great setting for a James Bond movie. We then had lunch at the winery’s restaurant - a 4 course meal with a flight of wine. We were served with an amuse bouche consisting of a mushroom and cheese empanada, a small mixed ceviche and a apple gazpacho with a rose wine to accompany it. Absolutely delicious! The starter was a golden crab pie served over vegetables and a glass of chardonnay. Again delicious! The main was Austral salmon in a goats cheese- basil crust served with a crusted beetroot side dish, this being served with a glass of merlot. It was mouth watering good. Then finally the dessert - a creme brulee a la Grand Marnier, this with an orange sauce, a berry sorbet and a hazelnut crumble with a glass of Lapostolle dessert wine. As with the rest of the meal, it was excellent. The best praise i can give for the meal is that it was probably the best lunch we have ever had!

What fantastic service! We had a very enjoyable (and thanks to our interpreter, a very informative) tour. We highly recommend this company - they went beyond the call of duty to make sure we had information provided in English, even after we had already paid and were committed to the Spanish only tour.

review_text: Estancias are working ranches, but I had no clue what to expect, and boy was I surprised! La Peninsula as they say was really a piece of heaven, with the best views, food, hospitality and no stone left unturned to make it a memorable day. We were picked up by Alejandro and Donald, the captain of the boat but who wore 10 caps or more, as he was also the sheep shearer, the person who carved our lamb, trains the sheep herding dogs and handles much more too! Did I mention Alejandro was the best guide and host ever! We started with the horse riding and I have never ridden before, but the simple instructions given by Alejandro, the super well trained white horses, and I got the best one Camy! She was a dream. All else was forgotten as we trotted along the Patagonian plains admiring the sheer magnitude and beauty of the unfolding landscapes. It was unbelievable and left me truly awestruck. Just when I thought nothing could beat this, we came back to an unimaginable Lamb meal, which had been cooking since 8 am on the traditional pit. I don’t need to tell you that was the best lamb I have ever eaten in my life, not just in Chile! The hosts did not make us feel like tourists but treated us like house guests forcing us to eat more and made sure the wine just kept flowing and kept refilling the wine glasses! We then encountered the sheep and we how the dogs are trained for sheep herding, which too was amazing! After that we were taken to the shed where the sheep go for their rearing and it was most interesting to learn all about it and how sheep rearing is now a dying profession, and thus sheep rearers are very hard to come by in today’s times. After the classic demo, and some tea and coffee, very sadly the day had to come to an end and we were transported back in the boat to Puerto Natales. I would strongly urge everybody who visitors to please make this trip to La Peninsula, it was a memorably day, which I am immensely grateful for! Nest time I would try to stay overnight for sure! Please do your self a favour and go! Kudos to the team of La Peninsula!

review_text: Elqui River Valley is nicknamed “Enchantment Valley” and after a visit yesterday that seems appropriate. It’s in the Coquimbo Region that forms the narrowest part of Chile where the Andes range runs closer to the South Pacific Ocean than anywhere else in the country. Having lived in the San Francisco Bay Area as well as the beautiful Napa and Willamette Valleys of California and Oregon and visited other spectacular wine-growing regions, the uniqueness of Elqui Valley surprised me. It truly has its own peaceful yet mystical and powerful presence. The vibrations make you want to stay, especially in the tiny town of Pisco Elqui. Many say “magic becomes reality” in the Valley not only because of the beauty, weather, and clear skies but also because it’s home to many “esoteric and extraterrestrial phenomena”. Its skies are the clearest in the southern hemisphere, which is why international organizations established astronomical observatories on the summits of Tololo and Pachón Hills. Considered a “power pole” the valley is associated with the UFO phenomena. The tour group visited a papaya plantation, ABA Pisquera, Puclaro Dam on the Elqui River, the city of Vicuña, and several small villages, including Paihuano, Montegrande, and Pisco Elqui. The valley’s climate is sunny almost 300 days a year making it a great location to recover from illness and stress. Our group of 15 was quiet and reserved. At lunch I sat with an Indian couple involved in the Chilean mining industry and an interesting, fun gay couple. Both couples were from Santiago. For those who don't know Pisco, it's a brandy produced in winemaking regions of Peru and Chile. Pisco production is an art and involves distilling grape wine into a high-proof spirit. The Chilean government regulates the process to ensure quality Pisco. Chileans consume most of the Pisco they produce. In addition to grapes and raisins, other crops in the Elqui Valley include papaya, mandarin, and avocado. Spanish settlers developed Pisco in the 16th century as an alternative to brandy imported from Spain. Pisco is popular and well-loved in Chile. Grapes cultivated in the Elqui Valley produce the best Pisco. Surrounded by vineyards and the Andes, the small village of Pisco Elqui is situated at about 4,300 ft. above sea level. It’s known for its craft Pisco distilleries. There is something very special about the village and it’s sought out by many. So far, the beautiful natural surroundings remain relatively unchanged by tourism. The main city in Elqui Valley is Vicuña, birthplace of Chilean poet Gabriela Mistral. Mistral was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1945 and the National Prize for Literature in 1951. Elqui Valley attractions include the Gabriela Mistral Museum, the Mamalluca Observatory, Cavas del Valle vineyard - considered the highest in Chile, and the Cerro Tololo Observatory. You must book observatory visits far in advance, so it was a disappointment not being able to view the sky through high-powered telescopes. I didn't know that Chile is the astronomy capital of the world and home to 42% of the world's astronomy infrastructure of telescopes. By 2018 it’s estimated to contain 70% of the global telescopic infrastructure. "One global scientific endeavor called the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) is a revolutionary instrument in its scientific concept, engineering design, and organization. It’s composed of 66 high-precision antennas working together at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths, with a possible extension in the future." It was a fascinating day!

review_text: This free museum is built above the train stop at Quinta Normal. Fabulous architecture with enclosing spaces, not vast galleries. I read only a small amount of Spanish, but it did not matter. There were translations on the key exhibits and the rest of the exhibits needed no explanation. The terror and fear screamed loudly and silently from the photos. This is a superb way to understand how easily an educated, sophisticated population can be cowed into subservience and forced to remain silent in the face of atrocities to their friends and families. The big question at the end of the visit, for me, was 'How, today, can a person live next to a neighbour who was part of the decades of inflicting terror and murder? How can a person deal with a family member who was part of inflicting the terror? How does one forgive those monsters still alive today?" And the museum clearly shows in the entrance exhibit that the long-lasting effects of a dicatorship and regimes of terror are found throughout the modern world, not just in Chile.

review_text: HORRIBLE. Long review as this was BAD in so many ways. When booking this tour, we were told by them that they are not like the other companies - no big buses with dozens and dozens of people, they want a very personal service, guide remains with group at all times, lots of time at each stop to take in the sights. This is the opposite of what happened. It was a large group of over 40 people in a large bus. The guide never spoke to us individually. The bus itself was incredibly uncomfortable. When the passenger in front of you reclines their seat, their head is literally under your nose. DISGUSTING. In order to avoid inhaling their hair and head, you have no choice to recline your seat back and do the same torture to the person behind you. Again, disgusting. There is zero leg room, to the point that you have to sit with your legs wide open with one knee on each side of the back of the passenger seat in front of you. You are then encroaching the space of the person next to you, who is also doing the same to the next person. And even then, it’s barely manageable and very very uncomfortable. The aisle between seats is only possible to walk when walking sideways. WORSE THAN THE SPACE ON AN ECONOMY FLIGHT. The seat itself is shaped in such a way that no matter what you do, your neck is strained. We both had neck pain that night and the next day. Additionally, we had been given the option of booking the tour with or without included lunch. We were told if we bring a lunch that there was a restaurant there for all to eat in. We opted for without and brought some food with us. When we got there, the guide dismissed us quickly by saying if you brought food, you have to eat outside and that we cannot eat with others in restaurant. Could we at least eat in the lobby/reception - no. We had to EAT OUTSIDE. IN THE COLD. IN THE STRONG WIND. AND IN THE RAIN. We were shocked. If we had been told that, we would have made sure to be more prepared by bringing a blanket or hats or warmers. DISRESPECTFUL. We have done previous tours that have been great. In this one, we were told the entrance fee ahead of time but upon arrival to ticket office, we all have to line up outside the ticket office of the Park and as well as the Cave. Keep in mind, many buses are coming in with tourists so you are waiting in long lines. In previous tours, the guide has always taken the entrance fee from the group upon arrival (I know it sounds sketchy but the price is pre determined through booking office). He takes all the entrance fees, goes into ticket line and purchases the whole groups tickets. Done in barely 5 minutes. We lost 35-40 minutes with this tour by standing in long lines. The guide made bland announcements as we passed certain sights and upon reaching sites to disembark, he continually said to get off the bus, take your pictures and get back to the bus. At one point, we had to do a trek through a beautiful path with sights of a lagoon to get to a stunning waterfall and sights of the Torres, and get back to the bus - all within 20 minutes! We had no time to stop for the view of lagoon or Torres. We had to zoom quickly to waterfalls just in time to take a few pics and rush back. No time to step back and take in the beauty. It’s not just about taking a picture or talk about it. It’s about the experience of being there, seeing these sights with your own eyes. Nope. Get out and take pic, get back. We understand this country is spectacular and there are so many sights to see and time is important. But this was TERRIBLE. Had we been told we will have 3 minutes to see a mind blowing sight, we would have booked a private tour. Or we would have rented a car and did it ourselves. Also, we were told we would see the Grey Glacier. We barely saw it from the restaurant window. Mind you, we weren’t allowed in restaurant. So we saw it through a series of windows. And driving by it when we left through the dirty bus windows. We could have seen that on Google Images in better quality. We felt rushed and pressured. TERRIBLE. To be honest, we were so disappointed we told ourselves to try to take a few extra minutes here and there. We were so wanting to absorb this beautiful country and to continually be rushed felt so stressful. Surely not what we brought our energies here for! He did not accompany the group to all the sights. He was nowhere to be found except for two of the sights. But he was sure to be at the restaurant for lunch and was even late getting to the bus for that one. Why was he not accompanying his group to the sites? What if something happened? What if someone got hurt? How would a bunch of tourists be provided help? Well, we found out just that. It was a crazy windy day and especially at the waterfall, the winds were so incredibly strong that I actually was knocked off the boardwalk and fell below on the ground. But before I fell, I slammed my leg on the boardwalk and a large rock and then landed painfully. No help in sight. Where was the guide? Apparently he had come briefly to the sight and gone back to the bus already. No guide was there to provide assistance. Anything could have happened and someone would have to trek down to the bus to find him to bring him back up. Very UNSAFE. We walked back to bus, I walked very slowly as I didn’t put weight on my hurt leg, and when we got there, all we got was a disapproving look for being late. My leg is swollen and I awoke to large purple bruising. AN AWFUL EXPERIENCE - Terrible travel and food accommodations. Tour company lied about its standards, guide was disinterested and unavailable and therefore unsafe. Do not recommend! Hello Optimus_mtl, We felt really disapponited for your experience with us. Kind regards from Patagonia

review_text: I booked the tour for May 26/27 and made my flight and hotel arrangements only to participate in the tour. The day before the tour, I tried to reach the tour operator Cali tours to check on pick up location when i f found out that the tour was cancelled. After that message, I received many emails from TripAdvisor providing me with the tours confirmation number and asking me to select pick up location. This made me believe that the tour will take place. I did try to call Cali tours but never got through. The day before the tour they finally responded telling me I should communicate via WhatsApp - This is when we found out that the tour was cancelled.. I only wonder how the tour would have been when simple coordination is already problematic. review_text: We visited Fundo Los Nichos in November 2016, primarily because I read the reviews on Trip Advisor. I learned a ton on the tour about pisco production and Elqui Valley - information I didn´t know after having lived in Chile for over 6 years. So it was indeed very informative. You need to speak spanish quite well to get the most out of the tour however. review_text: As we drove from Puerto Bories with TDP in the far distance we spotted hundreds of Guanacos grazing by the side of the road. Guanacos are part of the South American camelids group with Llamas, Alpacas and Vicunas. Closer to the mountains we saw Condors circling high above looking for food. Our first stop was to take photos of the Salto Grande waterfall, we were fortunate with the weather and some amazing shots of the thundering falls. Next stop was a picnic at Pehoe Lake absolutely stunning mountain peaks only TDP could supply. Hope you will forgive the pun but the icing on the cake was when we reached Grays Lake and walked right up to floating Icebergs. There was a section of the lake where the water had receded which enabled us to walk out to an island which was surrounded by bergs. A once in a lifetime experience.

review_text: We departed the 32km tracking from Punta Árbol. The one way track to cape Froward took us 6 days, but there is people doing the return trip in the same number of days. We wanted to do it slowly to have the chance to stop for longer in some places and take breaks during the day. It's a hard tracking, you have to be fit. You'll walk throughout slippery rocks, mud, forest, and rocky beaches. You'll also have to climb steep hills using a rope or grabbing tree roots... Quite an adventure! All your efforts and leg cramps will be tremendously rewarded with amazing views of the Estrecho de Magallanes and the Cordillera de Darwin. This is a must in Punta Arenas. You don't need a tourist guide to do this trekking,the way is properly marked with colour flags. You only need food, a good tent and sleeping bag, and energy. From cape Froward we took a zodiac back to Punta Árbol with Kayak Agua Fresca tourist company.

review_text: We actually visited Torres Del Paine as part of a South American cruise a couple of years ago. The cruise line chartered a plane out of Punta Arenas to Puerto Natales and we did a bus tour through part of the park. We had to go back and this time in March 2016 we spent 4 nights at Tierra Patagonia and did several hikes during our stay. Spectacular! The weather is unpredictable, the scenery is expansive, the lakes and rivers are a most gorgeous shade of blues and greens. From virtually every vantage point the towers and horns are visible. Hiking is spectacular as well as taking a boat trip to the Grey Glacier. Our trip was civilized and we slept in the upmost comfort, but overnight camping is available and plentiful throughout the park. We saw lots of guanacos (3,500 are reported in the park), wild foxes, lots of birds including flamingos and different varieties of ducks. There had been puma sightings, but we did not see any. We did, however, see an armadillo! There is kayaking, horseback riding, hiking as activities. I think any time of the year is good, but consider early summer for the wild flowers and fall to see the beech trees changing color.

review_text: We did the tour to Viña del mar and Valparaiso from Santiago. Julio was unwell but we had his sons, Mattias who chauffeured us around, and Lucas as the main guide. We had a wonderful experience seeing the fish market, with Lucas translating as we spoke with the fishermen/women. Amazing array at the wet market with the busy-ness and hubbub associated with a true working market, smells, splashes, fish guts included! It was instructive to see the recycling of offal into the waiting mouths of sealions and gulls. Lunch was a whole lot of fun with Mattias talking and Lucas translating to us about meal traditions. Lots of laughs and animated discussion. Then the walk around Valparaiso…. Lucas and Mattias walked with us showing classical buildings from the golden age of this city to the colourful bohemian neighbourhoods that it is so well known for. In total, it was like a day out with favourite family. We enjoyed it so much we requested another day tour and saw a whole other side of Santiago. But, that is another story! Sorry we didn’t meet you Julio, but your boys really excelled. Review of: A full Private Tour of Valparaiso from Santiago Dear David, your heartfelt recount of your days with Matias and Lucas has filled our hearts with immense pride—thank you for seeing the soul of our family in every moment shared. 🌊🎨 While I deeply regret missing the chance to meet you personally, reading how my sons turned your tour into a “day out with favourite family” is the ultimate reward for this proud father and guide. Matias’s laughter-filled lunchtime stories and Lucas’s passion for Valparaiso’s bohemian heartbeat (fish guts, sea lions, and all!) embody exactly what we stand for: travel that feels less like a service and more like kinship. Your willingness to dive into the raw, vibrant energy of the market—and then trust us with another day in Santiago—speaks volumes about the connection you forged. Please know that while I was guiding another group, my heart was thrilled to hear how my boys stepped up. They’ve grown up in these streets, and seeing them share Chile’s soul with such warmth and expertise is a father’s greatest joy. Your words are a reminder that travel’s true magic lies in the people who make foreign places feel like home. Should your adventures ever circle back to Chile, I’d be honored to finally meet you—perhaps over a pisco sour and tales of Valparaiso’s golden age. Until then, thank you for becoming part of our family story.** 👨👦🚗💙

review_text: What an amazing experience. Santiago is a very "cyclist friendly" city and we were on the blue bike lanes for the majority of the tour. review_text: I had a very similar experience to Maria P just a day after her accident. My 9 year old daughter had an accident on a horse which luckily didn't amount to more than a twisted ankle. The Trancura agency is one of the eldest and with better reputation in the area. That is why I was amazed as how bad they handled not one, but two accidents in our horse excursion. First of all some logistic issues which put me off. The excursion was supposed to start at 11:00. We were the first group to leave that morning and that is why I cannot comprehend how come the horses were not ready by the time we arrived and they left us waiting in the stables. We set off around noon. It was obvious that our guides had no experience with horses. Moreover, the horses were afraid of them. I am an experienced rider so the incompetency of the guides did not bother me at this point. The scenery is breathtaking and that made up for the implacable sun of the hour of the day. We stopped by a stream so that the horses could drink. The area was full of horse flies (tábanos) which make horses nervous and they can be a problem. This is when the accident occurred. Another rider's horse got nervous and pushed my daughter's horse who started prancing. As my girl was falling, the guide made an important mistake; instead of trying to stop the horse he started to pull my daughter. Imagine the scene, the horse in one direction and the girl in another. That is when I jumped out of my horse to get her. In the mean time the other rider's horse went against a wired fence and the rider got her legs ripped by the wire. While I accept accidents happen, I cannot accept a bad management of the situation by horse guides. As Maria said, the guides did not have a radio or any way to contact the main base. We finally made it to the Termas, a good day spoilt. In there we had to wait for a further hour until we could be taken to the base in Pucón and from there to the hospital. An excursion that should have taken 3 hours took six! No food and no water in the meantime. We did not get our money back, not even a follow up on the injury. I filled a complaint and haven't heard from anyone. We later learned that the guides were Tourism Students who had been waiters and wanted to do something more daring (!). This time Trancura Agency not only showed a lack of management and security but lack of basic decency and a poor costumer service. I am still waiting for a response from the owner/manager regarding a course of action for future activities on horses.

review_text: So, they tell you that you have to be there at 6:00AM when it is cold and the steam from the geysers meets the frigid air and is lovely. That may be true, and it might be worth it to get up at 4:30, but the geysers themselves bubble away 24 hours a day. They don't shoot into the air more at sunrise than they do at a more reasonable hour. We arrived after noon and the geysers were certainly in action. There was steam, but probably not as much as earlier. The water was scalding. It was very interesting, but maybe not the same as the much publicized experience. The sign at the entrance said that the admission price was CLP10,000 for adults and CLP3,000 for seniors. That was the Spanish sign. In English, the CLP3,000 for seniors was covered over. It seems that foreign seniors are not the same as national ones. Oh well. At the time that we were there, the thermal pool was closed, but we didn't care. Overwall, it was well worth the drive out from San Pedro.

review_text: On recent tour of SA we had originally booked flights from Santiago to Buenos Aires but found ourselves with a spare day so looked into hiring a car for a road trip but found it wasn’t possible to take a hire car across the border. No trains either. We came across a review somewhere about a bus trip and got excited about the thought of travelling by land through the Andes as we thought the views would be even more spectacular than flying. We were not disappointed. This route was one of the high lights of our whole trip. 5 hours of spectacular, dramatic. Incredible views with not many other vehicles around. Sadly, as usual, the photos we took do not do it justice at all to the point where I am slightly reluctant to show anyone! The terrain changes significantly from the green of Santiago, stark baroness of the Andes, then it’s quite something to see green again at the other end. We travelled with Andesmar, the coach was very clean and seats were large and comfortable. You aren’t able to book more than a month in advance but you can reserve seats we had two at the top front which really paid off. At the border, everyone had to get off and go through a passport check, all the luggage is taken off and the the bus searched. A little tip, it was really cold in the lofty hanger type building and not possible to get back on the bus for a jumper. Also, no loo roll on the bus so take your own. We had tea/coffee, long life bun and sandwich offered during the trip so best to take your own if you prefer something else as no opportunity to buy anything en route. I would definitely recommend this trip and would do it again even though it’s sited as a dangerous road I am guessing that certain times of the year are more dangerous as maybe the roads are busier. P.s. Mendoza is a good place to stop, lots of pavement cafes/restaurants and craft beer bars, every street is tree lined and of course it’s the home of Malbec!

review_text: I read all 5 star reviews so I need to add on to their collection. I’m a female trekker and have done trekking for more than 25 years now all over the world. Comfort and support are most important to me these days hence I’ll pay top dollar to a good agency. I use Climbing sa for few of my S.America expedition. They have been very good in Bolivia, Argentina and for Ojos summit so I didn’t think twice about using them when I wanted to attempt Llullaillaco. I paid USD 18K for 2 of us (excluding hotels, air tickets just the trips in San Pedro Atacama). 3 days of half-day trip, 2 practice easy hike to Machuca and a river crossing of 10km, plus 3 volcano day hikes to prepare for Llullaillaco. It started well with Natalie and driver picking us up from airport with no hiccups and Natalie is such a pleasant lady. Chris was introduced to us as a guide on day 1 and we went with him to do day hikes and some river crossing. Though he’s not good at reading the trekking route but he was pleasant and an extremely good driver. He showed his skills during the expedition nagivating difficult rocks on the way to Llullaillaco. The main guide Guillermo Paez started well too. He looks very accomodating, paint us a picture of “we have the best support during Llullaillaco, said he has three guides for 2 of us, two brand new sleeping bags of -40 degrees. We trusted him. The day we depart to start sleeping in refuge camp of Llullaillaco, he showed us his “brand new” sleeping bags. 1 was -40degree (not new), the other is old with plaster on it and maximum -18 degree. I questioned where are the 2 porters? I’ve planned this trip for almost a year. I always ask for 2 porters + 2 guides for 2 pax. 2 porters to carry load up high camp so guides are free of loads and can support us easily should we have a fall. Paez said only 3 guides and 2 guides will act as porter. He also told us summit day we can never start earlier than 7:30am even though itinerary has been 4am all year round. So we know we have to trek up to high camp 6,100m else there’s no way we can make it to summit as he told us we’ve to turnaround latest by 2pm. The day we are supposed to depart to start trekking up high camp, he told us we depart at ~6:30am from refuge camp. We’ve to witness the excruciating packing of Paez and the team. Finally we left ~ 8:45am. By the time we eventually start from Llullaillaco 5,038m to trek to high camp, it was 10am. The wind starts picking up so strong from ~12pm, Paez and Chris were slow as they are carrying so many things due to no porters. They have to tell 3rd guide Gerard who also has ~25kg to stop at 5,800m. We were knackered at 5,800m and it was already 5pm. They came up ~ 6pm. This whole Llullaillaco was planned to fail. Paez even gave us a huge mattress to BLOW UP at high camp with no pump. When things go belly up, Paez was quick to keep telling me “S*** happens” and I must learn to except things. S*** happens means when we suffer diarrhea, we vomit, we broke an arm, we sprained an ankle, we had a fall etc. This is call poor planning, never done an expedition before, and no interest to bring your client to summit. review_text: Your experience in the Atacama and Bolivian Altiplano region will depend heavily on the agency you choose and the guides you find! Me, my wife and my 4-year-old son went on a trip now in early September with all the tours and transfers contracted with Sol Andino Expeditions and I can guarantee that the experience was great. The agency has met all deadlines and matched, in addition to being punctual on all tours. The prices were also fair and cheaper than many other agencies I met. The contacts with the agency have always been enlightening and helpful, personally and via WhatsApp. Because we are with our 4-year-old son, we need some special care and the agency advised us on this. We organized the tours in order to gradually raise the altitude, and we finished the trip with the expedition to Salar de Uyuni, in a private tour, also by indication of the agency, which is definitely a determining factor for the success of the trip. The tours in Atacama were great and amazing, with incredible landscapes. Do not fail to make the astronomical tour that is really amazing and unforgettable, something untold. On the other hand, in one of the highlights of the trip, the Sol Andino put us on a tour with the EcoAventura to Piedras Rojas, this was the only tour that left us a little disappointed, because, as I mentioned the importance above, the Guide left a little to wish for, but nothing that prevented the admiration for being in that place. But there is a reservation for the agency to pay more attention. Next, we end our trip with the expedition to Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia. We again highlighted that we were with our 4-year-old son, but despite all the fear that we were, as well as all the recommendations seen on the internet, the expedition was a success. We know incredible and grandiose places, monuments that look like another world, that show all the grandiosity of life. We had the agency hit on the private tour, which provided us with more freedom and comfort. We also had the great and very important participation of the driver/Guide Milton, which was fundamental to our incredible experience. Milton was cordial, patient, helpful and attentive to our needs, being an indispensable character in our journey. He learned to contextualize us about all the places we visited, in addition to solving our doubts. As a driver he was also excellent, knew all the roads, drove safely and did not put us in any risk situation, no matter how bad the roads were, in addition to leaving us safe all the time. Finally, I want to thank Sol Andino for all exchange and attention. We hope to return again in the near future, this time in the summer, to be able to meet another aspect of this so amazing region of our planet!

review_text: Very beautiful! Puritama Thermas – A warm oasis in the middle of the desert Imagine being in the middle of the world's driest desert... and suddenly finding a small canyon with a river of thermal waters running between green vegetation and reddish rocks. This is the landscape of the Puritama Thermas, one of the most amazing and pleasant places of Atacama. Located about 30 km from San Pedro de Atacama, at an altitude of almost 3,500 meters, the therms are formed by eight natural swimming pools with thermal waters ranging from 28oC to 31oC, rich in minerals such as calcium, magnesium and sodium — great for relaxing muscles, improving circulation and relieving pain in the body. The site is well structured: there are wooden decks that connect the pools, bathrooms and simple dressing rooms, as well as areas to rest between a bath and another. The surrounding landscape is breathtaking: dry mountains at the bottom, typical desert vegetation and the sound of the water running gently.

review_text: Reserva Nacional Tamango is a beautiful protected area right outside of the town of Cochrane, just a 3 km walk to the entrance. There are trails for day hikes, and also camping if you want to spend a night or two in the park. It is supposed to be one of the best places to observe huemel, although my girlfriend and I did not see any. When we went the trails did not quite match what was on the map, so make sure you are clear on your route. Also, the biting flies (tabanos) were really bad, and we actually left the park a day early to get away from the swarms. The flies are supposed to be worst in January and start to disappear in February. But the scenery is quite nice and it is worth the visit, especially since the entrance is just a short walk from the town of Cochrane. There are also options to take a boat ride around the lake.

review_text: From all the places I've been to in to Chile this was the one that stunned me the most. I've been in the area for almost 2 months so I've explore well the region with sometimes the company of some locals as Bladimir who hosted me in his house as a volunteer. I've visited the hotel thermas of Malalcahuello, went in the National Reserve which was my best treeking experience so far, I've started biking in the asphalt road at 0900AM took a vecinal dirt road up to the foot of volcano Lonquemay, up till some point I could go biking then at maybe 600 meters MSL I've left the bike and went on trekking and climbed in the alternative unused trail to go up to the top of the volcano, getting almost at the top I was surrounded by an ice cap and my shoes slippery on it plus the weather changing forced me to climb down as quick as I could, it was like 4 hours to get up there wthout a defined trail, then 3 more to climb down. Exercise caution with the Tabanos, big flying mosquitoes, their bite are painful and those are flying up to 6000 feet, and generally visitors are the only meal available.

review_text: This tour is worth your time and money! Hector, the tour guide and Alejandro were amazing. Hector‘s tour in both Spanish, and English was seamless as he switched from one language to the other. He was funny and informative, answering all of our questions. Hector has a broad knowledge of history and did a great job explaining the geography and weather as we drove through the beautiful countryside. During the drive out of Santiago, we were entertained with an informative description of the areas of Chile. It may sound strange to stop at 10 AM for wine tasting, but Hector explained to us that later in the day it gets very very hot. The wine was lovely and the scenery at the In Sutu Vineyard. Is as well. Hector explained to us how the grapes are grown and a lot of the history of Chilean wine grapes. We spent a nice amount of time at the winery and did not feel rushed. Alejandro is a masterful driver, taking us up at the 26 curves in the road that goes up the mountain. The driving is even more amazing when you realize there are no guard rails on those roads and curves. The scenery just gets better and better as you go up. The Inca lagoon leaves me speechless with its beauty and the magical colors of the water. Lunch at the hotel was very good and the view of the lagoon from the tables by the window made it very special. If you go in the summer, make sure you walk down to the lake and put your feet in the refreshing (cold!) water. This tour is worth every penny for a delight of a day. Review of: Inca Lagoon in Andes Mountain Range - Visit Local Vineyard with Tasting included

review_text: We really enjoyed exploring this fascinating old house. There are several rooms to see downstairs, plus an exhibition of photos of the mine workers. We asked if there was anything more to see upstairs and a friendly lady very kindly agreed to show us. There is a museum exhibit of shells collected by a local man then sold to Pinochet. There is also a series of suites used by the children of the family, completely in contrast to the mine workers who could not even afford razors to shave with. The lady was clearly very passionate about the house and very knowledgeable about its history, the mining and the vast social differences present at the time. It turned out the family moved away only a year after the house was built, selling it all including contents (even the food in the cupboards) for 100 pesos....just because they could afford to do so! It was a very interesting visit. Free entry too - just a box for donations if you want to contribute.
